x12.scripture: Jesus taught, 'Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God' (Matthew 5:9). In the Book of Mormon, Jesus warns about using His name for violence (3 Nephi 11:29-30). Doctrine and Covenants 121:41-42 teaches that influence should be by persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, and love, not by force or compulsion. The plain message in all scripture is that war and contention are not Christ's way, even when using religious words or symbols.
x12.background: Before the Crusades, the Middle Ages in Europe were a time of strong religious faith, but also of fear, superstition, and hardship. Most people lived as farmers or peasants, working land owned by kings and nobles. The Roman Catholic Church was at the center of daily life. In lands east of Europe, Muslims ruled Jerusalem and much of the surrounding region, where Christians, Jews, and Muslims all lived. Travel was slow, and few could read or write. Stories of Jerusalem’s holiness were powerful, but few Europeans had ever been there. It was also a world where violence over faith and land was common, and leaders often used religion to gather people for wars, especially as the power of local kings grew and life was uncertain.

x13.talk: Why do you think it matters that we can read the scriptures for ourselves?
x13.child: A man named John Wycliffe gave people in England the first Bible they could read in their own language. He wanted everyone, not just church leaders, to know what God says. His work helped many people learn about Jesus for themselves.
x13.learn: From Wycliffe’s story, we learn that seeking and sharing truth can bless many people, even if it is difficult or risky. We see how one person’s faith and work can prepare the way for others, making it possible for families today to read scriptures in their own language. It teaches us to treasure the scriptures and the chance to learn from them personally, and to help others do the same.
x13.matters: Wycliffe’s work matters because it started opening the doors so ordinary people could read the scriptures for themselves. For families of faith, it helped begin the journey toward personal scripture study and seeking answers directly from God. This translation set a pattern followed by later reformers, making it possible for people like Joseph Smith, centuries later, to read and ponder the Bible and receive inspiration. Wycliffe’s faith and courage still bless people today as we are encouraged to search the scriptures ourselves.

sources.name: British Library: John Wycliffe's Bible
Encyclopaedia Britannica: John Wycliffe
The Bible in English – National Trust

x13.evidence: Historians have strong evidence that Wycliffe and his followers translated and hand-copied the Bible in English by 1382. Several copies of the Wycliffe Bible still exist in libraries and museums today. Letters from church leaders at the time criticized Wycliffe’s work, showing it was recognized and controversial. Records from Oxford and accounts from his opponents confirm his leadership and teachings. While none of the original manuscripts survive, the earliest hand-copied Wycliffe Bibles are treasured artifacts and important proof of this brave effort.
x13.happened: In the late 1300s, John Wycliffe, an Oxford scholar in England, created the first complete translation of the Bible into English. Before this, the Bible was mostly available only in Latin, a language that regular people in England could not read. Wycliffe believed deeply that all people should have the chance to read and understand God’s word for themselves, not just hear it explained by priests. With the help of his friends and students, he translated the whole Bible from Latin into the everyday English spoken by the people. Wycliffe also taught that the Bible, not church leaders or the pope, was the highest authority for Christians. Because of these brave acts, Wycliffe faced strong opposition from church leaders, but many people loved what he was doing. His followers were called Lollards, and they traveled across England sharing the English Bible and teaching others to read it.
x13.scripture: The scriptures teach about the value of knowing God’s word personally. In James 1:5, which was key for Joseph Smith, it says, 'If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God.' Psalm 119:105 says, 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.' In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 31:20 urges us to 'feast upon the words of Christ.' The principle connecting all these is that personal study and searching the scriptures help bring light and truth into our lives, just as Wycliffe hoped.
x13.background: At the time of Wycliffe, England was a country shaped by the power of the church and kings. Most people went to church every week, but few could understand Latin, and most were poor villagers or farmers who couldn’t read. Education was rare, mostly found in monasteries or among the wealthy. The church controlled not only religion but much of daily life. Only priests and scholars had access to the Bible, and its teachings were explained to people from church pulpits. Paper was still expensive, and books were copied slowly by hand. This made the idea of translating the Bible into English both daring and, to some leaders, dangerous. It was a world hungering for hope and light during hard times of war, disease, and change.

x14.talk: Why is it important for everyone to be able to read the scriptures for themselves?
x14.child: A man named Martin Luther made a list of things he thought needed to change in the church and put it on the church door. He wanted everyone to learn from the Bible, not just church leaders. Because of this, many Christian churches began, and people could read the Bible in their own language.
x14.learn: We can learn the importance of standing up for what we believe is right, even when it is hard or unpopular. We also see how seeking truth—especially through careful study of God’s word—can bring light not only to ourselves, but to others as well. Luther’s story reminds us that everyone can help make changes that lead to more truth and goodness in the world, and that technology and learning can be gifts from God when used wisely.
x14.matters: Martin Luther’s act of courage helped start the Protestant Reformation, a completely new chapter in Christian history. This movement led to people reading and interpreting the Bible for themselves, in their own language, and opened the door for new Christian traditions and beliefs. For families of faith, Luther’s insistence on scripture and personal faith reminds us that God wants His children to seek truth and use their agency. It also shows how technology—like the printing press—can help spread light and knowledge, echoing our belief that tools can be used for Heavenly Father’s work.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica - Martin Luther
Lutheran World Federation - Martin Luther: A Brief Introduction
Metropolitan Museum of Art - Martin Luther and the Reformation

x14.evidence: Historians agree that Martin Luther’s stand actually happened and that his 95 Theses were posted in 1517, though some debate whether he nailed them to the church door or simply mailed them to church leaders. There is strong record from letters written by Luther and those around him, as well as from church officials who responded quickly. The effect of his actions is shown in the quick spread of Reformation ideas and the many new churches that formed. Surviving copies of Luther’s writings, printed early and widely, further confirm the event and its great impact. Modern scholars also point to Luther’s translation of the Bible as a turning point for both religion and the German language.
x14.happened: On October 31, 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther nailed a paper listing 95 complaints, called the 95 Theses, to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, Germany. This church door acted as a sort of community bulletin board. Luther’s list was mostly about his deep worry that the Church was allowing people to buy pieces of paper called indulgences, which were supposed to forgive sins. Luther believed only God could forgive sins, not money or even church leaders. His action caught the attention of many people, from common townsfolk to powerful rulers, and spread quickly because the printing press could make many copies. Luther’s questions and courage led him to argue that the Bible, not the church leaders, was the highest authority for Christians. He taught that people are saved by faith in Jesus and God’s grace, not by paying money or following special rituals. His bold stand led to a huge split in Western Christianity and the beginning of many new Christian churches outside the Catholic Church. After several years of debate, Luther was put on trial and excommunicated, or officially cast out, by church authorities in 1521. Even after this, he continued teaching, writing, and translating the Bible into German so everyday people could read God’s word for themselves.
x14.scripture: The principle that scripture is a foundation for faith can be found in both the Bible and the Book of Mormon. In 2 Timothy 3:16-17, Paul teaches that 'All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.' The Book of Mormon reminds us in 2 Nephi 29:6 that God speaks to all His children and values His word in every nation. While neither talks about Martin Luther, both support the idea that scripture is for everyone, and that personal study and revelation can bring us closer to God.
x14.background: Martin Luther lived in a time when almost everyone in western Europe belonged to the Catholic Church and depended on priests to explain the scriptures. Bibles were mostly written in Latin, which only a few could read, and most people, including rulers and merchants, accepted that the Pope was the leader of all Christians in the West. Daily life for most Europeans meant a cycle of work, church attendance, and community gatherings, often shaped by religious festivals and teachings. The church governed much of life and law, and differences in belief weren't usually allowed. At the same time, new ideas about learning, called the Renaissance, were spreading, and the printing press made it easier to share books and pamphlets quickly.

x15.talk: Why do you think it’s important to make your own choices about following Jesus?
x15.child: A long time ago, some people believed you should only be baptized when you choose it yourself. They were very brave and kept their faith, even when it was hard. Today, many people still follow what they taught.
x15.learn: We learn from the Anabaptists that seeking truth sometimes takes courage, and that God values our agency—the power to choose for ourselves. Their example teaches us the importance of following Jesus through our own choices, even when it’s hard or others disagree. It also reminds us to treat others with kindness and respect, even when their beliefs are different from ours.
x15.matters: This moment in 1525 is important because it was one of the first times in modern Christian history that people stood up for the idea of making religious choices based on personal faith. The Anabaptists’ belief that baptism should be a covenant choice is a teaching that blesses many Christians today, and it would be confirmed later in the Restoration. For families of faith, their story is a reminder that standing for what you believe—kindly and bravely—can help restore lost truths. It also reminds us that sometimes, it takes great courage to live your conscience, even when others might not understand or agree.

sources.name: Encyclopædia Britannica – Anabaptist
Mennonite Church USA – History of the Anabaptist Tradition
BBC – Religion: Anabaptists

x15.evidence: Historians have many records from Zurich’s city council, church leaders, and even letters by the Anabaptists themselves, showing exactly what happened. Felix Manz’s execution is especially well-documented because it was a public warning to others. Over time, churches connected to the Anabaptists, like the Mennonites and Amish, have kept careful records tracing their beginnings to these 1525 baptisms. Today, historians widely agree that adult baptism by personal choice really was revived by the Anabaptists, and that they faced severe persecution. Archaeological finds, such as meeting places and secret letters, add further evidence. While some details of secret meetings are hard to confirm, the main events are clear and well-recorded.
x15.happened: In 1525, in the city of Zurich, Switzerland, a small group of Christians gathered in secret to make an important choice. Two of them, Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz, believed that baptism should be given only to people old enough to choose it for themselves, not to babies. On a cold night, Grebel baptized George Blaurock, and then Blaurock baptized the others, including Manz, by pouring water over their heads. This was a big moment because the city church, along with the Roman Catholic and the growing Protestant churches, taught that babies should be baptized soon after birth. The group became known as Anabaptists, meaning “re-baptizers,” because authorities felt they were breaking old rules by baptizing adults who had already been baptized as infants. The Anabaptists wanted people to make a personal decision to follow Jesus, just as Jesus himself was baptized as an adult. Their teachings spread quickly across Europe, but brought harsh punishments. Both Catholic and Protestant leaders saw their beliefs as dangerous. Thousands of Anabaptists were arrested and many were killed, including Felix Manz, who was drowned in the river as a warning to others. Yet, the group endured, and became the ancestors of Mennonites, Amish, and Baptists.
x15.scripture: In the New Testament, Jesus was baptized by John when He was an adult, as described in Matthew 3:13-17. The Book of Mormon teaches about believing and being baptized, such as in Mosiah 18:10 and 3 Nephi 11:23-27. Doctrine and Covenants 20:37 explains that baptism is for those who can show faith, repentance, and willingness to keep God’s commandments. These scriptures confirm the principle that baptism is a covenant for those who can choose it and understand its meaning.
x15.background: The early 1500s in Europe were times of big changes. After years of everyone following the same church traditions, bold thinkers like Martin Luther and Ulrich Zwingli began to question old practices, hoping to restore Christianity to how it was in the beginning. Zurich was a busy city in Switzerland, where people worked as farmers, merchants, and craftsmen. Most people belonged to the city church and rarely questioned its teachings. The Anabaptists grew out of Bible study groups led by teachers like Grebel and Manz, who read that Jesus was baptized as an adult, not as a baby. They wanted to follow the Bible as closely as possible, even if it meant going against the laws of their city. Daily life at this time could be dangerous for anyone who stood out or challenged the authorities. People relied on family and neighbors, but trust could be difficult when big changes were happening.

x16.talk: Why do you think it's important for us to have the freedom to make our own choices?
x16.child: John Calvin was a man who wanted to help people understand God better. He moved to a city called Geneva and taught people about God's love and how to live good lives. His teachings helped many people and are still remembered today.
x16.learn: John Calvin's life teaches us about the power of faith and determination in the face of adversity. His efforts to reform Geneva show how one person's dedication can influence an entire community and beyond. It also reminds us of the importance of understanding different theological perspectives and how they align or contrast with our own beliefs, encouraging thoughtful reflection on doctrines like agency and predestination.
x16.matters: John Calvin's work in Geneva was pivotal in shaping Reformed theology, which emphasized God's sovereignty and predestination. His teachings laid the foundation for Presbyterianism, Congregationalism, and Puritanism, traditions that significantly influenced religious practices in Europe and later in New England. For families of faith, understanding Calvin's emphasis on God's sovereignty can deepen appreciation for divine authority. However, his doctrine of predestination, suggesting that God has predetermined who will be saved, contrasts with the restored gospel's teaching that agency is central to Heavenly Father's plan, highlighting the importance of personal choice in salvation.

sources.name: Calvin's Geneva
John Calvin
Republic of Geneva
Assessing the 'TULIP' of Calvinism

x16.evidence: Historical records confirm John Calvin's significant influence on Geneva and the broader Protestant Reformation. Documents from the period detail his implementation of the Ecclesiastical Ordinances and the establishment of the Consistory, which structured church governance and discipline. The founding of the Academy of Geneva in 1559 under Calvin's guidance further solidified the city's role as a center for Reformed theology. Additionally, the influx of Protestant refugees into Geneva during Calvin's tenure is well-documented, illustrating the city's reputation as a haven for those seeking religious freedom. These historical accounts provide a clear picture of Calvin's impact on Geneva and the development of Reformed traditions.
x16.happened: In the 1530s, John Calvin, a French theologian, fled his homeland due to religious persecution and eventually settled in Geneva, Switzerland. There, he collaborated with reformer William Farel to establish a new church order. In 1536, they presented their plans to Geneva's leaders, who were initially hesitant but eventually adopted their reforms. However, disagreements over church governance led to Calvin and Farel's expulsion in 1538. Calvin spent the next few years in Strasbourg, ministering to a French refugee congregation. In 1541, Geneva's authorities invited him back, and he returned to implement his vision for the church. He introduced the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, which structured the church into pastors, doctors, elders, and deacons, and established the Consistory, an ecclesiastical court overseeing moral and religious discipline. Calvin's leadership transformed Geneva into a center of Protestantism, attracting refugees and influencing Reformed theology across Europe.
x16.scripture: The Bible teaches that God desires all people to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:3-4). The Book of Mormon emphasizes the importance of agency, stating that men are free to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death (2 Nephi 2:27). The Doctrine and Covenants reiterates that individuals are agents unto themselves (D&C 58:28). These scriptures affirm that while God is sovereign, He grants His children the freedom to choose their paths, aligning with the restored gospel's teachings on agency.
x16.background: During the early 16th century, Europe was undergoing significant religious upheaval. The Protestant Reformation, initiated by figures like Martin Luther and Ulrich Zwingli, challenged the doctrines and practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Geneva, a city-state strategically located between France and the Holy Roman Empire, became a focal point for these reforms. Prior to Calvin's arrival, Geneva had declared itself a republic and embraced Protestantism, but it lacked a cohesive religious structure. Daily life was marked by political tensions and the struggle to establish a new religious identity. The influx of Protestant refugees seeking safety from persecution added to the city's dynamic and evolving character.

x17.talk: Why do you think it's important that people can read the scriptures in their own language?
x17.child: A king wanted to make his own choices about his family, so he started a new church in England called the Church of England. This meant people in England did not follow the Pope anymore. Over time, this helped people read the Bible for themselves.
x17.learn: We learn that sometimes big changes in religion, even those begun for complicated or not-so-spiritual reasons, can still lead to greater blessings, like more people having access to God's word. We also see how faith can grow and thrive even during times of disagreement and change. This encourages us to trust that the Lord can work through any situation and use it for good.
x17.matters: The founding of the Church of England matters because it reminds us that faith and church life are sometimes shaped by human choices, not just by spiritual reasons. It helped open the door for people in England to read the Bible in their own language, which would have lasting influence on families, worship, and the culture of faith for centuries. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of seeking truth by personal study and prayer, even as we honor the ways the Lord leads His people through imperfect leaders and changing times. The culture started here would one day help prepare people to welcome the coming Restoration of the gospel.

sources.name: BBC - The English Reformation
Britannica - Church of England
UK Parliament - Act of Supremacy

x17.evidence: Historians agree there is strong evidence for what happened in England during the reign of Henry VIII. Many official records remain, including acts of Parliament, letters from Henry and his court, and writings of Thomas Cranmer. Churches and cathedrals built before and after this split can still be visited today. Archaeology supports the changing practices within churches, such as the removal of statues and changes in decoration. Some traditions went on for years, showing that the change was gradual, not instant. The production of English Bibles and new prayer books are also well documented. Although details of private conversations may be lost, there is no doubt about the major events and their aftermath.
x17.happened: In 1534, something remarkable happened in England that changed the way millions of people worshipped. King Henry VIII was the ruler at the time, and he wanted to divorce his wife, Catherine of Aragon, because she had not given him a son. The Catholic Church, led by the Pope in Rome, would not allow the divorce. In response, Henry VIII decided to separate England’s church from the authority of the Pope. This break from Rome was made official when Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, a law that declared the king the supreme head of the Church of England. At first, the Church of England (sometimes called the Anglican Church) kept most Catholic teachings and traditions, but it was now led by the king and not by the Pope. Important leaders in this new church included King Henry himself and Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury. This change started the English Reformation, which continued to shape English religion for many years. Over time, the Church of England would become more Protestant in its beliefs and practices, paving the way for important changes like the creation of the King James Bible and the rise of groups such as the Puritans.
x17.scripture: Although the scriptures do not talk directly about the events of the English Reformation or the Church of England, they do counsel us about the importance of seeking truth and being guided by God, not just by the traditions of men. James 1:5 invites anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives to all liberally. Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 speaks of the Lord's true and living church. These verses remind us to turn to God for guidance and not be afraid of change when it leads us closer to Him.
x17.background: Before 1534, almost everyone in England belonged to the Roman Catholic Church. The church was a powerful part of life, present in every village and town. People attended Mass, honored saints' days, and followed traditions handed down for centuries. Kings and queens ruled with the support of the church, and the Pope in Rome was recognized as the highest religious leader in all of Western Europe. King Henry VIII was a strong king who loved pageantry and tradition, but he was also determined to have a son who could inherit his throne. His marriage to Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish princess, lasted many years, but no surviving male heir was born. Henry’s desire to end his marriage challenged the church’s teachings about marriage and authority. Thomas Cranmer, a thoughtful church leader, became an important figure in helping Henry shape England's new religious path. For ordinary people, life was based on farming, family, and faith, but changes started to filter down as kings and church leaders argued over law and loyalty.

x18.t: William Tyndale Martyred - Bible in English
x18.talk: Why do you think it's important to have the Bible in our own language?
x18.child: William Tyndale wanted everyone to read the Bible in their own language, so he translated it into English. Even though it was dangerous, he worked hard so that people could understand God's word. Because of him, we can read the Bible in English today.
x18.learn: William Tyndale's life teaches us the value of dedication to one's beliefs and the importance of making God's word accessible to all. His unwavering commitment to translating the Bible into English, despite the personal risks, reminds us of the sacrifices made to ensure that future generations could read and understand the scriptures in their own language. It encourages us to cherish and study the scriptures, recognizing them as a vital source of guidance and inspiration in our lives.
x18.matters: William Tyndale's translation of the New Testament was a pivotal moment in Christian history. By making the scriptures available in English, he empowered ordinary people to read and interpret God's word for themselves, fostering a personal connection to their faith. His work laid the foundation for subsequent English translations, including the King James Version, which has had a profound influence on English-speaking Christianity. For families of faith, Tyndale's dedication and sacrifice underscore the importance of scripture in daily life and the value of having access to God's word in one's own language.

sources.name: William Tyndale's Betrayal and Death
William Tyndale: The Apostle of England
William Tyndale - World History Encyclopedia
Tyndale Bible - Wikipedia

x18.evidence: Historical records, including John Foxe's "Book of Martyrs," provide detailed accounts of Tyndale's life, his translation efforts, and his martyrdom. These documents confirm that Tyndale was arrested in 1535, imprisoned in Vilvoorde Castle, and executed in early October 1536. His final words, "Lord, open the King of England's eyes," are well-documented and reflect his hope that the scriptures would become accessible to all English-speaking people. Additionally, the subsequent authorization of the Great Bible by King Henry VIII in 1537, which heavily relied on Tyndale's translation, serves as evidence of the lasting impact of his work.
x18.happened: In the early 16th century, William Tyndale, a devoted scholar and translator, undertook the monumental task of translating the New Testament from its original Greek into English. His goal was to make the scriptures accessible to common people, believing that everyone should have the opportunity to read and understand God's word in their native language. Tyndale's translation was groundbreaking, as it was the first English New Testament translated directly from Greek texts. However, his work was deemed heretical by the Catholic Church, which held that scripture should only be available in Latin. Facing persecution, Tyndale fled England and continued his translation efforts in Europe. In 1535, he was betrayed by an acquaintance named Henry Phillips and arrested in Antwerp. After enduring over a year in prison, Tyndale was tried for heresy and, in early October 1536, executed in Vilvoorde, Belgium. He was strangled and then burned at the stake. His final words were a fervent prayer: "Lord, open the King of England's eyes." Remarkably, within a year of his death, King Henry VIII authorized the Great Bible, an English translation largely based on Tyndale's work.
x18.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of sharing God's word and making it accessible to all. In 2 Timothy 3:16-17, it is written: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works." This passage highlights the significance of scripture in guiding believers toward righteousness and good works, aligning with Tyndale's mission to provide the Bible in a language that all could understand.
x18.background: During Tyndale's time, the Catholic Church maintained strict control over religious texts, insisting that the Bible be available only in Latin, a language understood by the educated elite and clergy. This policy effectively barred the majority of the population from direct access to the scriptures. The early 16th century was also a period of significant religious upheaval, marked by the Protestant Reformation, which challenged the authority of the Church and advocated for reforms, including the translation of the Bible into vernacular languages. Tyndale, influenced by these reformist ideas and driven by his belief in the importance of scripture accessibility, dedicated his life to translating the Bible into English, despite the considerable risks involved.

x19.talk: Why do you think it is important to ask God for help when we are trying to understand what is true?
x19.child: A long time ago, church leaders met to talk about what they believed and how to make their church better. They made many rules and sent helpers around the world to teach and help others. Even though they tried very hard, more help from God was still needed.
x19.learn: We can learn from the Council of Trent that it takes both humility and courage to look for truth. Sometimes, people try their best to fix problems with the tools they have, but something more may be needed. For Latter-day Saint families, this event shows how important it is to trust in ongoing revelation and be open to God’s plans, even when they are bigger than we first imagine. It also encourages us to be patient and respectful when others see things differently than we do.
x19.matters: The Council of Trent matters for families of faith because it shows how even good people in a powerful church can struggle to find the original teachings of Jesus Christ. The council’s decisions shaped Catholic belief for centuries, and its push for reform helped improve honesty and education among priests. For those who believe in modern revelation, this event helps us see that sometimes real change in God’s work needs not just good intentions, but new authority and direction from heaven. It reminds families that seeking after truth and goodness is a serious task, and that Heavenly Father can use all things—even great disagreements—to help His purposes unfold.

sources.name: Vatican - The Council of Trent
British Library - The Council of Trent
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Council of Trent

x19.evidence: Historians have many records from the Council of Trent. There are official minutes, letters, and reports written by people who attended, allowing us to know in detail what was said and decided. Archaeological remains in Trent, such as the churches where leaders met, still exist today. Art and books from the time show how seriously this council was taken by Catholic rulers and believers. Catholic doctrine and practices, shaped by Trent, continue today; for example, the form of the Mass and the work of Jesuit missionaries around the world. The evidence shows this event is firmly part of the historical record, well documented by both friends and critics of the Catholic Church.
x19.happened: The Council of Trent was a very important meeting held by leaders of the Catholic Church between 1545 and 1563 in the city of Trent, Italy. It was called in response to a big challenge within Christianity called the Protestant Reformation, which had begun just a few decades before. The Protestants, led by men like Martin Luther, were calling for changes in church teachings and practices. At Trent, Catholic bishops and theologians met to talk about what the church truly believed. They firmly decided which doctrines to keep, such as the importance of both faith and church traditions, and which ideas they would not accept from the Protestants, like the belief that faith alone was enough for salvation. The Council also worked to fix some very real problems inside the church, such as corruption and uneducated priests. They passed strict rules to improve discipline among church leaders and encouraged better teaching and care for local church members. This meeting led to new energy and dedication among Catholics across Europe and started what is called the "Counter-Reformation"—a great effort to spread Catholic beliefs and fix what was wrong inside the church, including the forming of the Jesuits, who became famous missionaries.
x19.scripture: The Council of Trent is not mentioned in scripture, but the principles discussed there touch on several scriptural themes. James 1:5 in the New Testament says, 'If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God,' which became important for Joseph Smith centuries later. The Book of Mormon also talks about plain and precious things being lost from the Bible (1 Nephi 13:26-29). Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 speaks of the 'only true and living church,' highlighting the belief among Latter-day Saints that a full restoration of Jesus Christ’s church would require more than institutional reform, but divine guidance and authority.
x19.background: Before the Council of Trent, Europe was experiencing huge changes. The printing press had spread new ideas quickly. Church leaders controlled much of the learning and politics, but there was rising concern about how some used their power. Many people could not read, farmed for a living, and trusted their local priest to teach them about God. When Martin Luther and others began asking hard questions and translating the Bible into everyday language, it shook people's trust in the church. The world was also full of discovery, with new lands being explored, and kings and princes often picked sides between Catholic and Protestant. It was a time of both confusion and hope, as people wanted to live true to what they believed God wanted.

x20.talk: How do you feel when you read or hear words from the Bible?
x20.child: A long time ago, some very smart people made a new Bible so families everywhere could read about Jesus. Joseph Smith read this Bible and found a verse that said he could pray for help. God answered his prayer because of what he read.
x20.learn: We can learn that when people work together carefully, led by sincere hearts and real skill, they can create something that blesses millions for generations. Heavenly Father wants His children to have His word in a way they can understand. The King James Bible helps us see how honest effort and respect for God’s words can prepare the way for even greater blessings, like the Restoration.
x20.matters: The King James Bible matters deeply for both the world and Christian families. It became the foundation for English-speaking Christians, shaping how millions learned about God and Jesus. Its words are still memorized, quoted, and loved across generations. For members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the King James Bible is a special link to the Restoration. Joseph Smith read from this Bible and found James 1:5, which led him to pray and receive the First Vision. The King James Bible is a reminder that God's word can bless many when it is made plain and available, helping both individuals and whole nations draw closer to Heavenly Father.

sources.name: British Library - King James Bible
Encyclopaedia Britannica - King James Version
Church History Topics: Bible Translations

x20.evidence: Historians have many reliable records about the creation of the King James Bible. Letters, meeting notes, and early copies show that King James called for the translation, selected scholars, and set guidelines. The names and backgrounds of the translators are well documented, with many being leading teachers from universities like Oxford and Cambridge. Several original 1611 printings survive in libraries today. There are also drafts and notes that show how carefully the translators worked to compare sources and choose the best words. The influence of this Bible on the English language has been studied and confirmed by experts in literature, history, and religion. There is no serious doubt among historians that the King James Bible was created as described in 1611.
x20.happened: In 1611, in London, England, a special group of 47 scholars came together to create a new translation of the Bible in English. This work was ordered by King James I of England, who wanted a Bible that everyone in his kingdom could read and trust. The team spent several years carefully studying old Greek and Hebrew manuscripts and earlier English translations. They divided into groups to work on sections, then reviewed every verse together to check accuracy, clarity, and reverence. The result was the King James Version (KJV) of the Bible. This new translation quickly spread across England and then to America and other English-speaking lands. For hundreds of years, it became the main Bible used by English-speaking Protestants. Its language, style, and phrases influenced authors, poets, and speakers, shaping English literature and culture. The KJV Bible was so widely respected that even today, many churches still use its words in worship, study, and family devotion.
x20.scripture: James 1:5, found in the King James Bible, reads: 'If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.' This scripture helped Joseph Smith know he could pray for answers, leading directly to the Restoration. Other scriptures like 2 Timothy 3:16 ('All scripture is given by inspiration of God') and 2 Nephi 29 in the Book of Mormon speak about the value and blessing of having God's word in our own language.
x20.background: Before the King James Bible was made, there were several English Bibles, but many had mistakes or were hard for regular people to get. Earlier translations like William Tyndale’s and the Geneva Bible were important, but often faced political or religious opposition. The world of 1611 was a place of great change: England was growing in learning, exploration, and trade, but there was still tension between different Christian groups. Most people worked hard as farmers, tradespeople, or servants, and only some could read. Monarchs had strong power, and religion shaped almost every part of life, from laws to school lessons. Having a trustworthy, beautiful English Bible was a hope for both rulers and ordinary families.

x21.talk: Why do you think the Puritans wanted everyone, even children, to read the Bible for themselves?
x21.child: The Pilgrims and Puritans sailed a long way to find a place where they could pray and read the Bible the way they believed was right. They worked together, helped each other, and taught their children about God. Their love of prayer and scripture helped families like Joseph Smith’s many years later.
x21.learn: We can learn much from how the Puritans set patterns of prayer, Bible reading, and community living that have lasted generations. Their courage to start over in a new land out of faith and their efforts to teach their children show how strong families and communities can grow from daily devotion to God and to each other. We remember that the way we live our faith today can prepare the way for blessings and changes in the future that we might not yet see.
x21.matters: This story matters because the ways the Puritans organized their faith, homes, and communities shaped religious life and freedom in America for centuries. For families who cherish faith, the Puritans’ habits of reading scripture, trusting in prayer, and making decisions together left a powerful example. Their focus on living close to God, family, and community is the spiritual soil where the Smith family, including young Joseph, would later grow. The Puritan tradition taught each person to seek God personally—something that helped prepare hearts for great spiritual events, including the coming of the Restoration.

sources.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums – The Pilgrims, English and American Identity
Britannica – Puritanism
U.S. National Park Service – The Mayflower Compact
Church of Jesus Christ – Facts and Statistics: United States History

x21.evidence: Historians have a wealth of evidence about the Puritans’ journey and settlements. We have original writings like William Bradford’s 'Of Plymouth Plantation,' church records, and town documents that describe how they lived, worshipped, and governed. Archaeologists have found artifacts from early Plymouth and other settlements, such as homes, tools, and meetinghouses. Recent research continues at sites like Plimoth Patuxet Museums, confirming how early New England life centered around faith and community. The records from this period are among the best preserved and most studied of any early American colony.
x21.happened: In 1620, a group known as the Separatist Pilgrims left England on a small ship called the Mayflower, hoping to find a place where they could worship God in their own way. After a difficult voyage across the Atlantic Ocean, they landed at Plymouth in what is now Massachusetts. They wrote the Mayflower Compact, an agreement to govern themselves as a community guided by faith and cooperation. These Pilgrims were soon joined by many more Puritans—people who wanted to further purify their Christian faith. Between 1620 and 1640, nearly 20,000 Puritans crossed the ocean during what historians call the Great Migration. They built towns where churches, called congregational churches, were the heart of daily life. Each church governed itself and deeply encouraged everyone to read the Bible, pray sincerely, and seek a personal relationship with God. Leaders like William Bradford, John Winthrop, and Cotton Mather helped guide these communities, teaching that prayer, worship, and study should fill daily living. The homes, schools, and towns shaped by these Puritans became a lasting center of Christian faith in New England.
x21.scripture: Several scriptures reflect Puritan values. In James 1:5, the Bible urges, 'If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God...'—a call to prayer that shaped the Puritan spirit, just as it did Joseph Smith. 2 Nephi 32:3 in the Book of Mormon tells us to 'feast upon the words of Christ,' pointing to the importance of studying scripture every day. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches, 'Seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom.' These passages match the Puritans’ deep commitment to prayer, Bible study, and teaching each other.
x21.background: Before these events, England was in a time of great religious change. The Church of England had split from the Roman Catholic Church, but many felt it still held onto old traditions. The Puritans were Christians who wanted to purify the church further, focusing on simple worship, Bible study, and heartfelt prayer. Daily life in England was hard for them, as they often faced punishment for their beliefs. Many worked as farmers, weavers, and tradespeople. In New England, life was challenging but full of purpose. Everyone worked together, lived simply, and gathered often to learn and pray. The seasons were harsh, and food was not always certain, but faith and community kept them going.

x22.talk: Why do you think people write down what they believe about God?
x22.child: A long time ago in England, a big group of church leaders wrote down what they believed about God and how to follow Him. Their words helped many people learn about their faith for hundreds of years. People in different churches sometimes believe different things, but many want to follow Jesus the best they can.
x22.learn: We can learn that faithful people have always tried to express and share their understanding of God. Even when those teachings differ from what we know today, their careful thinking and devotion remind us to be thoughtful about our own beliefs. It also teaches us that written statements of belief can help families and churches teach, protect, and remember their faith. As we learn about others' doctrines and reflect on our own, we grow in kindness, respect, and understanding.
x22.matters: The Westminster Confession matters greatly because it became a standard for Presbyterian doctrine—helping people agree on what they believe and how they live as followers of Jesus. For a family of faith, this event reminds us that Christians throughout history have sought answers, written out beliefs, and tried to teach one another clearly. It also shows that, while churches may differ on how they understand God and His ways, many have acted sincerely to know Him better. These differences can remind us to learn with humility, respecting various traditions while drawing closer to what we believe is true.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica - Westminster Confession
The National Archives - Westminster Assembly
Presbyterian Historical Society - Westminster Confession of Faith

x22.evidence: There is strong historical evidence for the Westminster Assembly and its work. The records of the Assembly, including minutes and original documents, are preserved and available for study by historians. The Confession and catechisms were published soon after the Assembly finished, and churches began using them immediately. Copies from the 1600s survive in libraries and archives today. Scholars confirm the role of these documents in shaping Presbyterian and Reformed churches, and their wording remains the basis for teaching in many denominations. While interpretations of the Confession's meaning can vary, its history is well documented and widely accepted.
x22.happened: Between 1646 and 1648 in Westminster, London, a group known as the Westminster Assembly gathered many ministers and some laymen—people who were not clergy, but members of the church—to write documents that would organize and explain the core beliefs of the Reformed, or Presbyterian, churches. This work happened during a difficult time in England, with civil war and questions about how churches should be organized and what exactly Christians should believe. The Assembly created the Westminster Confession of Faith and two catechisms (teaching guides in question-and-answer format). These writings pulled together ideas about God, Jesus Christ, salvation, scripture, and the church, marking them down so everyone could understand what the Reformed churches agreed on. These documents help members learn, discuss, and defend their beliefs, and they are still used almost 400 years later by Presbyterians and other Reformed Christians.
x22.scripture: The Westminster Confession says that God does not have a body, parts, or passions, a view drawn in part from John 4:24, which teaches that God is spirit. Latter-day Saint scripture adds more: in Joseph Smith’s First Vision (Joseph Smith—History 1:17), Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ appear as two distinct, embodied beings. Doctrine and Covenants 130:22 also says, 'The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man’s; the Son also.' These teachings help explain why beliefs about God’s nature are different in various Christian faiths. We see that scripture invites careful study, prayer, and openness to revelation.
x22.background: The people at the Westminster Assembly were living during a time of great change and uncertainty. England was struggling with a civil war between supporters of the King and Parliament, which included debates over how much power the Church and religious leaders should have. Everyday life was challenging: news spread slowly, books were rare, and most people learned about religion by listening to sermons or reading catechisms aloud in their homes. Many wanted the church to be closer to what they believed was described in the Bible, while others liked the old ways supported by the King. The Assembly was asked by Parliament to help solve these disputes and to guide the faith of the nation.

x23.talk: How can we make our faith more personal and heartfelt in our daily lives?
x23.child: Long ago, a man named Philipp wanted people to feel close to God, not just follow rules. He wrote a book to help them pray and read the Bible together.
x23.learn: From Pietism, we learn the importance of balancing correct beliefs with personal devotion and moral living. It teaches that faith is not just about understanding doctrines but also about experiencing a personal relationship with God and expressing that faith through love and good works. This approach can deepen our spiritual lives and positively impact our communities.
x23.matters: Pietism shifted the focus of Christianity from strict adherence to doctrine to a personal, heartfelt relationship with God. This emphasis on individual devotion and moral living prepared the way for later religious revivals, such as the First and Second Great Awakenings. For families of faith, Pietism serves as a reminder that true religion involves both understanding God's teachings and living them out daily. It encourages believers to seek a personal connection with God and to express their faith through love and good works.

sources.name: Pietism - Wikipedia
From the Archives: The Pia Desideria (Pious Desires) | Christian History Magazine
Pietism - New World Encyclopedia

x23.evidence: Historical records confirm that Philipp Jakob Spener published "Pia Desideria" in 1675, outlining his vision for church renewal. The book's proposals, such as small group Bible studies and active lay participation, were implemented in various communities, leading to the spread of Pietism. Count Zinzendorf later established the Moravian Brethren community, further promoting these ideas. The movement's influence is evident in the subsequent religious revivals and the emphasis on personal faith in Protestant Christianity.
x23.happened: In 1675, Philipp Jakob Spener, a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt, Germany, observed that many Christians were more focused on theological debates than on living a Christlike life. Concerned about this, he wrote a book called "Pia Desideria" ("Pious Desires"), suggesting ways to renew the church by encouraging personal devotion and heartfelt faith. Spener proposed six key ideas: studying the Bible earnestly in small groups, recognizing that all believers share in the church's spiritual work, practicing faith through good deeds, approaching others with kindness instead of criticism, training pastors to be both knowledgeable and devout, and preaching that inspires genuine faith. This movement, known as Pietism, emphasized a personal connection with God over formal rituals. It spread throughout Germany and beyond, influencing many Christians to seek a more heartfelt and active faith.
x23.scripture: The Bible teaches that faith should be active and personal. In James 1:22, it says, "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only." Similarly, in Doctrine and Covenants 59:5, believers are instructed to "love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy might, mind, and strength." These scriptures align with Pietism's emphasis on heartfelt devotion and living one's faith through actions.
x23.background: In the 1600s, after the Reformation, many churches focused heavily on correct doctrine and formal practices. While this ensured clear teachings, it sometimes led to a faith that felt distant and impersonal. Daily life was challenging, with wars and economic hardships affecting many. People longed for a faith that provided personal comfort and guidance. Philipp Jakob Spener, influenced by earlier devotional writers like Johann Arndt, saw the need for a more personal and practical Christianity. He believed that faith should transform one's heart and daily actions, not just be about agreeing with certain teachings.

x24.talk: How can we, like John Wesley, show kindness and share our faith with others in our daily lives?
x24.child: John Wesley wanted everyone to know about Jesus, so he traveled far and wide, telling people about God's love. He started groups called 'Methodists' to help people grow in their faith and help others.
x24.learn: From John Wesley's life and the rise of Methodism, we learn the power of personal conviction and the impact of dedicated service. His commitment to reaching out to those neglected by society teaches us the importance of inclusivity and compassion in our faith practices. The emphasis on personal holiness and community service reminds us that faith is both an inward journey and an outward expression. Wesley's adaptability in methods, such as open-air preaching, encourages us to find innovative ways to share our beliefs and serve others.
x24.matters: Methodism's emphasis on personal holiness, social justice, and accessible preaching brought Christianity to many who felt overlooked by the established church. Its spread to the American frontier contributed to the religious environment that influenced early American society. For families of faith, Methodism serves as a reminder of the importance of personal devotion, community service, and the belief that God's grace is available to all. The movement's focus on disciplined living and outreach can inspire families to live out their faith actively and compassionately.

sources.name: Methodism - Wikipedia
John Wesley - Wikipedia
History of Methodism - Methodist Heritage
The beginnings of Methodism - The Methodist Church in Singapore

x24.evidence: Historical records, including John Wesley's extensive journals and letters, provide detailed accounts of his life and the development of Methodism. These documents confirm his extensive travels, preaching engagements, and the growth of Methodist societies. The establishment of Methodist chapels and the formation of organized societies across England and America are well-documented. Additionally, contemporary accounts from both supporters and critics offer insights into the impact of the movement. The survival of these records and the continued existence of Methodist congregations worldwide serve as tangible evidence of the movement's historical significance.
x24.happened: In the early 18th century, John Wesley, along with his brother Charles and friend George Whitefield, initiated a movement that would become known as Methodism. While studying at Oxford University, they formed the 'Holy Club,' a group dedicated to prayer, Bible study, and serving others. Their methodical approach to faith earned them the nickname 'Methodists.' In 1735, the Wesley brothers traveled to the American colony of Georgia to minister to settlers and Native Americans. During the voyage, John was deeply impressed by the unwavering faith of Moravian Christians during a violent storm, leading him to question his own spiritual assurance. After an unsuccessful mission in Georgia, he returned to England and, influenced by the Moravians, experienced a profound spiritual awakening on May 24, 1738, at a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. He described feeling his 'heart strangely warmed' and gained a deep assurance of salvation. This experience propelled him into a ministry of open-air preaching, reaching those neglected by the established Church of England. Over his lifetime, Wesley traveled approximately 250,000 miles and delivered around 40,000 sermons, emphasizing personal holiness and God's grace available to all. Methodism spread rapidly, reaching the American frontier and playing a significant role in the religious landscape of the time.
x24.scripture: The Bible emphasizes the importance of faith and works in the life of a believer. James 2:17 states, 'Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.' This aligns with Methodism's focus on personal holiness and active service. Additionally, the Book of Mormon teaches about the grace of God and the necessity of faith leading to good works, as seen in 2 Nephi 25:23: 'For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.' These scriptures underscore the balance of faith and action central to Methodist teachings.
x24.background: In the early 18th century, England was undergoing significant social and economic changes. The Industrial Revolution was beginning to reshape society, leading to urbanization and the growth of a working-class population. The Church of England, the established church, often failed to address the spiritual needs of these new urban communities. John Wesley was born in 1703 in Epworth, Lincolnshire, to Samuel and Susanna Wesley. His father was an Anglican clergyman, and his mother was known for her strong faith and discipline. At Oxford University, John and his brother Charles sought to deepen their faith through disciplined practices, forming the 'Holy Club' with like-minded students. Their commitment to regular prayer, Bible study, and service to others set them apart, leading to the nickname 'Methodists.' This period of religious fervor and the desire for a more personal faith experience laid the groundwork for the Methodist movement.

x25.talk: Have you ever felt extra close to Heavenly Father or Jesus, maybe during a prayer or a song?
x25.child: A long time ago, people in America felt a special excitement about God. Many wanted to know Him better, so they went to big meetings led by caring preachers who helped them feel Jesus’s love. Families felt their hearts change and wanted to follow Him.
x25.learn: We can learn that spiritual renewal often comes when people seek God sincerely and study His word together. That search invites the Spirit and can bring people from different backgrounds closer. The Great Awakening also teaches families to respect different ways people may feel or express their faith, while remembering that the desire to come closer to Heavenly Father is something all His children can share.
x25.matters: The First Great Awakening matters because it shaped how Americans think about faith, freedom, and community. It cut across old boundaries, teaching people that spiritual experiences could happen to anyone, not just the well-educated or powerful. This movement prepared future generations to ask big questions about what they believed and why. For families of faith, it shows that times of spiritual hunger often lead people back to the scriptures and prayer, helping them seek truth together. The joy, new hope, and sometimes confusion that sprang up during these years became the religious background of Joseph Smith's childhood, and later, the beginnings of the Restoration.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Great Awakening
George Whitefield and the Great Awakening – Yale Divinity School

x25.evidence: Historians have detailed records and journals of the revival meetings and sermons from this time. Jonathan Edwards’s and George Whitefield’s writings are preserved, and letters between ordinary people describe how the awakenings changed communities. Church membership records show a jump in baptisms and new members. Some ministers wrote about emotional outpourings—crying, shouting, and confessing faith—which were unusual for that time. Scholars agree the movement was widespread and long-lasting, though not every detail is felt equally among all denominations. The event is well-documented through newspapers, diaries, church records, and later reflections by those who experienced it. The First Great Awakening is considered a foundational chapter in American religious history.
x25.happened: Between 1730 and 1745, the First Great Awakening swept across the American colonies. During these years, preachers like Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield, and Gilbert Tennent traveled from town to town, speaking to huge crowds outdoors and in meetinghouses. Their message was simple but powerful: every person can feel God’s Spirit, repent, and come to Christ. Edwards delivered famous sermons, like “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,” which made people think deeply about their spiritual lives. George Whitefield was known for his loud, passionate voice and moving words that could make people cry or rejoice. This revival was not just in one church—it crossed lines between different Protestant groups. People who had always attended quiet, routine services found themselves feeling strong emotions and wanting a fresh, personal faith. Tens of thousands reported life-changing conversion experiences. The movement brought together Baptists, Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and others, helping them see each other as fellow Christians. Ordinary men and women, young and old, rich and poor, all felt God was speaking to their hearts. The Great Awakening changed the way people worshipped and talked about religion in America, making faith feel personal and alive.
x25.scripture: The First Great Awakening echoes teachings from the Bible on seeking a personal relationship with God, such as James 1:5 (“If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God”), which inspired Joseph Smith to pray for guidance. The Book of Mormon invites all to “come unto Christ” (Moroni 10:32). Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 speaks of the Lord’s Church being restored because so many “have strayed from mine ordinances.” These passages remind families that sincere prayer and searching the scriptures can invite the Spirit to guide us personally, as it did for many during the Awakening.
x25.background: Before the First Great Awakening, most colonial churches in New England and the middle colonies were calm and formal. People usually sat quietly while the minister spoke from a pulpit. For many, faith was part of daily routine, but it rarely stirred their hearts. Life itself was full of work—farming, building, keeping family safe. Society was shaped by English roots, strict church rules, and leaders who expected people to follow the old ways. Yet, many people hungered for something deeper. Families read the Bible at home, but competition among denominations and questions about ‘the right way’ led to confusion. Some churchgoers felt that ministers sounded more like teachers than messengers from God. The Great Awakening entered a world where travel was slow, letters were precious, and most news came by word of mouth. These revivals disrupted normal patterns in exciting—and sometimes troubling—ways.

x26.talk: Why do you think people feel stronger in their faith when they worship together with others?
x26.child: A long time ago, people traveled from far and wide to gather in big open fields to pray, sing, and listen to stories about God. These gatherings helped them feel closer to God and each other.
x26.learn: The Cane Ridge Revival teaches us about the power of community in fostering spiritual growth and the importance of accessible religious gatherings. It reminds us that faith can flourish in diverse settings and that collective worship can lead to profound personal and societal transformations.
x26.matters: The Cane Ridge Revival and similar camp meetings had a lasting impact on American religious life. They democratized religion by emphasizing personal choice in salvation and encouraged the formation of new denominations that prioritized individual faith experiences over traditional hierarchical structures. For families of faith, these events underscore the importance of community in spiritual growth and the power of collective worship. They also highlight how religious fervor can inspire societal change and the spread of faith-based values.

sources.name: Second Great Awakening
Cane Ridge Revival
Camp meetings: a Methodist invention?

x26.evidence: Historical records, including eyewitness accounts and contemporary reports, provide detailed descriptions of the Cane Ridge Revival. Estimates of attendance range from 10,000 to 20,000 people, with some accounts suggesting that the number could have been as high as 25,000. The revival's influence is evident in the rapid growth of Methodist and Baptist congregations in the years following, as well as the establishment of new denominations like the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ). The emotional expressions observed during the revival, such as falling, jerking, and shouting, were documented by multiple sources, indicating a widespread and intense spiritual experience.
x26.happened: In the early 1800s, a wave of religious enthusiasm swept across the American frontier, leading to the rise of camp meetings—large outdoor gatherings where people came together for days of preaching, prayer, and communal worship. One of the most notable of these was the Cane Ridge Revival, held in August 1801 in Bourbon County, Kentucky. Organized by Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone, the event drew an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 attendees, a remarkable number considering Kentucky's total population at the time was around 200,000. The meeting featured preachers from various denominations, including Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist, who delivered sermons simultaneously from different platforms. Attendees experienced intense emotional responses, such as falling to the ground, shouting, and singing, which were seen as manifestations of the Holy Spirit's influence. This revival not only invigorated personal faith but also led to the formation of new denominations and a surge in church memberships across the frontier.
x26.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of gathering together for worship and the power of communal faith. In the New Testament, Hebrews 10:25 encourages believers not to forsake assembling together, highlighting the significance of communal worship. Additionally, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:8-10 describes the people of Alma gathering at the waters of Mormon to hear the word of God and enter into a covenant, illustrating the strength found in collective faith experiences.
x26.background: At the turn of the 19th century, the United States was expanding westward, with settlers establishing communities in frontier regions like Kentucky. These areas often lacked established churches and ordained ministers, creating a spiritual vacuum. The Second Great Awakening emerged in this context, emphasizing personal salvation and direct experiences with God. Camp meetings became a practical solution for these dispersed populations, providing opportunities for communal worship and religious instruction. The Cane Ridge Revival was a culmination of this movement, bringing together people from various backgrounds to share in a profound spiritual experience.

x27.talk: What do you think it means to try to be like the very first Christians?
x27.child: Some people decided to leave behind old church rules and just follow the Bible the best they could. They wanted to be like Jesus’ church from the scriptures. Many good things happened because they tried very hard to follow what Jesus and His friends taught.
x27.learn: We can learn from the Restoration Movement that it is good to seek truth and to look carefully at our beliefs and traditions. Even when people do their best to follow God with what they have, there may always be something more that He wishes to restore or teach. This movement also reminds us that sincere study of the scriptures can change hearts, families, and even the course of churches. Finally, it shows that sometimes big changes begin with simple questions and honest searching.
x27.matters: The Restoration Movement mattered because it was one of the strongest calls to return to the roots of Christianity in American history. It showed that many people longed to follow Jesus as closely as possible, even if it meant leaving behind tradition or popular opinion. For families of faith today, it is a reminder that searching the scriptures and asking hard questions can be good, that God can guide ordinary people to make important changes, and that unity in Christ matters. It also helps us consider what it really means to follow Christ’s original church and teachings.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Restoration Movement
Christian History Institute – The Stone-Campbell Movement
Church History Topics: Sidney Rigdon

x27.evidence: Historians agree that the Restoration Movement happened much as described. Letters, church records, and journals show Barton W. Stone and the Campbells were real people with sincere religious concerns. Their writings are still read today and document their ideas very clearly. Sidney Rigdon is well documented as a preacher among the Campbellites before he met Joseph Smith and moved with his congregation into the early restored Church. There are church buildings, published debates, and membership records that mark the growth of these movements, as well as contemporary newspaper articles describing their gatherings. The historical evidence is open and strong on this subject.
x27.happened: Between 1809 and 1832, a group of Christian believers in the United States, mostly in Kentucky and Virginia, felt something important was missing from the churches around them. Led by men like Barton W. Stone and Alexander Campbell, they wanted to leave behind all the creeds and traditions that people had built up over time and instead get back to what Jesus and His apostles taught in the New Testament. They believed that by closely reading the Bible—all of it, but especially the teachings about the church—Christians could unite and be the kind of church that Jesus had set up long ago. At first, Stone and Campbell led separate groups, but they were moving toward the same goal: a simple, honest faith rooted directly in the scriptures. In 1832, these two movements joined together. Many people, including Sidney Rigdon, who would later join the early Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, were part of these changes. Their effort is why many churches today exist that try to pattern themselves exactly after the early Christians.
x27.scripture: The principle at the heart of the Restoration Movement—returning to the original teachings of Christ—matches passages like Ephesians 4:5, which says there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism.” In the Book of Mormon, 3 Nephi 27:8-10 explains that Christ’s true church must be called in His name and built upon His gospel. Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 declares that the Lord is “well pleased that there should be a living church.” These show that wanting to follow the true church is a desire God honors, but they also teach that divine authority and revelation matter alongside scripture study.
x27.background: America in the early 1800s was a country still growing, where many people were moving west and building new communities. Religion was often very important in daily life. Churches sometimes argued over beliefs and rules, and there were many different denominations. Barton W. Stone came from a Presbyterian background, while Thomas and Alexander Campbell started as Presbyterians but broke away because they felt church rules did not always fit what the Bible said. Many people in these times did not have much money, and church life often meant gathering in simple meeting houses or under trees. The Bible was read in homes and shared among families, making it the center of Christian life for many.

x28.talk: How can we keep trusting Heavenly Father when things don’t turn out as we expected?
x28.child: William Miller thought Jesus would come back in 1844, and lots of people got ready. When it didn’t happen, many were sad, but some kept believing and helped start the Seventh-day Adventist Church. It shows how people can learn and grow even when things don’t go as they hoped.
x28.learn: We can learn to be humble about things we don’t fully understand, especially when it comes to God’s promises or timing. Mistakes or disappointments do not mean the end but can lead to new growth and deeper faith. This story can help families talk about how to follow the Spirit, seek truth, and patiently trust God’s unfolding plan.
x28.matters: Adventism’s birth reminds families how faith and hope can help people cope with disappointment. The movement also shows the power and risk of trying to predict God’s timing. For the world, the Seventh-day Adventist Church became a global faith helping millions, especially in health and education. For families who trust in God’s plan, this story reassures us that God’s work unfolds in His own time, and we grow when we patiently seek deeper understanding, learning from both our mistakes and our hopes.

sources.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church Encyclopedia Britannica
‘William Miller and the Advent Crisis’ Smithsonian Magazine
Adventist Heritage Center, Andrews University

x28.evidence: Historians have found many letters, diaries, and newspaper articles that confirm what happened among the Millerites and their followers. There are first-hand accounts from people who waited on hillsides or sold their belongings in hope. Church records and personal writings also show how the Seventh-day Adventist Church was organized after the disappointment. Scholars agree on the main facts, though details about personal motivations and spiritual experiences are sometimes debated. The records of beliefs, meetings, and leadership, especially regarding William Miller and Ellen G. White, are well preserved and studied in both church-run and outside archives.
x28.happened: In the early 1800s, a farmer named William Miller in New England started reading the Bible very carefully. He became convinced that he could use Bible prophecies, especially from the book of Daniel, to predict the year Jesus Christ would return to earth. After much study, Miller concluded that Christ’s Second Coming would happen in 1844. He shared this message with thousands, and many believed and prepared, sometimes even selling their possessions and gathering in hope. But when the year 1844 passed and Jesus did not return, people were deeply let down. This event is now known as the Great Disappointment. While many lost faith or went their own way, others kept studying and praying, looking for new understanding. Among them was Ellen G. White, who felt inspired to help guide the faithful. With others like Hiram Edson and Joseph Bates, Ellen White became a key leader in founding the Seventh-day Adventist Church, which began taking shape in the years following the disappointment and was officially organized in 1863. This new group emphasized observance of the Sabbath on Saturday, healthy living, and a belief that prophecy could still guide faithful followers.
x28.scripture: The Bible gives many teachings about Christ’s return. Jesus said, 'But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only' (Matthew 24:36). This warns believers not to try to predict the exact time. In modern scripture, Saints are taught to watch and be ready (Doctrine and Covenants 45:44) and that the Second Coming will happen as the gospel reaches every nation (Matthew 24:14; Doctrine and Covenants 65:2). These passages help show why it’s wise to trust in the Lord’s timing and not rush ahead of Him.
x28.background: The United States in the early 1800s was a place of great religious excitement, often called the Second Great Awakening. People were eager to know God’s will and were open to new churches and ideas. Most folks lived on farms or in small towns, and life could be hard with much work and simple comforts. Many read their Bibles regularly, and Bible study groups were common. Millerites, as followers of William Miller were known, came from varied backgrounds, but most were ordinary people, like farmers or merchants, hoping for a better world. At this time, epidemics, wars, and hard times made people especially long for Christ’s return.

x29.talk: How could we help someone in our neighborhood who needs a friend or a meal?
x29.child: Long ago in London, two kind people decided to help anyone who was hungry, lonely, or cold. They made a group called the Salvation Army to care for others, sharing food and love. Today, they help people all around the world, just like Jesus did.
x29.learn: From the Booths and the Salvation Army, we learn that faith grows brightest when it leads us to serve those who are most in need. We can remember that every act of kindness—no matter how small—can be part of God’s work. When families help others together, they build trust and love in their own homes, as well as with the people they meet. Serving like Jesus lifts everyone involved.
x29.matters: The founding of the Salvation Army matters to families of faith because it shows how Christian service isn’t just about words—it’s about action. William and Catherine Booth taught that we come closest to Christ when we care for the needy, feed the hungry, and lift up those who feel forgotten. Their legacy lives on every time someone volunteers at a soup kitchen or donates clothes to a shelter. When families serve together, they follow a pattern set by Jesus and echoed by the Booths: loving God by loving all His children, especially those who have the least.

sources.name: The Salvation Army - Official History
Britannica - Salvation Army
BBC - The Salvation Army: Origins

x29.evidence: The history of the Salvation Army is very well documented, with journals, letters, newspapers, and records kept by the organization itself showing its early work and growth. Scholars have studied how the Army’s uniforms, open-air meetings, and military-style ranks helped attract attention and respect among those often ignored by society. People alive at the time wrote about the Booths and their followers, and the transformation they saw in whole neighborhoods. The Salvation Army’s continuing worldwide work is widely recognized and measured by independent organizations that track humanitarian service.
x29.happened: In 1865, William and Catherine Booth, who were devoted Christians within England’s Holiness Movement, started what they called the Christian Mission on the tough streets of London’s East End. The Booths saw people who were suffering from poverty, addiction, and hunger—many of whom felt unwelcome or ignored in traditional churches. Instead of only preaching sermons, the Booths took their message of hope straight to the streets, bringing food, friendship, and shelter to those most in need. They soon organized their helpers using the structure and language of an army, not to fight with weapons, but to spread kindness and serve others. This group became known as The Salvation Army. They wore uniforms, used ranks like “captain” and “soldier,” and sang hymns outdoors, drawing crowds of people who may never have entered a church. Over time, the movement grew, offering practical help—soup, soap, and salvation, as their slogan went. Today, the Salvation Army serves in 131 countries and cares for millions through shelters, food banks, hospitals, and disaster relief, all while sharing their faith in Christ through their loving actions.
