x29.scripture: Jesus’ teachings in Matthew 25:35-40 guide much of the Salvation Army’s work, especially His words, “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in.” The Book of Mormon echoes this in Mosiah 4:16-19, urging believers not to let the beggar “putteth up his petition to you in vain.” Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-28 also reminds us that we should be “anxiously engaged in a good cause.” All these verses teach that practical service—caring for others’ physical needs—is part of living the gospel of Jesus Christ.
x29.background: In the mid-1800s, London was a crowded, dirty, and often dangerous city, especially for the poor. Factories and rapid growth brought jobs, but also pollution, slums, and families sleeping on the streets. Many churches stayed away from these rough parts of town, focusing on the wealthy or middle class. William Booth had grown up poor and worked hard as a Methodist preacher. Catherine Booth was strong in her faith and believed everyone needed both spiritual and practical help. They joined the Holiness Movement, a group of Christians who taught that a person should live a holy life, caring for others as Jesus did. The Booths’ decision to step onto the streets and invite hurting people into God’s family—often when nobody else would—made their work stand out in their own day.

x30.talk: How do you feel when you pray and sing to Heavenly Father?
x30.child: Long ago in Los Angeles, people gathered in a small church to pray together and ask for God’s help. Many felt God’s power and spoke new words, sang, and felt happy inside. Soon, people around the world heard about it and wanted to join, too.
x30.learn: We can learn that God can inspire people in times and places we might not expect. Faith and unity can bring people together, even when society is divided. The revival shows that spiritual hunger is something people have felt throughout history, and that sincere prayer can lead to new understanding and blessings. It’s also a reminder that it is wise to seek spiritual experiences with humility and kindness.
x30.matters: The Azusa Street Revival matters because it changed how millions of Christians around the world think about worship and spiritual gifts. Today, over 700 million people are part of Pentecostal or charismatic Christian groups. For families of faith, the story reminds us that God can work through anyone, in any place, and that faith can bring people together across differences. It also shows that spiritual gifts and heartfelt worship are still important to many Christians, connecting back to stories of the early church.

sources.name: Christianity Today: The Azusa Street Revival
Encyclopedia Britannica: Pentecostalism
PBS: The Azusa Street Revival

x30.evidence: Historical records, newspaper articles, personal diaries, and letters from the time clearly show that the Azusa Street Revival happened as described. First-hand accounts describe the powerful spiritual experiences people had, and these match records from visitors who published reports of what they saw. Photos exist of the small building used for the meetings. Historians agree that the revival played a big role in spreading Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity globally in the 20th century. While some outsiders at the time criticized the meetings or did not believe the reports, the volume and consistency of sources make the basic story well established.
x30.happened: In 1906, a remarkable spiritual event began in a small wooden building on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, California. Led by William Seymour, an African American preacher, a group of Christians gathered to pray and seek what they called the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In their meetings, people reported speaking in tongues (using languages they had not learned), being healed from sickness, and worshipping God with great emotion and music. The meetings were often loud and joyful, and people came from many different backgrounds and races to join. Word of these meetings spread quickly, and before long, visitors from across the United States and even other countries came to experience what was happening. This became known as the Azusa Street Revival. The excitement and spiritual experiences at Azusa set off a movement called Pentecostalism, which focused on the gifts of the Spirit, especially speaking in tongues, healings, and prophecy. Over the next century, the movement grew rapidly around the world, with churches forming in many different countries.
x30.scripture: The New Testament in the Bible describes the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit filled Christ’s apostles and they spoke in languages they did not know (Acts 2:1-18). Paul also taught about spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians chapters 12 and 14, listing gifts like tongues, prophecy, healing, and faith. The Book of Mormon speaks of spiritual gifts among believers in Moroni 10:8-18. The Doctrine and Covenants, in Section 46:9-26, teaches that the gifts of the Spirit, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing, are given to help and bless others, not to show off.
x30.background: Life in early 1900s Los Angeles was busy and growing, with people coming from all over the country and the world to seek new opportunities. The United States was becoming more urban, and new inventions like cars and electric lights were changing daily life. Many churches were already well established, but most worship services were very formal. Some people felt something was missing and longed for more direct experiences with God, like those described in the New Testament. William Seymour grew up in the deeply divided and often racist South but believed that in God's eyes all people were equal. The people drawn to Azusa Street included men, women, children, Black, White, Latino, and Asian worshippers, together in a time when society often kept groups apart.

x31.talk: How do you feel when someone speaks to you in your own language or listens to what you believe?
x31.child: Long ago, the biggest church in the world decided to make its meetings easier for everyone to understand. Leaders met and chose to use words people know, so more could join and sing. This taught us that Jesus wants everyone to feel welcome and loved.
x31.learn: We learn that God’s work moves on as people seek Him together. Change can feel difficult, but it can also bring new understanding and help us serve others better. When we value both tradition and new ways to share God’s love, families can help build bridges, encourage understanding, and stand strong in faith. Honest and kind conversations with people of other beliefs can strengthen our own testimony, remind us of what we cherish, and open our eyes to the goodness in God’s wider family.
x31.matters: Vatican II is important because it showed that God’s work can move forward in new ways as the world changes. For a family of faith, this teaches us that tradition and personal connection with God can go together. By putting the gospel in everyone’s own language and inviting respectful conversation with other Christians and faiths, Vatican II made faith more active and welcoming. This spirit of dialogue encourages us to learn from others and stand firm in what we know to be true, trusting that light and truth come from God and can be shared with all.

sources.name: Vatican II Documents - Vatican.va
Britannica - Second Vatican Council
US Conference of Catholic Bishops: Vatican II
BBC History - Vatican II

x31.evidence: There is strong historical evidence for Vatican II. Over 2,000 bishops attended, along with many observers, including women and non-Catholic Christians. The council’s documents, speeches, and even video recordings are preserved in the Vatican archives and available online. Scholars agree about the changes that happened, including the shift to worship in the local languages, emphasis on religious liberty, and opening to dialogue. The effects can still be seen today in Catholic parishes around the world. Modern historians, church leaders, and participants have written many books and articles about their experiences, making this a well-documented event.
x31.happened: From 1962 to 1965, leaders of the Roman Catholic Church came together in Rome for a series of meetings known as the Second Vatican Council, or Vatican II. Called by Pope John XXIII, and continued under Pope Paul VI, this council welcomed bishops from all over the world to discuss how the Church could better serve people in modern times. One of the biggest changes was allowing the Mass, the most important worship service, to be held in people’s local languages instead of only in Latin. This helped more people understand and participate fully in worship. The council also encouraged Catholics to talk kindly with people from other faiths, both Christian and non-Christian, and recognized that truth and goodness could be found outside their church. Many traditions were updated, and the Church became more open, hoping to be a light to everyone, not just Catholics. The council gave special attention to the dignity of all people and the importance of reaching out with charity and understanding.
x31.scripture: The Bible encourages unity and understanding. In the book of Acts, chapter 2, the Holy Ghost helps the disciples speak in many languages so everyone can hear the good news. Jesus teaches in Mark 12:31 to love our neighbors as ourselves, which includes listening and respecting others’ faith. Modern scripture like Doctrine and Covenants 46:13 tells us that all have spiritual gifts, and 2 Nephi 29:7-9 reminds us God speaks to all nations. While Vatican II is not directly in scripture, these principles of openness, unity, and hearing God in many places touch its purpose.
x31.background: The years before Vatican II were a time of quick change. After two world wars had shaken the world, many people wondered about the place of faith in a modern, scientific age. In the 1960s, the world saw rising hopes for peace, civil rights, and new friendships between different countries. The Catholic Church was very large and had followers on every continent, but many church practices seemed old-fashioned to ordinary members. Most church services were conducted in Latin, which few people outside priests understood, making it hard for families and children to join in fully. Leaders realized it was time to talk together about guiding the Church in a changing world—asking how they could better share Christ’s love with all.

x32.talk: Can you think of a time when you worked with someone different from you to help someone else?
x32.child: A long time ago, Christians met in a big meeting to try to help each other and learn to be friends, even though they were a bit different. Heavenly Father wants us to love and work with everyone. When we are kind and try to understand others, good things can happen.
x32.learn: From this event, we can learn that even when people have different beliefs or backgrounds, they can find ways to work together for good. We also see that it can take courage to start a conversation with someone who is different from us, but Heavenly Father can help us reach out in love. The WCC teaches us about respect, kindness, and trying to build bridges rather than walls. For Latter-day Saints, this is a reminder of the gospel value of seeking peace and friendship with all.
x32.matters: The founding of the World Council of Churches matters to the world because it shows the power of people coming together, even when they are different. It is important for families of faith because it reminds us that Jesus wanted His followers to be united in love and purpose. The WCC offers a way for Christian churches to work side by side in service, prayer, and learning, even if they aren’t always in agreement. For Latter-day Saint families, it can help us remember the value of reaching out kindly to all God’s children.

sources.name: World Council of Churches official history
Encyclopedia Britannica: World Council of Churches
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Refugee Work of the WCC
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Official Statement on Religious Freedom and Pluralism

x32.evidence: Historians have carefully recorded the founding of the World Council of Churches, and its work over the years is well documented in its records and meeting minutes. The organization’s creation in 1948 is supported by many contemporary news reports and academic studies. Minutes, photographs, and witness accounts from Amsterdam that summer show the seriousness and hope these church leaders felt. Today, anyone can visit the headquarters or read their documents online. The WCC’s ongoing humanitarian efforts, such as helping refugees or leading peacemaking missions, are often reported by journalists and partners. This evidence shows that the WCC meeting truly happened and continues its work today.
x32.happened: In 1948, in the city of Amsterdam, leaders and members from 352 Christian churches in 44 countries gathered to create something new called the World Council of Churches. These churches included many kinds of Christians, especially from Protestant and Orthodox backgrounds, who wanted to work together more closely. Their goal was to find ways to help each other and bring Christians into better understanding through shared prayer, study, and service. Dr. W.A. Visser ’t Hooft, a respected leader from the Netherlands, became the group’s first General Secretary. The council did not try to make everyone the same, but to encourage Christians to talk openly about their faith, help those in need, and share their beliefs with the world. Over time, the World Council of Churches grew to include more than 350 different churches and to represent about 580 million Christians around the world. Their meetings give a place for Christians to discuss beliefs and world problems, and to do good together through humanitarian and peacemaking efforts.
x32.scripture: There are several passages in scripture about unity among believers. In the Bible, Jesus prays, "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee" (John 17:21). Paul taught the early saints to "be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment" (1 Corinthians 1:10). The Book of Mormon explains that when the people of Christ have His spirit, “there were no contentions and disputations among them, and every man did deal justly one with another” (4 Nephi 1:2). Doctrine and Covenants 38:27 teaches, "If ye are not one ye are not mine." These teachings remind us that unity is a holy desire from God.
x32.background: The world in 1948 was still healing from the pain of World War II. Many nations were rebuilding, and people were searching for hope and unity. Christianity was spread across many countries and practiced in many ways. Protestant and Orthodox Christians had long histories of both working together and disagreeing. Daily life for church members often meant going to worship services, reading scripture, and helping neighbors, but there were also deep divisions over beliefs and traditions. The idea of Christian unity was not new, but after centuries of separation, many church leaders believed it was time to find common ground. Movements toward cooperation had started in the 1800s, but this was the first large organization aiming to unite such a wide range of churches.

x33.talk: How do you think Jesus feels about people who follow Him in different places around the world?
x33.child: Around the world, lots of people love Jesus and try to follow Him, even if they live far away or worship in different ways. Some get to go to church in big buildings, but some have to meet quietly at home. We are all part of a big family of people who believe in God.
x33.learn: One important lesson is that God’s message can take root anywhere—sometimes in grand cathedrals, sometimes in small homes, and always in people’s hearts. We can learn to be grateful for our freedom to worship, and we can remember to pray for those who do not have it. Knowing that so many people around the world seek God can help us feel connected as part of a global family, and encourage us to listen, learn, and show respect for others’ ways of worship.
x33.matters: This moment matters greatly because it shows that faith in Jesus Christ is not just a memory from the past but is living and growing in families and communities worldwide. For families of faith, it can remind us that Heavenly Father’s love reaches across every border and into every heart. Even as traditions differ, the teachings of Christ about love, forgiveness, and caring for the poor continue to guide millions. It also invites us to recognize that we are part of a much larger family of believers, each trying to follow God’s light in their own way. Recognizing our brothers and sisters worldwide can help us act with greater kindness and understanding.

sources.name: Pew Research Center - Global Christianity: A Report on the Size and Distribution of the World's Christian Population

x33.evidence: Recent global data from research organizations and churches support that Christianity remains the world’s largest religion, with around 2.4 billion adherents. These numbers come from careful studies of church membership rolls, census reports, and surveys in many countries. Organizations like the Pew Research Center and the World Christian Database regularly collect and report this information. Archaeology and written history confirm the long journey of Christianity from its beginnings in the Middle East, through Europe and the Americas, and now with much growth in Africa and Asia. There are well-documented examples of churches and Christian communities across every continent, and reports from China verify that millions still meet privately to worship. These trends are reliably tracked by expert demographers and respected news sources.
x33.happened: Since the year 2000, Christianity has continued to be the world’s largest faith, with about 2.4 billion people calling themselves Christians. This includes many traditions—Roman Catholic, Protestant, Eastern Orthodox, and new Christian movements that have grown up in different lands. Catholics make up the largest group, led by the Pope in Rome. Protestants are a collection of smaller groups like Presbyterians, Baptists, and Pentecostals, many of whom worship in unique ways in churches all around the globe. The Orthodox churches, rooted in places like Greece and Russia, look much as they have for centuries. In Western Europe, where many churches once crowded every town square, fewer people today attend church, but Christianity is thriving in unexpected places, especially in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. In these regions, families and communities are building new churches, schools, and hospitals, often under great challenges. In countries like China, millions of Christians meet quietly in homes because they are not always free to worship openly, while in Africa, Christians gather in joyful services, often with music and dancing. Leaders like Pope Francis, pastors, and patriarchs guide their people, and together, they work to meet both spiritual and physical needs in a world facing many changes.
x33.scripture: Jesus taught His followers to go and teach all nations (Matthew 28:19-20), promising to be with them always. In the Book of Mormon, the risen Christ explained He would gather all His people from every nation (3 Nephi 16:3). Doctrine and Covenants 1:2, speaking of the last days, teaches that the gospel will be heard by all people, wherever they live. These scriptures show God’s desire for everyone to learn of Him and feel His love, and the worldwide spread of Christianity reflects this hopeful vision.
x33.background: The world in 2000 was connected in ways never seen before. Airplanes, the internet, and television brought news and ideas from any place to almost anywhere else. Before this, Christianity spread first from Israel, then through Europe and the Americas, often alongside the rise and fall of empires. Daily life for Christians in 2000 could look very different depending on where they lived—many in the West had freedom to worship and a church nearby, while some in Asia or the Middle East needed to keep their faith private. Technology made it easier to share beliefs, but also brought new questions about faith in a changing world. This new era saw greater attention to issues like poverty, justice, and caring for others, reflecting Jesus’s teachings. Families often gathered for worship in churches, homes, or even outdoors, reflecting both old traditions and new ways of gathering.

x40.talk: What is something we can do at home to help our family feel closer to Heavenly Father?
x40.child: A long time ago, a church leader wrote a letter to help families love each other and stay close to God. He said families can be like a little church at home, learning and loving together every day. Families can help each other choose the right and feel happy.
x40.learn: Familiaris Consortio teaches us that strong families start at home, with love, faith, and patience. It reminds us that family is not just about living together but about growing together, praying together, and helping each other. Even when the world changes, families can stick together and teach their children what matters most. When families put God at the center of their lives, they help each other become kind, faithful, and strong.
x40.matters: Familiaris Consortio matters because it became a guidebook for Catholic families trying to live faithfully in a quickly changing world. It gave parents confidence that teaching faith at home is as important as church activities. The letter didn’t just shape Catholic thinking; it caught worldwide attention from Christians of many faiths because it spoke deeply about love, unity, and the promise of marriage. For Latter-day Saint families, it’s interesting to see the Catholic Church teaching about home-centered faith and marriage as a covenant—ideas that later echoed in the Family Proclamation. These shared beliefs remind us that families everywhere can reach for God’s help to love and serve each other.

sources.name: Vatican: Familiaris Consortio (English text)
Encyclopedia Britannica: John Paul II
United States Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB): About Familiaris Consortio

x40.evidence: There is clear historical evidence for the publication of Familiaris Consortio. The text is officially recorded and available through the Vatican and widely discussed by historians, theologians, and family scholars. Church documents from the 1980 Synod of Bishops show the careful preparation and prayer that went into creating it. The teachings in the document shaped many Catholic activities and resources for families in the decades that followed. Its influence can be seen in later Church statements by other faiths, including the Latter-day Saint Proclamation on the Family. No major historian disputes the document’s release or its importance within Catholicism and modern Christian history.
x40.happened: On November 22, 1981, Pope John Paul II released a special letter called an Apostolic Exhortation titled Familiaris Consortio, which means 'The Family in the Modern World.' This letter was written to all Catholic Christians, focusing on what families mean and what it looks like to live as a family with faith today. Pope John Paul II described the family as a 'communion of persons,' which means a group of people joined together in love and responsibility. He taught that marriage is a sacred promise — a covenant — that should last throughout life between one man and one woman. He called families 'the domestic church,' saying that the home is where faith is taught first, prayer is learned, and service to others begins. The document explained how families can serve each other, welcome children, and help their communities. When Familiaris Consortio was published, it gathered the thoughts and prayers of bishops from all over the world after they met in the Vatican in 1980 to talk about families. This document remains one of the most important Catholic teachings about families in recent history.
x40.scripture: Scriptures that touch on the principles of Familiaris Consortio talk about the love and unity in families. The Bible teaches in Ephesians 5:25, 'Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church,' showing deep respect in marriage. In The Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:14-15 instructs parents to teach their children to love and serve one another. Doctrine and Covenants 68:25 also commands parents to teach children in faith and prayer. Each of these Scriptures supports the idea of the home as a sacred place where families grow in love for God and each other, which is exactly what Familiaris Consortio hoped to encourage.
x40.background: In the years before Familiaris Consortio was written, many families were facing changes and challenges. The late 1970s and early 1980s brought new social ideas about marriage, divorce, and the roles men and women had in families. Pope John Paul II, a Polish Pope known for his deep faith and connection to families, listened carefully as Catholic bishops from around the world met to talk about what families needed most. Daily life for many was changing—more women were working outside the home, laws about marriage and divorce were shifting, and technology was beginning to transform how people worked and spent their time together. The Catholic Church wanted to offer guidance and encouragement to families trying to stay close and faithful amidst all these changes, which led to the creation of Familiaris Consortio.

x41.t: Charter of the Rights of the Family
x41.talk: Why do you think the family is important, and who do you believe gave us families?
x41.child: A long time ago, church leaders wrote a letter to the world saying families are special, and no government made families—God did. They wanted everyone to remember how important it is to love and protect our families.
x41.learn: From this event, we can learn that many people around the world—and across Christian faiths—believe strongly in the natural and sacred purpose of the family. It shows that when families face challenges, leaders can use their voices to remind society of what matters most. The Charter of the Rights of the Family encourages us to hold onto the truth that families should be places of safety, love, and teaching, and that these blessings are not given by governments, but by God.
x41.matters: This event matters because it made a worldwide statement that families have rights which are not given by governments, but come from their very nature as created by God. For families of faith, including Latter-day Saint families, this supports the idea that the family has a purpose and a dignity that no law or court can take away. It showed the world that churches care deeply about protecting families, and that many people believe families are the building blocks of a good society. Even today, governments and groups sometimes refer to this charter when discussing laws about marriage and children.

sources.name: The Holy See—Charter of the Rights of the Family (official English text)
Encyclopedia Britannica—Pope John Paul II
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—The Family: A Proclamation to the World
United Nations—The family: A natural and fundamental group unit of society

x41.evidence: Historians can clearly trace the creation and publication of the Charter of the Rights of the Family in 1983. The Vatican holds copies in its archives, and many governments and religious bodies received formal copies at the time. News reports and religious journals also covered its release and impact. The text of the charter is available in many languages, and it has been referenced in United Nations conversations about family and children's rights. Academic studies on the charter show how it influenced global discussions about families and law, especially in relation to Catholic social teaching.
x41.happened: On October 22, 1983, the Holy See, which is the government of the Roman Catholic Church based in Vatican City, published a special document called the Charter of the Rights of the Family. This charter was presented to all people, governments, and organizations around the world who have a part in caring for families. The document says very clearly that the family is not an idea invented by a government, but a real, natural group that has its own important rights. It tells the world that a family begins with marriage between a man and a woman, and that families have the special job of bringing children into the world and raising them. The Charter also says these family rights exist before any country or government, and that no government has the power to give or take away these rights. This declaration was written by the Pontifical Council for the Family, with Pope John Paul II leading the church. The Charter was meant to remind everyone that families are the foundation of society and should be protected, not changed or taken apart by laws or politics. It was sent on to many leaders, trying to help shape how the world treats family life. Twelve years later, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints would share its own Family Proclamation, which also teaches that the family is created by God and cannot be invented or changed by governments.
x41.scripture: Many scriptures teach about the family and its importance. In Genesis 2:24, the Bible says that a man shall leave his parents and be joined to his wife, and they shall be one flesh, showing marriage as the beginning of the family. The Book of Mormon, in Mosiah 4:14-15, teaches parents to love and care for their children and to teach them to walk in the ways of God. The Doctrine and Covenants 68:25-28 commands parents to teach their children faith, repentance, and baptism. While no scripture uses the language of 'rights,' these teachings all underline that the family is part of God’s plan and exists before any government or law.
x41.background: The Charter of the Rights of the Family was written in the early 1980s, a time of great change. Many countries were debating new laws about marriage, divorce, and family life. In some places, governments wanted more control over family matters, such as how children are raised or who is counted as a family. Pope John Paul II was a strong leader for the Roman Catholic Church during this time. He and others saw that families in many countries were under pressure and sometimes overlooked or weakened by the changes happening in society. Daily life for many believers still centered around family meals, church teachings, and traditions, but new ideas from media and politics were challenging old ways. The Charter was written to answer these changes with a deep belief in the natural, God-given role of the family.

x42.talk: Why do you think God made boys and girls different?
x42.child: A long time ago, some church leaders wrote a paper about how boys and girls are special and have different jobs in families and church. They believed God made us this way to help each other.
x42.learn: From the Danvers Statement, we learn the importance of seeking guidance from Scripture when addressing societal changes. It teaches that while cultural norms may shift, grounding our understanding of roles and relationships in biblical teachings can provide clarity and stability. This approach encourages families to reflect on how they can honor God's design in their daily lives.
x42.matters: The Danvers Statement holds significance as it represents a concerted effort by evangelical leaders to define and uphold traditional gender roles based on their interpretation of Scripture. For families of faith, it provides a framework for understanding the complementary roles of men and women in marriage and church life. This perspective aligns with the belief that gender distinctions are divinely ordained and essential for the proper functioning of family and church structures.

sources.name: The Danvers Statement - CBMW
Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood - Wikipedia
Recovering Biblical Manhood and Womanhood - Wikipedia

x42.evidence: The Danvers Statement is a well-documented historical document. It was drafted in December 1987 and published in November 1988 by the CBMW. The statement has been referenced in various publications and discussions on gender roles within evangelical Christianity. Its publication in Christianity Today in January 1989 further solidified its presence in evangelical discourse. The CBMW's website provides access to the full text of the statement, ensuring its availability for study and reference.
x42.happened: In December 1987, a group of evangelical leaders gathered in Danvers, Massachusetts, to address concerns about changing views on gender roles within the church and society. This meeting led to the drafting of the Danvers Statement, which was finalized and published by the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood (CBMW) in November 1988. The statement affirms that both men and women are created in God's image, equal in personhood but distinct in their roles. It emphasizes that these differences are part of God's design and are meant to complement each other in marriage and church leadership. The Danvers Statement was later published as a full-page advertisement in Christianity Today in January 1989, bringing its message to a broader audience.
x42.scripture: The Bible offers guidance on the roles of men and women. In Genesis 1:27, it states that God created both male and female in His image, highlighting their equal value. Ephesians 5:22-33 discusses the relationship between husbands and wives, emphasizing love and respect. 1 Timothy 2:12 addresses roles within the church, suggesting distinct functions for men and women. These passages have been foundational for those advocating the complementarian view expressed in the Danvers Statement.
x42.background: During the 1980s, Western society experienced significant shifts in attitudes toward gender roles, with increasing advocacy for gender equality in all spheres of life. Within evangelical circles, this period saw debates between those advocating for traditional roles and those supporting egalitarian views. In response to these cultural changes, leaders like John Piper and Wayne Grudem sought to articulate a biblical perspective on manhood and womanhood, leading to the formation of the CBMW and the drafting of the Danvers Statement.

x43.talk: What do you think helps our family stay strong and happy together?
x43.child: A long time ago, a church leader wrote a letter to all families to remind them how special families are. He wanted everyone to remember what words like marriage and family really mean. He hoped this would help families feel close and strong.
x43.learn: We can learn that words matter and that truths about family life can be passed down and kept safe even when the world changes around us. The Pope’s letter teaches us to value the words we use and the promises we make to each other, and to protect the good things in family life that help us stay strong and close to Heavenly Father. History shows that when families work together and remember what really matters, they can be a blessing to all.
x43.matters: This letter matters because it called the world to remember simple truths at a moment when those truths were being questioned. For families of faith, like members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, it reminds us to cherish the words and covenants that bring our families together. Pope John Paul II was concerned that if we lose the real meaning of marriage, parenthood, and family, we lose something precious. The letter points families to roots that can steady them in confusing times—much like the Family Proclamation would do a little later for Latter-day Saints.

sources.name: Vatican - Letter to Families (Gratissimam Sane)
United Nations - International Year of the Family, 1994
Catholic News Agency - Explainer: What is Pope John Paul II’s ‘Letter to Families’?

x43.evidence: The Letter to Families is a public, written document with an official date, translations, and widespread distribution by the Vatican. The text can be easily found and read today, and historians recognize it as one of the key moments when Pope John Paul II addressed modern changes in family life. Outside of church settings, the letter is often studied by scholars who want to understand how Christian leaders responded to shifting views about family and marriage at the end of the 20th century. There is no real debate about whether the letter was issued or what its main messages were—though people do discuss its impact and how much influence it had in different communities.
x43.happened: On February 2, 1994, Pope John Paul II wrote a special letter to families around the world called Gratissimam Sane, or the "Letter to Families." This letter was not just for bishops or priests but was written directly to all families, moms and dads, grandmas and grandpas, and kids. The Pope wrote it because, in that year, the United Nations had chosen to focus on the family, naming 1994 the International Year of the Family. The Pope wanted to remind everyone that families are at the very heart of society and God’s plan. He spoke about something he saw happening: that many people were starting to use words like "marriage" and "family" in ways that didn’t match their true meaning. He called this a "crisis of truth," where people can get confused if the real meaning of important words changes. He encouraged families to keep living by the love, respect, and trust that help them grow strong and happy. The letter was an invitation to think deeply about what makes families work and why they matter so much, even in a changing world.
x43.scripture: Scriptures teach a lot about the importance of families. In Genesis 2:24, the Bible says a man leaves his parents and joins with his wife to become one family. The Book of Mormon, in Mosiah 4:14-15, teaches parents to raise their children in love and truth. Doctrine and Covenants 49:15–16 reminds us that marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God. Each of these passages points to how families have a purpose in God’s plan and why words like marriage and family matter so much in scripture.
x43.background: The early 1990s were a time of big change around the world. The Cold War had just ended, and people in many countries were trying to rebuild and find new ways of living together. The United Nations, seeing how important family is to every country, set aside 1994 as the International Year of the Family. This meant families and their challenges were in the spotlight. At this time, families were facing lots of new pressures, from both changing laws and new philosophies about what marriage and family should look like. Pope John Paul II had himself grown up in difficult times, having lost his own mother as a child and lived through war and hardship in Poland. He understood how tough life could be, but also how faith and family could bring hope and strength.

c04b.talk: Why do you think it's important for families to follow the teachings of the prophets?
c04b.child: Long ago, some people in Hawaii wanted to get married, but the law didn't let them because they were the same gender. This made many people talk about what marriage means. Church leaders taught that marriage is special between a man and a woman, and families are very important.
c04b.learn: This period teaches the importance of vigilance and proactive guidance in times of societal change. It illustrates how legal decisions can prompt religious organizations to reaffirm and articulate their doctrines, providing clarity and direction to their members. The events also highlight the role of prophets and leaders as watchmen, tasked with foreseeing challenges and offering counsel to navigate them.
c04b.matters: The Hawaii Supreme Court's decision in Baehr v. Lewin was a catalyst for the national debate on same-sex marriage, influencing subsequent legal battles and legislative actions across the country. For families of faith, this period underscored the importance of understanding and articulating their beliefs regarding marriage and family structures. The issuance of "The Family: A Proclamation to the World" by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints provided clear guidance on these doctrines, emphasizing the divine nature of marriage between a man and a woman and the central role of the family in God's plan. This reaffirmation served as a foundation for members to navigate the evolving societal landscape while adhering to their faith principles.

sources.name: The Family: A Proclamation to the World
Baehr v. Lewin: Hawaii Supreme Court Case Summary - LegalClarity
Historical Context and Background of The Family: A Proclamation to the World | Doctrine and Covenants Central

c04b.evidence: The historical record confirms the sequence of events: the filing of the lawsuit in 1991, the Hawaii Supreme Court's decision in 1993, and the subsequent actions by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, including the issuance of "The Family: A Proclamation to the World" in 1995. These events are well-documented in legal archives and church publications. The Hawaii Supreme Court's ruling is recognized as a pivotal moment in the legal discourse on same-sex marriage, influencing both public opinion and legislative actions in the years that followed.
c04b.happened: In May 1991, three same-sex couples in Hawaii applied for marriage licenses but were denied based on existing state laws that defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman. These couples filed a lawsuit against the state, leading to the landmark case Baehr v. Lewin. In May 1993, the Hawaii Supreme Court ruled that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples constituted sex-based discrimination under the state's constitution. The court remanded the case for further proceedings, requiring the state to demonstrate a compelling interest to justify the exclusion. This decision marked the first time a state supreme court recognized that excluding same-sex couples from marriage could be unconstitutional, igniting a nationwide conversation on the topic. In response, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints issued "The Family: A Proclamation to the World" in September 1995, reaffirming its doctrines on marriage and family. The Church also sought to intervene in the Hawaii case in February 1995, emphasizing its commitment to traditional marriage values.
c04b.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the role of prophets as watchmen who warn of impending challenges. Ezekiel 33:2-6 illustrates this principle, describing a watchman who sees danger from afar and sounds the alarm to protect the people. Similarly, Amos 3:7 states, "Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets." These passages highlight the belief that prophets are divinely appointed to foresee and address societal issues, guiding the faithful in times of change.
c04b.background: In the early 1990s, societal attitudes toward same-sex relationships were evolving, with increasing advocacy for LGBTQ+ rights. However, legal recognition of same-sex marriages was virtually nonexistent in the United States. Hawaii's unique cultural and legal landscape became a focal point for this issue. The plaintiffs in Baehr v. Lewin challenged the state's denial of marriage licenses, arguing that it violated their constitutional rights. The Hawaii Supreme Court's 1993 decision was unprecedented, as it applied strict scrutiny to the state's marriage laws, requiring the government to provide a compelling reason for excluding same-sex couples. This legal development prompted various religious organizations, including The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, to articulate and reaffirm their positions on marriage and family.

c04c.talk: How can we show kindness to people who believe different things than we do?
c04c.child: In 2015, the United States made a law that all people can marry who they love, even if they are the same gender. Families in the Church believe marriage is between a man and a woman, but we also try to be kind and loving to everyone. We can ask Heavenly Father to help us do both.
c04c.learn: From this event, we can learn that the laws of countries and the teachings of faith do not always move at the same speed, and it is important to understand both. We can also see how changes in laws shape how families, schools, and churches work together. Most of all, we are reminded that kindness, listening, and respect are needed in times of change. Even when we hold to what we believe, we can show love for others and ask for guidance from Heavenly Father as we teach and learn.
c04c.matters: This event matters because it changed the laws about marriage in the United States for everyone, touching families, schools, churches, and workplaces. For families of faith, it brings two faithful duties: loving and respecting all of God’s children and standing by the teachings found in sacred doctrine about marriage. The challenge for many is how to live and teach both these commitments together, with kindness and honesty. Changes like this call families to talk heart-to-heart about what they believe, how they can show respect for others, and how they can trust in God’s timing.

sources.name: Obergefell v. Hodges | Supreme Court decision
Church Statement on Supreme Court Ruling on Same-Sex Marriage
Britannica: Obergefell v. Hodges
National Constitution Center: Explaining Obergefell v. Hodges

c04c.evidence: The Supreme Court's decision is documented in public records, which show not only the votes of the justices and the words they wrote, but also thousands of pages of legal arguments, stories from families, and statements from states and organizations across the country. Scholars and news outlets documented the rapid shift in public opinion over the decade before 2015, with more Americans coming to support legal same-sex marriage. There is clear historical evidence that Obergefell v. Hodges changed laws and daily life for many, as states revised their records and practices right after the ruling. The Church’s official statements and teaching materials from this time also reflect the real ways families and leaders responded, striving to keep faith and kindness at the center of their conversations.
c04c.happened: On June 26, 2015, the United States Supreme Court made a historic decision in a case called Obergefell v. Hodges. The Court decided, by a vote of five justices to four, that the Constitution requires all fifty states to allow and recognize marriages between two people of the same sex. This meant that no matter where someone lived in the United States, they could legally marry the person they loved, even if they were the same gender, and the state had to accept that marriage. The Court said that the Fourteenth Amendment, which promises people equal protection under the law, meant that marriage rights could not be denied just because of gender. The decision was named after Jim Obergefell, who wanted his marriage to his partner recognized after his partner died. Because of this ruling, thousands of couples across the country could have their marriages officially recognized, even in places where local laws had said otherwise.
c04c.scripture: There are no scriptures that directly discuss legal rulings on marriage by governments, but the Bible and modern scripture do teach about loving one another (John 13:34-35), honoring God's commandments about marriage and family (Genesis 2:24; The Family: A Proclamation to the World), and being peacemakers in a changing world (Matthew 5:9). Doctrine and Covenants 42:22 encourages marriage between husband and wife, as does the Proclamation. At the same time, Jesus’ example of reaching out in love to all people (Luke 10:27) stands as the foundation for how we treat others.
c04c.background: When this decision happened, the world had been changing its ideas about marriage and family. Several countries, starting with the Netherlands in 2001, had already made same-sex marriage legal. In the United States, Massachusetts became the first state to allow same-sex marriage in 2003. These changes followed many years of discussion about civil rights and equality, including debates about what marriage meant in the eyes of the law. For many, daily life included watching these debates play out on television or hearing about them at school or church. Many people had strong feelings on both sides, and families often had to talk through these changes together. Faith communities, including The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, were asked to consider how to respond to the new laws while holding to their beliefs.

cv01.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wanted us to learn the gospel at home as well as at church?
cv01.child: President Nelson taught us to hold gospel lessons at home, not just at church. When we had to stay home, we were ready because we had already practiced. Learning about Jesus with your family can happen anywhere, even in your living room.
cv01.learn: We learn that sometimes Heavenly Father prepares answers long before we understand why we need them. Trust in the Lord’s timing can bring peace, especially when change feels uncomfortable or new. As we embrace opportunities to teach and learn together as families, we can feel more connected to each other and to Him. In times of need, what we have learned and practiced together at home can become a strong foundation.
cv01.matters: This change matters deeply for both the world and families of faith. It put responsibility and confidence into the hands of parents and individuals, encouraging everyone to create meaningful gospel experiences in their own homes. When COVID-19 caused meetinghouses everywhere to close suddenly in early 2020, families who had learned the 'Come, Follow Me' routine found that Sunday worship could still continue. They did not need to start from scratch — they already had tools and habits for home-centered worship. For members of the Church, it was a loving reminder that Heavenly Father asks His people to prepare and trust Him even before the need is clear.

sources.name: Church Newsroom — Home-Centered, Church-Supported Worship
General Conference Announcement — President Russell M. Nelson October 2018
Ensign — A Home-Centered, Church-Supported Plan for Learning

cv01.evidence: The historical record is clear: this change was widely announced and documented by the Church itself and widely reported by reputable news organizations. The Church provided detailed instructions and resources for members worldwide, and many studies on religious practice show that home-based religious learning can increase faith and family unity. The worldwide response — both in adapting to the two-hour block and in smoothly shifting to home worship during the 2020 pandemic — is a matter of public record. Church leaders have since reflected on the wisdom and timing of the change, noting how prepared members were when meetinghouses closed.
cv01.happened: On October 6, 2018, during the General Conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints held in Salt Lake City, Utah, President Russell M. Nelson announced a remarkable change in the way church members would worship and learn together. Instead of spending three hours at church every Sunday, families and individuals would now meet for just two hours, with much of the gospel learning shifting from the meetinghouse to their own homes. This new approach introduced a unified curriculum called "Come, Follow Me," designed to be used by children, youth, and adults, encouraging families to study the gospel together during the week. President Nelson explained that church is to be "home-centered and church-supported," turning old routines upside down for millions across the world. This adjustment wasn't about doing less, but about making learning and worship more personal and more flexible to meet different family needs. The change officially started in January 2019, giving everyone time to adjust and prepare.
cv01.scripture: This event echoes scriptural patterns where God invites His people to teach and worship in the home. Moses taught Israel to teach their children daily in Deuteronomy 6:6-7. In the Book of Mormon, Alma urged families to "teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness" (Mosiah 4:15). Doctrine and Covenants 68:25-28 specifically instructs parents to teach children faith, repentance, and gospel basics at home. These passages show that the principle of home-centered learning is long-standing in the Lord’s plan.
cv01.background: Before this change, members of the Church across the globe followed a consistent pattern—Sundays meant going to the same church meetings: Sacrament, Sunday School, and classes for men, women, children, and youth. Classes lasted for three hours altogether, and most gospel learning happened within church walls. For families, this sometimes meant that gospel teaching was mainly something organized by the ward or branch, with home study being a helpful extra if time allowed. The world in 2018 saw rapid changes in how people communicated, learned, and spent time together. Technology, busy schedules, and shifting family patterns made it harder for many to keep up. The Church's new approach fit a growing hope for families to be the center of strength, learning, and faith — supported, but not replaced, by what took place at church.

cv03.talk: How can we make our home a place where we feel close to Heavenly Father?
cv03.child: When church meetings were paused because of sickness spreading, families had church at home. They read scriptures together and took the sacrament with their family. This showed that we can worship Heavenly Father anywhere, not just in church buildings.
cv03.learn: This experience teaches the importance of spiritual preparedness and adaptability. By establishing strong gospel habits at home, individuals and families can maintain their faith and worship practices even when traditional structures are disrupted. It also highlights the Church's commitment to following prophetic counsel and seeking divine guidance in times of uncertainty.
cv03.matters: The Church's swift response to the pandemic underscored the importance of adaptability and the central role of the home in gospel learning. Families took on greater responsibility for their spiritual growth, with fathers and sons administering the sacrament at home and families engaging deeply with the 'Come, Follow Me' curriculum. This period reinforced the principle that the home is a sacred space for worship and learning, preparing members to rely on personal revelation and family-centered worship in times of crisis.

sources.name: Update: Gatherings of Church Members Temporarily Suspended Worldwide
First Presidency Temporarily Closes All Latter-Day Saint Temples
Come, Follow Me (LDS Church)

cv03.evidence: Historical records from March 2020 document the Church's announcements regarding the suspension of public gatherings and temple closures. News outlets reported on these unprecedented measures, highlighting the Church's commitment to member safety and public health. The successful transition to home-centered worship was facilitated by the prior implementation of the 'Come, Follow Me' program, which had already encouraged members to engage in personal and family scripture study. This preparation allowed for a smoother adaptation to the new circumstances imposed by the pandemic.
cv03.happened: In March 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic spread globally, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints took unprecedented steps to protect its members. On March 12, the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles announced the temporary suspension of all public gatherings worldwide. This included stake conferences, leadership conferences, public worship services, and all branch, ward, and stake activities. Leaders were encouraged to conduct essential meetings via technology, and bishops were advised to work with stake presidents to ensure the sacrament was available to members at least once a month. Shortly thereafter, on March 25, the Church temporarily closed all temples worldwide. These measures were taken after consulting with local Church leaders, government officials, and medical professionals, and seeking the Lord’s guidance. Despite the closures, the Church encouraged members to continue their ministering efforts and follow the Savior’s example to bless and lift others.
cv03.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of worshiping God in all circumstances. In Doctrine and Covenants 59:9, the Lord commands, 'And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day.' While traditional worship settings were unavailable, members found ways to fulfill this commandment within their homes, demonstrating that worship is not confined to church buildings but can occur wherever the faithful gather.
cv03.background: Before the pandemic, the Church had already begun emphasizing home-centered gospel learning. In 2018, the 'Come, Follow Me' program was introduced, encouraging individuals and families to study the scriptures at home. This initiative was part of a broader effort to strengthen faith and testimony outside of traditional Sunday worship. By 2020, members were accustomed to this approach, which proved invaluable when public gatherings were suspended. The world at that time was grappling with the rapid spread of COVID-19, leading to widespread lockdowns and restrictions on gatherings to curb the virus's transmission.

cv06.talk: Can you think of a time when you learned something new that changed what you thought before?
cv06.child: Sometimes, even experts learn new things that change what they thought before. It's important to keep learning and be open to new ideas.
cv06.learn: This period teaches the importance of humility and openness to new information. It reminds us that human knowledge is ever-evolving, and what is considered certain today may be revised tomorrow. For families, it emphasizes the value of teaching children to seek truth diligently, question respectfully, and balance faith with reason.
cv06.matters: The evolving nature of health guidelines during the pandemic underscores the importance of adaptability in the face of new information. For families of faith, this serves as a reminder that while human understanding is limited and subject to change, seeking divine guidance can provide clarity. It also highlights the need for critical thinking and personal responsibility in making health decisions, balancing trust in scientific expertise with individual discernment.

sources.name: CDC: Delta variant may cause mild COVID among fully vaccinated people
CDC: Fully-vaccinated people can still spread the delta variant - YouTube
CDC Real-World Study Confirms Protective Benefits of mRNA COVID-19 Vaccines

cv06.evidence: Scientific studies have shown that while COVID-19 vaccines significantly reduce the risk of severe illness and death, breakthrough infections can occur, especially with variants like Delta. The CDC reported that in a Massachusetts outbreak, approximately 74% of cases were among fully vaccinated individuals, indicating that vaccinated people could still transmit the virus. This led to updated mask recommendations for vaccinated individuals in certain settings. Regarding myocarditis, the CDC acknowledged reports of increased cases among young males following mRNA vaccination and updated vaccine information to reflect this risk. These instances demonstrate the dynamic nature of scientific understanding and the necessity for ongoing research and data analysis.
cv06.happened: During the COVID-19 pandemic from 2021 to 2026, several health guidelines and statements were revised as new information emerged. Initially, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) stated that vaccinated individuals did not carry the virus. However, by July 2021, data indicated that vaccinated people infected with the Delta variant could carry high viral loads and potentially transmit the virus to others. This led the CDC to update its guidance, recommending that vaccinated individuals wear masks indoors in areas of substantial or high transmission. Additionally, the six-foot social distancing rule, widely promoted to reduce virus spread, was later acknowledged to lack a firm empirical basis. The emphasis on extensive surface disinfection was also reconsidered, as evidence suggested that COVID-19 primarily spreads through respiratory droplets rather than contaminated surfaces. Furthermore, cases of myocarditis, particularly in young males following mRNA vaccination, were initially downplayed but were subsequently confirmed and added to vaccine labeling. The origin of the virus also remained a topic of debate. Early in the pandemic, the lab-leak hypothesis was dismissed by many experts. However, by 2023, agencies like the CIA, FBI, and Department of Energy considered a research-related origin plausible, though with varying degrees of confidence. In July 2026, Senator Rand Paul released over 1,000 pages of Dr. Anthony Fauci's daily journals. When questioned about them, Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment, choosing not to answer.
cv06.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of seeking knowledge and wisdom. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it states, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." This encourages individuals to pursue both secular and spiritual understanding. Additionally, Moroni 10:4-5 invites believers to ask God for truth, emphasizing personal revelation as a means to discern right from wrong.
cv06.background: The COVID-19 pandemic, which began in late 2019, led to unprecedented global health challenges. Governments and health organizations worldwide implemented various measures to curb the virus's spread, including lockdowns, mask mandates, and social distancing guidelines. Vaccines were developed at an accelerated pace, with mRNA vaccines like Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna receiving emergency use authorization in late 2020. As the pandemic progressed, new variants of the virus emerged, such as the Delta variant, which was more transmissible and led to increased cases even among vaccinated individuals. The rapid evolution of the virus and the urgency to provide public guidance meant that health recommendations were frequently updated as new data became available.

nt01.talk: Why do you think the shepherds and wise men wanted to see baby Jesus?
nt01.child: Long ago, in a town called Bethlehem, a special baby named Jesus was born to Mary and Joseph. Angels told nearby shepherds about His birth, and they went to see Him. Wise men followed a bright star to find Jesus and gave Him gifts.
nt01.learn: The story of Jesus' birth teaches us about humility, faith, and the fulfillment of God's promises. Mary and Joseph's trust in God's plan, despite challenges, encourages us to rely on divine guidance. The shepherds' eagerness to witness and share the good news reminds us of the joy found in Christ's message. The Magi's journey illustrates the importance of seeking truth and recognizing the divine in our lives. This event invites us to reflect on the significance of Jesus' arrival and how it shapes our faith and actions.
nt01.matters: The birth of Jesus Christ is central to Christian faith, marking the moment when Heavenly Father sent His Son into the world to offer salvation to all humanity. For families of faith, this event underscores the importance of humility, obedience, and trust in God's plan. Mary and Joseph's willingness to accept their roles, despite societal challenges, serves as a model of faith and devotion. The shepherds' immediate response to the angelic announcement highlights the joy and urgency in sharing the good news. The Magi's journey symbolizes the recognition of Jesus' significance beyond the Jewish community, emphasizing that His message is for all people. This event invites families to reflect on the gift of Jesus' life and teachings, encouraging them to live in ways that honor His example of love, service, and sacrifice.

sources.name: National Geographic: Is there historical evidence for the Star of Bethlehem?
Encyclopedia.com: Nativity of Christ
National Geographic: Biblical stories of Jesus' birth reveal intriguing clues about his times

nt01.evidence: Historical records confirm the existence of King Herod and the Roman census, aligning with the Gospel accounts. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions Herod's reign and the political climate of Judea during that period. Archaeological findings in Bethlehem and Nazareth provide context to the settings described in the narratives. However, specific details like the exact date of Jesus' birth and the nature of the Star of Bethlehem remain subjects of scholarly debate. Some astronomers suggest that the star could have been a planetary conjunction or a comet, but definitive evidence is lacking. Despite these uncertainties, the convergence of historical, cultural, and textual analyses supports the plausibility of the Gospel accounts.
nt01.happened: Around 2,000 years ago, in the small town of Bethlehem in Judea, a remarkable event unfolded. Mary, a young woman engaged to Joseph, gave birth to a baby boy named Jesus. This birth was extraordinary because Mary was a virgin, and the child was conceived through the Holy Spirit. On the night of His birth, shepherds were tending their flocks nearby when an angel appeared to them, announcing the arrival of the Savior. A multitude of angels then filled the sky, praising God and proclaiming peace on earth. Guided by this heavenly message, the shepherds hurried to find the newborn lying in a manger. Sometime later, wise men from the East, often called Magi, observed a unique star in the sky. Interpreting it as a sign of a significant birth, they traveled to Jerusalem, seeking the newborn King of the Jews. King Herod, upon hearing this, felt threatened and inquired about the child's whereabouts. The Magi continued their journey, following the star to Bethlehem, where they found Jesus with Mary. They presented Him with gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed for their country by another route. Joseph, also warned in a dream, took Mary and Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod's decree to kill all male infants in Bethlehem. After Herod's death, the family returned and settled in Nazareth, fulfilling various prophecies about the Messiah.
nt01.scripture: The birth of Jesus is detailed in the New Testament. Matthew 1:18-2:12 describes Joseph's dream, the visit of the Magi, and the flight to Egypt. Luke 2:1-20 recounts the census, Jesus' birth in a manger, and the shepherds' visit. Prophecies about the Messiah's birth are found in the Old Testament, such as Isaiah 7:14, which speaks of a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, and Micah 5:2, predicting the ruler's birth in Bethlehem. These passages collectively affirm the fulfillment of God's promises through Jesus' birth.
nt01.background: At the time of Jesus' birth, Judea was under Roman rule, with King Herod the Great serving as a client king under the Roman Emperor Augustus. The region was a melting pot of cultures, with Jewish traditions deeply rooted in daily life. The Jewish people were anticipating the arrival of the Messiah, a prophesied leader who would deliver them. Bethlehem, a small town with historical significance as the City of David, was bustling due to a census decreed by Caesar Augustus, requiring individuals to return to their ancestral homes for registration. This decree led Joseph and Mary to travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Daily life was modest, with families engaged in agriculture, shepherding, and trade. Homes were simple, and hospitality was a valued virtue. The social and political climate was tense, with the Jewish population yearning for liberation from Roman oppression and the fulfillment of ancient prophecies.

nt02.talk: How do you feel knowing Jesus understands everything you go through and can help you?
nt02.child: Jesus loved us so much that He suffered and died, then came back to life again. Because He did this, we can be forgiven and live again too. We can always ask Jesus for help when we feel sad or have made a mistake.
nt02.learn: The atonement teaches us that no one is ever alone in their hardest moments. Jesus knows exactly how we feel, and He offers help and forgiveness, no matter what. Because of Him, there is always hope—things can change and hearts can heal. We can learn that forgiving others and ourselves is possible, and that even the worst days can become beginnings again because Jesus made it so. The atonement invites us to love more deeply and to remember how precious each person is to Heavenly Father.
nt02.matters: For families who follow Jesus, His atonement makes all the difference. Because He suffered everything for us and rose from the dead, we are promised that our own mistakes can be forgiven and that we will rise again as He did. It means families can be eternal, and even sad times can be mended. The atonement is a gift offered to all. It helps us feel hope when life is hard and teaches us how much Heavenly Father and Jesus love us. In moments when we make mistakes, feel sad, or are afraid, we can turn to Jesus and remember that He understands perfectly and will help us heal and move forward. This truth is at the very heart of the gospel and all God's work with His children.

sources.name: Jesus Christ’s Atonement Is Central to God’s Plan
The Death & Resurrection of Jesus Christ (Encyclopædia Britannica)
Archaeology and the Tomb of Jesus (Biblical Archaeology Society)
Tacitus and Josephus on Jesus (PBS Frontline)

nt02.evidence: Historians agree that Jesus of Nazareth lived, taught, and was crucified in Jerusalem, as accounts outside the Bible support this. There are references to Jesus’ death on a cross by Roman historians such as Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus. Archaeological discoveries have given us details about crucifixion, Jewish burial customs, and locations like Gethsemane and ancient tombs similar to what the Gospels describe. However, the resurrection itself is a matter of faith, not something history or science can confirm or deny directly. The written records from Jesus’ followers were shared soon after His death. These documents form the heart of the New Testament and have been carefully studied for centuries. While there is strong support for Jesus’ life and death as real events, the miracle of the resurrection is believed because of the faith and testimony of witnesses recorded in scripture and by personal spiritual experiences today.
nt02.happened: About two thousand years ago, in the city of Jerusalem, something happened that believers consider the most important event in the history of the world. Jesus Christ, who had taught and loved the people, went with His friends to a quiet garden called Gethsemane. There, He prayed to God the Father and felt all the pain, sadness, and mistakes of everyone who would ever live. This was beyond what we can imagine, but Jesus did it because He loves each person deeply. He accepted all the sorrow and sin so we can be forgiven. That night, Jesus was arrested by people who feared His teachings. He was taken to leaders who decided He should die. After a long night and day of questioning and suffering, Jesus was put on a wooden cross outside the city on a hill called Golgotha. He was treated cruelly and died there, giving His life willingly. His followers placed His body in a tomb cut out of rock. On the third day, the stone was rolled away, and Jesus rose from the dead. He was alive again, never to die. This means that because of Jesus, every person will one day live again, and everyone can be forgiven if they turn to Him. His atonement—suffering, death, and resurrection—is the center of the gospel and history.
nt02.scripture: The Bible tells the story of Jesus’ atonement in Matthew 26–28, Mark 14–16, Luke 22–24, and John 18–21. The Book of Mormon explains even more about why Jesus went through these things, especially in 2 Nephi 9 and Alma 7:11–13, where it says He suffered pains and sicknesses so He would know how to help us. Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 teaches in Jesus’ own words about His suffering in Gethsemane. All these scriptures show us that the atonement was for everyone, so we can return to live with Heavenly Father again if we come unto Christ.
nt02.background: Jerusalem at that time was the center of Jewish religious life under Roman rule. The people were waiting for a promised Savior, but most did not expect Jesus to be that person. Their lives were simple but busy, focused on families, worship at the temple, and working to provide. Roads were dusty, homes were small stone dwellings, and daily life involved preparing food, caring for animals, and following religious customs. The Roman government controlled much of what happened, collecting taxes and keeping peace by force. Many people felt the weight of strict laws and hoped for someone to save them from trouble. Into this world came Jesus, teaching love, forgiveness, and faith in God. His teachings were new for many, and His kindness drew crowds. Some leaders felt threatened by Him and looked for reasons to trap Him. The story of Jesus’ last days brings together the hopes, fears, and beliefs of many ordinary people in a remarkable way.

nt03.talk: How would you feel if Jesus came to visit your family today?
nt03.child: Jesus came to visit the Nephites after He was resurrected. He let everyone touch His hands and blessed each child one by one. Jesus loves everyone and wants to bless us too.
nt03.learn: From this story, we learn that Jesus knows each of us by name and wants to bless us personally. We also see that even after hard times or sadness, hope and light can return. The story encourages us to look for Christ’s hand in our lives and to treat all people as children of God, worthy of love and kindness. Families can find comfort in knowing Christ’s compassion for every child, everywhere.
nt03.matters: This event matters because it shows that Jesus Christ cares for all of God’s children, wherever they live. For families of faith, it teaches that God is present and loving, that Christ’s Atonement reaches everyone, and that extraordinary blessings can come after trials. For the world, the story invites us to see Christ as the Savior for all people, not just those in one part of the world. It reminds us that faith, hope, and personal experiences with God are possible for everyone.

sources.name: “Jesus Christ Visits the Americas,” Book of Mormon Stories, churchofjesuschrist.org
Book of Mormon: 3 Nephi 11-18, churchofjesuschrist.org
“Who are the Nephites?,” Church History Topics, churchofjesuschrist.org

nt03.evidence: There is no direct archaeological or historical evidence outside of the Book of Mormon to confirm the visit of Jesus Christ to the Americas. Scholars and archaeologists have studied ancient American civilizations, but no physical artifact or inscription has been found to directly support the Book of Mormon account. Some researchers believe there are similarities between ancient teachings about a great white god and the Christ story, but these are debated and not accepted as proof. For believers, the strongest evidence is the spiritual witness received through prayer and study of the Book of Mormon itself. Many view this as a matter of faith rather than scientific proof.
nt03.happened: According to the Book of Mormon, after Jesus Christ’s resurrection in Jerusalem, He appeared to a group of people in the ancient Americas called the Nephites. This happened at a place called Bountiful, likely in the region we now call the Americas, sometime around the year 34 AD. The Nephites had just passed through a great destruction and darkness that covered the land for days. As the people gathered, they heard a voice from heaven. Suddenly, Jesus Christ descended from the sky, clothed in white. The people were so surprised and full of wonder that at first they did not dare approach Him. Jesus spoke gently, inviting each person, one by one, to come forward and feel the wounds in His hands, feet, and side, so each could know for themselves that He was truly the risen Lord.
nt03.scripture: The main record of this event is found in the Book of Mormon, specifically 3 Nephi chapters 9 through 18. These chapters describe Christ’s visit, His teachings, and how He blessed each child personally. While the Bible does not mention Christ visiting the Americas, Peter taught in Acts 10:34 that God is “no respecter of persons.” Modern scripture, such as Doctrine and Covenants 10:51–53, refers to the Book of Mormon as a witness that Christ visited “other sheep.”
nt03.background: The Nephites were descendants of a family who left Jerusalem about 600 years earlier. They had built cities and societies in the Americas, trying to live their laws and teachings. Life was a mix of farming, building homes, making clothing, and worshipping God. Before Christ’s visit, the people had suffered great destruction because of their wickedness, but those who survived gathered at the temple in Bountiful. They had been taught to watch for signs of Christ’s death and resurrection, and now they longed for hope and peace.

nt04.talk: How do you think Paul felt when he was far from home, sharing something so important to him?
nt04.child: Paul traveled far and wide to tell people about Jesus. He wrote letters to his friends to help them stay strong in their faith. Because he shared the gospel, people all over the world came to know about Jesus.
nt04.learn: From Paul, we learn that when we are willing to listen to Heavenly Father and act with faith—even when it’s scary or hard—we can help His work move forward. Paul’s journeys remind us that one person can make a big difference when guided by the Spirit. His story also shows us that challenges will come, but Heavenly Father can turn even hard times into ways to help others and grow in faith. We can use the tools and opportunities we have today to bless others, just like Paul did long ago.
nt04.matters: Paul’s missionary journeys matter because they show how the gospel spread quickly all across the Mediterranean world. For families of faith, Paul’s story encourages us to share what we believe with others, even when it’s not easy. Paul used the technology of his day—Roman roads and ships—to help Heavenly Father’s work. It reminds us that the tools and inventions we have, like the internet or phones, can be blessings if we use them to do good and lift others. Paul’s courage and love for others teach us that faith can travel far and change lives, one heart at a time.

sources.name: Bible Odyssey: Paul the Apostle
Church of Jesus Christ: Paul’s Missionary Journeys
British Museum: Ephesus—A Church of Paul
Smithsonian: The Apostle Paul and His Letters

nt04.evidence: Historians agree that Paul was a real person and an important early Christian leader, though not all details of his journeys can be confirmed exactly. The Roman roads he traveled—many of which have been found by archaeologists—match the cities Paul visited according to the Acts of the Apostles.
