Ancient letters written by Paul, like Romans and Corinthians, are among the earliest Christian writings and are accepted by scholars as authentic. Archaeologists have discovered ancient synagogues, marketplaces, and homes in cities Paul visited, such as Ephesus and Corinth, helping us picture daily life. However, the specific routes and all events described in Acts still include some debated details, as records from that time are few.
nt04.happened: After the resurrection of Jesus Christ, a man named Paul, who was once called Saul, began a remarkable journey. Paul traveled all over the Roman Empire, starting around the year 45 AD. He wasn’t alone; sometimes he traveled with Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, and others. Paul journeyed across what is now Turkey, into Greece, and later to Rome itself. He walked on Roman roads, sailed across the Mediterranean, and visited cities large and small. In these places, he taught people about Jesus, started small groups of new believers called branches, and wrote letters to help them grow in faith. Paul faced many challenges. He was sometimes welcomed and sometimes thrown out of cities; he was even put in jail and shipwrecked more than once. Despite these hardships, Paul traveled about 10,000 miles. The letters he wrote—like those to the Romans and Corinthians—are still read and cherished as books in the New Testament. These writings helped early Christians and shape Christian faith today.
nt04.scripture: The Bible tells Paul’s story mainly in the book of Acts (chapters 13-28) and through Paul’s own letters, such as Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, and others. Doctrine and Covenants 18:28 hints that every disciple is called to share the gospel, just as Paul did. The scriptures teach that God prepares the way for His work (Isaiah 45:2; Doctrine and Covenants 84:88), which can help us see how Roman roads helped the gospel spread in Paul’s day. The Book of Mormon also teaches the importance of sharing the gospel in Mosiah 28:3.
nt04.background: The world Paul lived in was busy and connected. The Roman Empire stretched across much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. People traveled on well-built roads, spoke common languages like Greek or Latin, and traded goods from far-off lands. Many cities were crowded and full of different religions and beliefs. Before Paul became a Christian, he was a strict Pharisee named Saul, who even tried to stop Christians. But after a powerful spiritual experience on the road to Damascus, Paul changed completely and chose to teach others about Jesus Christ. Most people still lived simply—working as farmers, craftsmen, or traders—and families ate together in small homes. Life could be hard, but it was also a time of great learning and new ideas.

sd01.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to be kind and respectful to our parents?
sd01.child: A long time ago in China, a wise teacher named Confucius taught people to respect and listen to their parents. He said families work best when they love and honor each other. This idea helps families everywhere feel safe and happy.
sd01.learn: We can learn from Confucius that loving and respecting our parents is a key to building a peaceful home and a strong society. Family lessons are some of the most important things we carry through life. By making our homes places where everyone feels loved and listened to, we live up to what both prophets and wise teachers have taught, showing that Heavenly Father’s truth is the same across time and cultures.
sd01.matters: Confucius’ teaching shapes how over a billion people today think about family and loyalty. For families of faith, it’s a powerful reminder that Heavenly Father placed the truth about loving and honoring parents deep in many hearts and cultures. These teachings draw families closer, forming a strong base for kindness, patience, and wisdom. For Latter-day Saints, it connects beautifully with the Fifth Commandment, the Family Proclamation, and the promise in Malachi that the hearts of children would turn to their fathers. We see that Heavenly Father’s love is not limited to one place—He has carefully taught His children about the gift of family, wherever they live.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Confucius
BBC – Religion: Confucianism
The Analects of Confucius – World History Encyclopedia
Church of Jesus Christ – The Family: A Proclamation to the World

sd01.evidence: Historians agree that Confucius lived and taught in 6th-century BC China. His words were gathered by followers in a collection called the Analects, compiled after his death and studied for generations. Ancient Chinese records and archaeological finds support the practices of honoring ancestors and elders in that era. While daily family life from so long ago is hard to reconstruct in detail, the importance given to family ties and respect for parents in early Chinese society is well-attested. Though some stories may be shaped by legend, the main ideas Confucius taught are confirmed by historical texts and have clearly influenced how families are valued in East Asia today.
sd01.happened: In the year 551 BC, in what is now eastern China, a wise teacher named Confucius was born. As he grew, Confucius noticed many troubles in his land: leaders argued, families quarreled, and people seemed to forget what was truly good. Seeing this, Confucius began to teach that the very heart of a strong society is the family. He shared the concept of 'filial piety,' which means showing deep respect, honor, and care for one’s parents and ancestors. To him, honoring your father and mother was not just a family rule, but the very foundation of all other virtues. Confucius believed that when children respect their parents, they learn how to respect others, trust leaders, and care for friends. His teachings quickly spread, shaping homes and communities far beyond his own home. People listened, wrote down his lessons, and taught them to their children. For thousands of years since, many across East Asia have built their families and lives on these principles, making Confucius one of history’s most influential teachers.
sd01.scripture: The Bible teaches in Exodus 20:12, 'Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land.' Paul repeats this in Ephesians 6:1-3, saying that honoring parents is the first commandment with promise. The Book of Mormon often shows families teaching and supporting each other (see Mosiah 4:14–15). In 'The Family: A Proclamation to the World,' Latter-day Saints are reminded that “the family is ordained of God.” Malachi 4:6 prophesies that the hearts of children will turn to their fathers, a truth that reaches across many cultures, including Confucius’ teachings.
sd01.background: Confucius lived in a time called the Spring and Autumn period, around 2,500 years ago. China was then split into many small states that often fought each other. Families worked hard just to get by, usually farming the land with simple tools, and most lived with parents, grandparents, and children together. Stories and lessons were passed down from elders, and respect for those older than you was a way of life. Before Confucius, people already honored ancestors, but rulers often put their own power above family bonds. Confucius watched leaders make selfish choices and saw how families lost trust in leaders and each other. He wanted to help people find peace by returning to good, loving homes as the center of society. His lessons did not focus on gods or rituals but on how people should treat each other every day, especially within the home.

sd02.talk: Can you think of a time when you chose to be kind to someone, even if it was hard?
sd02.child: A long time ago in India, a man named Buddha taught people to be kind to everyone and to help others when they are sad. He said that showing compassion is one of the most important things we can do. Many people even far away learned from his gentle teachings.
sd02.learn: Buddha’s example reminds us that when we notice others’ suffering and act with real kindness, we grow closer to truths Heavenly Father wants all His children to know. We can learn to look beyond differences in background or belief, seeing each person as a beloved child of God. Seeking peace and comforting those who suffer is a way of serving the Lord, and it prepares our hearts to receive even greater truths about His love.
sd02.matters: Buddha’s teachings still matter today because they remind us that kindness is powerful and that being gentle with others is a strength, not a weakness. His teachings on compassion challenge families everywhere to think about how they treat every person, teaching mercy even when it is hard. For families of faith, the Lord asks us to show mercy and love, just as He does. When we see Heavenly Father’s hand helping people on different paths to seek goodness and truth, we see that He has been reaching out to all His children, everywhere, across all times.

sources.name: BBC - Religion: Buddhism
Metropolitan Museum of Art - Buddha and Buddhist Art
Britannica - Buddhism
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - Charity: The Pure Love of Christ

sd02.evidence: Most historians agree that the Buddha was a real person who lived and taught in northern India around the 6th century BCE. The earliest written records of his life and teachings come from centuries after his death, based on oral traditions passed from disciple to disciple. Archaeological discoveries, such as ancient monasteries and early Buddhist symbols dating back to the 3rd century BCE, show the wide early spread of his teachings. While some details of his life story are shaped by legend, there is strong evidence that a wise teacher known as the Buddha did exist and shaped world history deeply, particularly in South and East Asia.
sd02.happened: Around the year 563 BCE, a prince named Siddhartha Gautama was born near what is now the border of Nepal and India. From a young age, Siddhartha lived a sheltered life of comfort, but he grew troubled when he saw people suffering. Wanting to understand why pain and hardship existed, he left his royal life behind to search for answers. After years of seeking, he meditated deeply under a tree and found enlightenment, realizing truths about suffering, kindness, and the nature of life. He became known as the Buddha, meaning 'the awakened one.' The Buddha traveled across northeastern India, teaching that every living being deserves compassion and that everyone can find peace by living wisely and kindly. His message was gentle: suffering comes, but it can be healed by changing our hearts. This teaching, centered on mercy and deep care for all life, would spread far beyond India over centuries, reaching millions across Asia and eventually the world.
sd02.scripture: The Savior teaches, 'Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful' (Luke 6:36). The Book of Mormon adds, 'if ye have not charity, ye are nothing' (Moroni 7:46). Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 teaches that we should influence others 'by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' The principle of compassion—looking on others with love and mercy—is consistent across scripture and is one of the highest callings Heavenly Father gives His children.
sd02.background: The world into which Siddhartha Gautama was born was shaped by ancient kingdoms, traders, and spiritual traditions. People farmed rice and wheat, tended livestock, and lived in villages or growing cities. Religion played a central part in daily life. Long before the Buddha’s time, many in northern India followed the teachings found in the Vedas, practicing rituals and honoring a variety of gods. Caste divisions separated society into strict classes. Most did not question these customs, believing them to be unchangeable. But some thinkers and seekers were beginning to look for deeper meaning and a better way to live, feeling unsettled by the suffering all around them. Into this world of searching and tradition, the Buddha brought a new idea: that anyone, regardless of birth or class, could live with kindness and wisdom, and that every life mattered.

sd03.talk: What is something in nature that makes you feel grateful to Heavenly Father?
sd03.child: Long ago in Japan, people believed Heavenly Father’s love could be seen in nature. They washed their hands and hearts to stay clean and said thank you for every good thing they had. These ideas helped Japanese people welcome the gospel when it came.
sd03.learn: From the seeds of Shinto, we can learn to notice and thank Heavenly Father for every good thing around us—even the smallest blessings. Keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean is not just about health, but also about honoring our bodies and homes as gifts from God. Shinto’s gentle attention to nature invites us to look for the divine in the world, treating each other and the earth with care and kindness, as Christ taught us to do.
sd03.matters: This matters because Shinto shaped how people in Japan view the world—not only long ago, but even today. Shinto’s focus on gratitude, purity, and reverence for the earth agrees with gospel teachings about honoring Heavenly Father’s gifts and caring for our families. When Latter-day Saint missionaries arrived in Japan, they found many people already practiced these virtues, making the gospel familiar and welcome in important ways. For families of faith, remembering Shinto’s seeds can help us see how Heavenly Father works with many cultures, preparing hearts and shaping traditions so His goodness can reach every corner of the earth.

sources.name: British Museum: Shinto
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Shinto and Nature in Japanese Art
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Gospel Topics - Gratitude

sd03.evidence: Historians agree that Shinto’s beginnings date back to ancient times, but because it grew up before written history, we rely on archaeology and early written records to understand it. By the 8th century, Japanese texts such as the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki were written to record myths and practices already long established. Archaeological finds, like old shrines and ritual objects, show that people honored nature and practiced cleansing rites thousands of years ago. Shinto has shaped Japanese culture for centuries, and its values—especially respect for purity and the natural world—continue to be visible in modern Japanese society. Although the exact details of earliest beliefs are debated, the importance of gratitude, purity, and harmony with creation is strongly supported by both tradition and evidence.
sd03.happened: In the earliest days of Japan, before written records began, families and small villages looked out onto misty mountains, deep forests, and rushing rivers, and felt awe. They believed all around them were kami, or divine spirits, living not just above but within rocks, trees, water, and the wind. Out of this reverence for nature and its gifts grew what is now called Shinto, which means “the way of the gods.” People honored the kami in quiet ceremonies, offering prayers, food, and music to show their gratitude for the earth’s provision and to seek harmony with each other and with nature. Purity was essential, as families believed that spiritual impurity could bring misfortune. Rituals to cleanse hands, faces, and even hearts—often performed at rivers or special shrines—became part of daily life. These customs didn’t set rules for everyone in the same way but grew gently out of care for the blessings Heavenly Father put all around them, helping neighbors and families to live thankfully and in peace. Over centuries, these seeds of gratitude, reverence, and purity shaped much of Japanese life, and their influence can still be seen today.
sd03.scripture: The scriptures teach that the earth was created by God as a gift for His children (Genesis 1:1, Doctrine and Covenants 59:16–20). We are taught to receive these gifts with gratitude and use them wisely. The Book of Mormon reminds us often to give thanks in all things (Mosiah 2:20–21; Alma 34:38), and the Lord asks us to be pure in heart and action (Matthew 5:8). While Shinto is not mentioned by name, its gratitude, cleanliness, and reverence for creation echo these scriptural principles.
sd03.background: Long before Japan became one country, it was home to many clans and small villages, each caring for their families, their rice fields, and their traditions. Most people lived close to the land, growing rice, fishing, and gathering what they needed from forests or the ocean. The world was seen as full of mystery, and the changing seasons were both beautiful and sometimes harsh. There were no large temples at first—only simple shrines made of wood, sometimes by sacred trees or near springs. Families shared stories, valued cleanliness and order, and believed with deep respect that nature and the family were holy. There was little contact with the outside world, and writing would not arrive until centuries later through China. In this gentle, green, misty world, the roots of Shinto grew quietly across the islands.

sd04.talk: What do you think it means that people in other lands learned about the soul and right choices, just like we do?
sd04.child: Long ago in India, people taught that every person has a special soul and that what we do matters forever. They believed in caring about right and wrong, just like we do. God wanted everyone to learn about kindness and truth.
sd04.learn: We can learn that God’s light reaches every nation, and that sincere questions about the soul and justice can lead people to important truths. Studying how others have sought and understood God helps us recognize what we share with them and deepens our gratitude for living truth. The story of Hindu thought reminds us to look for eternal values in ourselves and in others, even when we seem very different.
sd04.matters: The core Hindu beliefs about the soul, justice, and duty remind us that God has helped all His children, wherever they live, learn important truths over time. For families of faith, it is meaningful to see how ancient people sought and found light. Their teachings about the eternal soul and the effects of our choices help us understand that God's truths can be found across the world. This also prepares hearts to recognize gospel principles like eternal life, the law of justice, and the duty to serve, showing that God loves and teaches all His children.

sources.name: BBC Bitesize: Hindu Beliefs
Encyclopedia Britannica: Hinduism
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Early Hinduism

sd04.evidence: There is strong historical and archaeological evidence for early Indian civilization and its rich spiritual life. The Vedas, composed in Sanskrit around 1500–500 BCE, are some of the oldest religious texts still used today and contain hymns, rituals, and discussions of philosophy. Archaeological sites like those of the Indus Valley Civilization show a highly organized society before and during the early Vedic period. Scholars agree that over many generations, the ideas of Brahman, atman, karma, and dharma developed and were gathered into the sacred texts of Hinduism. While details of personal religious life from so long ago are sometimes debated, the existence and importance of these beliefs are well established by the evidence.
sd04.happened: Around 1500 years before Jesus lived on earth, in the vast and diverse land of India, early Hindu people taught and wrote about deep spiritual ideas. Although many gods and goddesses were worshipped in Hinduism, their thinkers spoke of Brahman, one unchanging, supreme reality that is the source of everything. They believed that every person has an atman, or soul, that is eternal and truly part of this one great reality. The laws of karma meant that everything a person did, good or bad, would have effects, and the idea of dharma guided people to live with righteousness, kindness, and duty to others. These teachings were written in ancient texts called the Vedas and Upanishads, which became the foundation of Hindu philosophy. These ideas encouraged people to look beyond the visible world and to live thoughtfully, understanding that every action has consequences and that everyone is part of something eternally good and real.
sd04.scripture: In the Bible, Ecclesiastes 12:7 speaks of the spirit returning to God who gave it, echoing the idea of an eternal soul. Doctrine and Covenants 93:29 teaches that "man was also in the beginning with God," and that intelligence or the light of truth cannot be created or made. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 42:15-23 explains the law of justice and mercy, showing how choices have eternal consequences. While not about Hinduism directly, these scriptures affirm that the soul is eternal and that justice and duty are part of God's eternal plan.
sd04.background: India during this time was home to many small kingdoms and farming villages. Families worked together to grow crops or care for animals. Life was closely tied to nature, the cycles of the seasons, and strong family traditions. The people gathered around fires, shared stories of gods and heroes, and honored the sacred rivers and mountains. Over generations, spiritual seekers in India asked deep questions: What is the purpose of life? What happens after death? How should we treat each other? The answers they found became the heart of the Hindu faith and influenced how millions of people lived, prayed, and cared for their families.

sd05.talk: Why do you think it's important to choose good thoughts, words, and actions every day?
sd05.child: Long ago, a man named Zoroaster taught that we should always choose to do good things, think good thoughts, and say kind words. He believed that by doing this, we help the world become a better place.
sd05.learn: Zoroaster's teachings remind us of the importance of making conscious choices between good and evil in our daily lives. They highlight the belief that our actions, thoughts, and words have significant consequences, not only for ourselves but for the world around us. This understanding encourages us to strive for righteousness and truth, knowing that our choices contribute to the greater cosmic battle between light and darkness.
sd05.matters: Zoroaster's teachings have had a lasting impact on religious thought. The concepts of a cosmic struggle between good and evil, the importance of personal choice in moral matters, and the promise of resurrection and final judgment have influenced other major religions, including Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. For families of faith, understanding Zoroastrianism can provide insight into the shared themes and values that connect different religious traditions, emphasizing the universal importance of choosing righteousness and truth.

sources.name: Zoroastrianism | HISTORY
Zoroaster - Wikipedia
Zoroastrianism - Wikipedia

sd05.evidence: Historical and archaeological evidence about Zoroaster's life is limited, and scholars debate the exact time and place of his existence. Some suggest he lived around 600 B.C., while others propose earlier dates. The primary sources of information are the Gathas, hymns attributed to Zoroaster, found within the Avesta, the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism. These writings provide insights into his teachings and the religious practices of his followers. Additionally, archaeological findings, such as fire temples in Iran, offer glimpses into the rituals and structures associated with Zoroastrian worship.
sd05.happened: Around 600 B.C., a man named Zoroaster, also known as Zarathustra, introduced a new way of understanding the world in ancient Persia, which is now Iran. He taught that life is a constant battle between Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord of light and truth, and Angra Mainyu, the spirit of darkness and lies. Zoroaster encouraged people to choose good thoughts, good words, and good deeds to support Ahura Mazda. He also spoke of a future time when the righteous would be resurrected, and good would triumph over evil. His teachings laid the foundation for Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest monotheistic religions.
sd05.scripture: The Book of Mormon teaches about the importance of choosing between good and evil. In 2 Nephi 2:27, it states, "Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man. And they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death." This aligns with Zoroaster's emphasis on the individual's choice between supporting Ahura Mazda or Angra Mainyu.
sd05.background: Before Zoroaster's time, the people of Persia practiced a polytheistic religion, worshiping many gods. Daily life was centered around agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade. The society was organized into tribes, and their beliefs were deeply connected to nature and the elements. Zoroaster's teachings introduced a shift towards monotheism, emphasizing the worship of a single, supreme god, Ahura Mazda, and the moral responsibility of individuals to choose between good and evil.

sd06.talk: Why do you think people want to know what happens after we die?
sd06.child: Long ago, Egyptians believed that after you die, your heart was weighed to see if you had been good and honest. If your heart was light, you could live again and be happy forever. They wanted to be good so they could have a wonderful life after this one.
sd06.learn: From Ancient Egypt, we learn that Heavenly Father has let many peoples search for and remember truths about eternal life. Searching for what is good, honest, and true is something many families have done throughout time. This helps us value our own beliefs about life after death and encourages us to be kind and good, because our choices matter—both now and forever.
sd06.matters: Understanding how Ancient Egyptians cared so deeply about life after death helps us see that questions about what comes next are ancient and universal. For families of faith, it shows that important truths about resurrection and judgment can be found across different peoples and times. These ideas help us teach children that God’s truths are planted everywhere, even in distant lands and old stories, and that seeking to live well is a message that stretches back thousands of years.

sources.name: The British Museum - Ancient Egyptian Beliefs in the Afterlife
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Ancient Egyptian Religion
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - Resurrection

sd06.evidence: Many tombs, like the pyramids and the Valley of the Kings, hold wall paintings and texts that describe the journey of the soul and judgment before the gods. The Book of the Dead, a series of ancient Egyptian instructions, has been found in many graves and spells out the trial of the heart and the idea of life after death. Archaeologists have carefully studied mummies and tomb carvings, showing this belief shaped art, writing, and daily life. These discoveries help us understand their faith and lives in real detail, though what each person personally believed may have been different. This evidence is widely accepted by historians and museum experts.
sd06.happened: Around 2000 BC in Ancient Egypt, people believed deeply in life after death. They thought that when someone died, their soul started a long journey to the next world. Egyptians pictured a place called the Hall of Judgment, where the soul’s heart would be weighed against a feather belonging to the goddess Ma’at, who stood for truth and justice. If a person’s heart was light, meaning they had lived a good and honest life, they could pass on to a happy afterlife. If not, their soul faced sadness or even destruction. Egyptians also believed that one day, the body would be restored and the soul would live again, so they carefully preserved bodies through mummification. Even their burial tombs and treasures were meant to help souls live well after death. These beliefs shaped everyday actions because Egyptians thought how they lived would matter forever.
sd06.scripture: The principles of resurrection and judgment are taught throughout scripture. In the New Testament, Paul explains, “As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). The Book of Mormon also promises a resurrection: “The spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form” (Alma 11:43-44). Abraham himself, who visited Egypt, was taught about eternal truths (Abraham 1). These scriptures affirm that God’s plan includes judgment and resurrection, echoing some of the hopes seen long ago in Egypt.
sd06.background: Ancient Egypt was one of the world’s earliest great civilizations, rising along the Nile River in North Africa. By 2000 BC, powerful pharaohs ruled over cities, farms, and temples. Most Egyptians worked as farmers or craftspeople and lived in small, mud-brick homes. The world around them was full of change, but Egypt’s rich soil allowed for plenty of food, giving people time for building, learning, and religion. Religion touched all parts of life; Egyptians honored many gods and told stories about the afterlife to help them deal with death and hope for peace after this life. Their ideas about the soul and resurrection became a central part of their culture.

sd07.t: African Traditional: God the Creator Father
sd07.talk: Can you think of different names people use for God around the world?
sd07.child: Long ago, many African people believed in one great Creator who made everything. They called Him names like 'Father' or 'Great One.' Even though they thought He was far away, they felt close to Him through their ancestors and spirits.
sd07.learn: This historical perspective teaches us that the knowledge of a Supreme Creator is a common thread woven through diverse cultures. It reminds us of the innate human desire to connect with the divine and understand our place in the universe. Recognizing these shared beliefs can foster greater respect and appreciation for different cultural expressions of faith. It also encourages us to seek common ground in our spiritual journeys, acknowledging that while practices may differ, the fundamental yearning to connect with a higher power unites us all.
sd07.matters: The widespread belief in a Supreme Creator God across various African cultures highlights a universal human inclination to seek understanding of life's origins and moral order. For families of faith, this shared recognition of a singular, benevolent Creator underscores the idea that knowledge of God has been present among all peoples throughout history. It suggests that divine truths can be found in diverse cultural expressions, reflecting a common spiritual heritage. This understanding fosters respect for different traditions and emphasizes the importance of seeking harmony and connection with the divine in various forms.

sources.name: African Traditional Religions: Beliefs and Practice
African Traditional Religions
God, divinities and spirits in African traditional religious ontology
African Traditional Religions

sd07.evidence: Anthropological and ethnographic studies have documented the consistent belief in a Supreme Creator among various African societies. For example, the Yoruba people worship Olodumare as the ultimate creator, while the Akan people honor Nyame in a similar role. These findings are supported by oral traditions, rituals, and cultural practices that have been passed down through generations. The prevalence of this belief across diverse and geographically separated communities suggests a deep-rooted and widespread recognition of a singular Creator. While the specifics of worship and the names attributed to the Supreme Being vary, the underlying concept remains remarkably consistent, indicating a shared spiritual understanding among these cultures.
sd07.happened: Around 900 BCE, numerous African societies held a shared belief in a supreme Creator God, often referred to by names signifying 'Father' or 'Great One.' This deity was viewed as the ultimate source of life and moral authority. For instance, the Yoruba people of present-day Nigeria called this god Olodumare, while the Akan of Ghana referred to him as Nyame. These cultures believed that the Supreme Being created the universe and established the natural order. Although considered distant and not directly involved in daily human affairs, this god was revered as the foundation of existence. To bridge the gap between the Supreme Being and humanity, people honored lesser deities and ancestral spirits, who acted as intermediaries. These spirits were believed to influence various aspects of life, such as health, fertility, and community well-being. Rituals, offerings, and prayers were directed toward these intermediaries to seek guidance and favor, reflecting a deeply spiritual worldview that emphasized harmony between the physical and spiritual realms.
sd07.scripture: The scriptures affirm the existence of a singular, supreme Creator. In the Bible, Genesis 1:1 states, 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.' Similarly, the Book of Mormon declares, 'Behold, I am Jesus Christ. I created the heavens and the earth...' (3 Nephi 9:15). These passages align with the African traditional belief in a Supreme Being as the originator of all things. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:41 teaches that God 'is in all things, and is through all things, and is round about all things,' emphasizing His omnipresence and sustaining power, concepts resonant with African views of a pervasive Creator.
sd07.background: In the centuries leading up to 900 BCE, sub-Saharan Africa was home to diverse communities with rich cultural traditions. These societies were primarily agrarian, relying on farming, hunting, and gathering for sustenance. Social structures were often organized around extended families and clans, with elders holding significant authority. Oral traditions played a crucial role in preserving history, laws, and spiritual beliefs. The environment, with its vast savannas, dense forests, and mighty rivers, deeply influenced daily life and spiritual practices. Natural phenomena were often attributed to the actions of spiritual beings, leading to rituals aimed at ensuring favorable conditions for agriculture and communal prosperity.

sd08.t: Greek Philosophy: The Logos and Divine Reason
sd08.talk: Why do you think it matters that people everywhere have learned about Jesus, even when they speak and think differently?
sd08.child: Long ago, Greek thinkers wondered if a wise guide—a kind of invisible rule—helped keep the whole world in order. Later, the Bible used their word for this, Logos, to teach about Jesus and His power. Heavenly Father can use smart ideas from anywhere to teach us important truths.
sd08.learn: We can learn that ideas and cultures from long ago can become important tools in God’s hands, even if they seem far from our faith at first. Truth can be found in many places, and Heavenly Father can use all kinds of knowledge to prepare the world for His purposes. Studying history helps us appreciate how God prepares people and languages for His gospel to be understood everywhere.
sd08.matters: The idea of the Logos helped prepare people’s minds for the message of Jesus Christ. When Christian apostles and writers came along, they used words and ideas from Greek philosophy, like Logos, to help explain Jesus Christ’s divinity to people who spoke Greek and thought in these terms. For families of faith, this shows how Heavenly Father can use tools from anywhere—even philosophy and language—to help His gospel reach people’s hearts. Understanding ancient ideas like the Logos can help us see how God prepares the world for important moments, like the coming of Christ.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Heraclitus
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Logos
PBS: The Greeks—Words and Deeds
Church of Jesus Christ Study Helps: John 1

sd08.evidence: Many ancient sources, like the writings of Heraclitus, Plato, and later Stoics, help us know what Greeks thought about the Logos and the Forms. Original texts from Plato, such as 'The Republic' and 'Phaedo,' are still studied today. Modern archaeological finds, such as inscriptions and very old manuscripts, confirm these philosophers' teachings were discussed in real Greek cities around 500 BC. The spread of Greek culture and language across the Mediterranean, especially after Alexander the Great’s conquests, further amplified these ideas. Scholars agree that Greek philosophical concepts directly influenced early Christian writings, especially in how they described Christ and His divine nature.
sd08.happened: Around 500 years before Jesus was born, Greek thinkers began asking deep questions about the world around them. Among these thinkers were philosophers like Heraclitus, Plato, and Stoics, who all discussed something called the 'Logos.' Logos is a Greek word that means 'word,' 'reason,' or 'order.' These Greeks taught that there was a guiding principle of reason in the universe—a force that makes sense of what we see and keeps everything ordered. Plato, a famous philosopher, also taught that beyond the things we see—like trees, rocks, and people—there are perfect, unchanging ideals called Forms, like perfect truth, beauty, and goodness. He believed these Forms were more real than anything in the world and that our souls could know them. As time went on, these ideas became very important in Greek culture and helped set the stage for new ways of thinking about life, God, and the world.
sd08.scripture: The Gospel of John begins, 'In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). This passage uses the Greek term Logos to name Jesus Christ as the divine, guiding force in creation. Modern scripture teaches that God is a God of order (Doctrine and Covenants 88:34–40), and His creations are governed by laws and reason. These ideas echo the ancient Greek search for order and truth beyond what we can see.
sd08.background: At this time, Greece was not a single country but a collection of city-states like Athens, Sparta, and Corinth, spread around the Mediterranean Sea. People lived in small towns with lively markets and spent time discussing big questions in public spaces. Religion was a part of daily life, but the Greeks also loved to debate and wonder about the gods, nature, and the meaning of life. Travel and trade brought them into contact with other cultures, sharing ideas and goods. Before the great philosophers, stories about gods explained almost everything, but now, some Greeks wanted logical answers, using their minds to understand the world instead of just relying on old myths.

sd09.talk: How can we show that everyone is our brother or sister, no matter where they come from?
sd09.child: A long time ago, some people called Stoics taught that being good is what really matters. They believed everyone is important and should be treated like family. Their ideas helped people understand the gospel of Jesus when it was shared later.
sd09.learn: We learn that honest and kind ideas can prepare people’s hearts for greater truth that comes later. Stoicism teaches that everyone is worthy of respect because we all share something deep within. It reminds us to look for truth wherever it is found, and to treat everyone as brothers and sisters, even if they seem different from us. Like the Stoics, we can try to live with courage and kindness each day.
sd09.matters: The Stoic teaching that everyone shares the same inner worth helped prepare people to hear the gospel that Paul and other apostles shared years later. When Paul wrote that in Christ ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free’ (Galatians 3:28), he was sharing radical good news in words people could understand. For families who believe each person is a child of Heavenly Father, this story shows that truth can be prepared across cultures and centuries. Stoicism’s sense of brotherhood and personal virtue helped make the world ready to hear the idea that all are equal before God and deserve kindness.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
BBC History: The ancient philosophy of Stoicism
ChurchofJesusChrist.org: All Are Alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33)

sd09.evidence: We know about Stoicism from many surviving writings by Stoic teachers like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. Ancient histories and Roman letters mention public lectures and discussions of Stoicism in Rome and other cities from the second century BCE onward. Evidence from ancient inscriptions and documents shows that Roman society began to use Stoic ideas to discuss law and fairness, though the world was still far from equal. Modern historians see the influence of Stoic vocabulary and ideas in early Christian writings, including Paul’s letters, showing that these ancient teachings were well known and discussed at the time. Archaeologists have found statues and household items featuring Stoic maxims, showing how widely respected the school was.
sd09.happened: Around 100 years before Jesus was born, the Stoic philosophers were teaching in Rome and throughout the Mediterranean. Their main idea was that virtue, or good character, was the only thing that truly mattered and could make someone happy. To the Stoics, things like wealth, health, or honor were not real goods; they could come and go, but virtue stays with you always. One of their most surprising ideas for their time was that all human beings, not just Romans or Greeks, share a common rational nature—meaning everyone can think, choose, and do good. This meant everyone was like a brother or sister, no matter where they were born, what language they spoke, or if they were free or enslaved. The Stoics believed that external troubles like sickness, poverty, or other people's actions can't take away your inner peace if you live by reason and try to be good. They often gathered in public places, like porches (‘stoa’ in Greek), to teach and discuss these ideas, inviting anyone to listen. Their teachings made such an impact that even people who weren't philosophers picked up the ideas in their daily lives, and later Christian teachers like Paul would use similar words to explain the gospel.
sd09.scripture: Paul’s letters reflect Stoic ideas when he says that nothing can separate us from God’s love (Romans 8:38-39), and when he teaches about spiritual gifts given to everyone (1 Corinthians 12). The Book of Mormon teaches that God ‘inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female’ (2 Nephi 26:33). While Stoicism is not scripture, its principle—that each person has value and should be treated as a brother or sister—echoes plainly in these sacred texts.
sd09.background: By the time Stoicism was spreading, Rome ruled much of the known world. People in the Roman Empire spoke many languages and came from different cultures. The city of Rome was crowded and busy, with senators, merchants, soldiers, slaves, and freedmen from many nations. Most people believed some were born better than others, and slavery was very common: slaves were often seen as property, not people. Earlier, Greek philosophers had searched for wisdom about how to live well, but few had said that everyone was truly equal. Stoic teachers took ideas from thinkers before them and brought them to the heart of Roman life, making them something “for everyone,” not just a few scholars. Ordinary people might not have become Stoics, but they could hear and share the Stoic ideals. Their attitude towards others—slaves, women, foreigners—was more respectful than was usual at the time, even if not every Stoic lived up to their own teachings.

sd10.talk: How can we show respect for the world Heavenly Father created for us?
sd10.child: Long ago, people in places like Ireland and Scotland believed that the world around them was very special and close to heaven. They thought that trees, rivers, and mountains were gifts from God and should be treated with care. They also believed that being kind and welcoming to others was very important.
sd10.learn: From Celtic Christianity, we learn the importance of seeing the divine in the world around us. Recognizing the sacredness of creation can inspire us to be better stewards of the environment and to appreciate the beauty and wonder of nature. It also teaches us the value of community and hospitality, encouraging us to build strong, supportive relationships with others and to serve those in need.
sd10.matters: Celtic Christianity's emphasis on the sacredness of creation offers a perspective that aligns with the gospel's teachings about the earth as a divine gift. This tradition reminds us to see the world around us as a reflection of God's handiwork and to treat it with respect and care. For families of faith, embracing this view can deepen our appreciation for nature and encourage us to be stewards of the environment. It also highlights the importance of community and hospitality, values that strengthen family bonds and foster a sense of belonging and service to others.

sources.name: Celtic Christianity
Ancient Celtic religion
Celtic Animism

sd10.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide insights into Celtic Christianity. Writings from the early medieval period, such as the works of Saint Patrick and Saint Columba, reveal a faith deeply connected to nature and community. Artifacts like the intricately decorated Celtic crosses and illuminated manuscripts, such as the Book of Kells, reflect a fusion of Christian symbolism with traditional Celtic art, emphasizing the sacredness of creation. These sources collectively illustrate a tradition that honored both the Creator and His creation.
sd10.happened: In the early 5th century, as the Roman Empire's influence waned in the British Isles, a distinctive form of Christianity emerged among the Celtic peoples of Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and Brittany. This tradition, known as Celtic Christianity, integrated Christian teachings with the Celts' deep reverence for nature. They viewed creation as sacred, believing that the divine permeated the natural world, making every place a 'thin place' where heaven and earth were closely connected. This perspective led them to see every person as bearing the image of God, and they considered creation itself a form of revelation. Community and hospitality were central to their faith, reflecting their belief in the interconnectedness of all life. Monastic communities flourished, with figures like Saint Patrick in Ireland and Saint Columba in Scotland leading missionary efforts that preserved and spread Christianity during a time of significant upheaval.
sd10.scripture: The scriptures teach that the earth and all things in it were created by God and are good. In Genesis 1:31, it states, 'And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.' The Doctrine and Covenants also emphasizes the sacredness of creation, instructing us to 'behold the glory of the Lord, and the riches of eternity' in the things He has made (D&C 88:47). These passages encourage us to recognize the divine in the natural world and to treat it with reverence.
sd10.background: Before the arrival of Christianity, the Celtic peoples practiced a polytheistic religion deeply intertwined with nature. They believed that spirits inhabited natural features like rivers, mountains, and trees, and they held rituals to honor these spirits. Daily life was closely connected to the land, with communities relying on agriculture and livestock. The transition to Christianity began in the 4th and 5th centuries, as missionaries introduced the new faith. Rather than completely abandoning their previous beliefs, the Celts integrated Christian teachings with their existing reverence for nature, leading to a unique expression of Christianity that honored both the Creator and His creation.

sd11.talk: Why do you think people from different places have stories about gods who come to visit them?
sd11.child: Long ago, people in places like Mexico and Guatemala believed in a special god called the Feathered Serpent. This god was part bird and part snake, showing how the sky and earth are connected. They built big temples to honor him, and during certain times of the year, shadows would make it look like a snake was moving down the temple steps.
sd11.learn: The story of the Feathered Serpent teaches us about the deep spiritual connections ancient cultures sought with the divine. It reminds us that across different societies, there is a common yearning to understand our origins and purpose. Recognizing these shared narratives can foster greater appreciation for the diverse ways humanity seeks and experiences the divine.
sd11.matters: The enduring presence of the Feathered Serpent across Mesoamerican cultures highlights a shared spiritual framework and the importance of deities that bridge the earthly and the divine. For families of faith, this underscores the universal human desire to understand and connect with higher powers. The narratives of a divine figure arriving from the east and promising to return resonate with themes of prophecy and fulfillment found in various religious traditions, including Christianity. Such parallels invite reflection on the ways different cultures perceive and anticipate divine intervention.

sources.name: Kukulkan - World History Encyclopedia
Kukulkan: The Legend of the Feathered Serpent | Mayan.org
Kukulkan - Mesoamerican Pantheon Deity | Mythos Atlas

sd11.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as the Temple of the Feathered Serpent in Teotihuacan and the Temple of Kukulkan in Chichen Itza, provide tangible evidence of the widespread veneration of this deity. Iconography depicting a feathered serpent appears in various artifacts, murals, and sculptures across Mesoamerica, indicating its significance. Historical records from Spanish chroniclers and indigenous codices also reference the Feathered Serpent, though interpretations vary. Some scholars suggest that the legends of a light-skinned deity arriving from the east may have been influenced by post-conquest narratives, making it challenging to separate pre-Columbian beliefs from later interpretations.
sd11.happened: In ancient Mesoamerica, the Feathered Serpent, known as Quetzalcoatl to the Aztecs and Kukulkan to the Maya, was a revered deity symbolizing the union of earth and sky. This god was associated with creation, wind, rain, and the morning star. The earliest depictions of the Feathered Serpent appear in Teotihuacan around 200 AD, but the concept likely originated earlier with the Olmec civilization. Over time, the worship of this deity spread across various cultures, including the Maya and Aztecs. In Maya tradition, Kukulkan was both a god and a cultural hero who brought knowledge and civilization. The Temple of Kukulkan at Chichen Itza is a testament to his significance, where during the equinoxes, a shadow resembling a serpent descends the pyramid's staircase, symbolizing the god's arrival. Some legends describe the Feathered Serpent as a light-skinned figure who arrived from the east and promised to return, a narrative that has intrigued scholars and believers alike.
sd11.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the Feathered Serpent, the Book of Mormon records Christ's appearance to the Nephites in 3 Nephi 11. This event shares thematic similarities with Mesoamerican legends of a divine teacher who came from the east. Additionally, the Bible speaks of God's outreach to all nations, as in Acts 17:26-27, emphasizing that He 'hath made of one blood all nations of men... that they should seek the Lord.' These passages suggest that divine manifestations are not limited to a single people or region but are part of a broader, universal plan.
sd11.background: Mesoamerica, encompassing regions of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras, was home to advanced civilizations like the Olmec, Maya, and Aztec. These societies developed complex social structures, impressive architectural feats, and rich mythologies. Daily life was deeply intertwined with religious beliefs, with deities governing aspects like agriculture, weather, and celestial events. The Feathered Serpent emerged as a central figure in this spiritual landscape, embodying the connection between the earthly and the divine. The Olmecs, often considered the 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica, laid the foundation for many religious concepts, including the Feathered Serpent, which subsequent cultures adapted and integrated into their own belief systems.

sd12.talk: Why do you think people in different places all believe in a loving Creator?
sd12.child: Long ago, Native American people believed in a loving Great Spirit who made everything. They prayed to thank Him and tried to live in harmony with the earth. This helps us remember that Heavenly Father loves all His children, all around the world.
sd12.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father’s truth and love are not bound by time or place. He has always reached out to His children, giving them ways to know Him even if they never had the Bible or the Book of Mormon. Learning about others’ faith traditions can help us be more humble, more appreciative, and more willing to see God’s hand everywhere. It also teaches us that gratitude and respect for creation are holy habits.
sd12.matters: This belief in a Great Spirit matters because it shows how God’s light can reach every heart, no matter when or where they are born. For families of faith, it is a gentle reminder that Heavenly Father’s love and truth can be found everywhere—a lesson of respect for all His children. When later missionaries taught Native Americans about God the Father, many already understood Him as a loving, all-powerful Creator. This shows that seeds of truth had already been planted. Respecting this heritage can help us see God’s hand moving in every nation.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: Native American Religions
Encyclopedia Britannica: Native American religions
Purdue University: Native American Spirituality

sd12.evidence: Historians and anthropologists who have studied Native American beliefs find strong evidence that many Indigenous North American communities held a foundational belief in a supreme Creator or Great Spirit. While every tribe had unique names, stories, and traditions, the similarity of a single, loving, creative force is widely noted in oral histories and traditional practices. Early Jesuit missionaries in the 1600s wrote about meeting people who already believed in a single Creator. Today, records and oral histories shared by Native elders, as well as studies from university and museum programs, confirm that this tradition was embedded in society long before Europeans arrived. Artifacts, stories, and ceremonies reflect these deep beliefs, even as details varied by region and tribe.
sd12.happened: Long before European explorers ever set foot in North America, hundreds of Native American nations lived across forests, plains, deserts, and mountains. Though each nation had its own traditions, languages, and stories, many shared a gentle and deep belief in what they called the Great Spirit. This Great Spirit was seen as the Creator of all things—the earth, the sky, people, and animals—and was understood as a good and loving power. When people wanted to show gratitude for a good harvest, a child’s healing, or the beauty of nature, they offered prayers or ceremonies to the Great Spirit. These ceremonies often focused on harmony: being in balance with each other, with the land, and with the animals. Every year, families gathered in circles, listened to elders tell of the Great Spirit, and gave thanks for life and the world they were given. This sense of a loving, watchful Creator runs like a strong, quiet river through the history and memory of many Indigenous peoples.
sd12.scripture: In Acts 17:22-28, Paul teaches that God ‘is not far from every one of us’ and that He gives ‘life, and breath, and all things’ to all people. The Book of Mormon confirms that the Lord speaks to all nations (2 Nephi 29:7) and that ‘all are alike unto God’ (2 Nephi 26:33). These passages support the idea that Heavenly Father has given light and witness to all His children, reaching across languages and cultures—even before the fullness of the gospel was shared with them.
sd12.background: Around 2,500 years ago, the land we now call North America was home to many different societies. These peoples farmed, hunted, and fished. They built villages, traded, and cared for each other. Children learned from their elders not just how to survive, but how to live in a way that respected all living things. Religion and daily life were closely joined. The world was seen as full—every stream, stone, and star had meaning. Most nations honored those who had come before and felt responsible to those who would follow after. Even though languages and customs were different from place to place, the idea of a great Creator or Great Spirit was a thread tying many together. In this way, Indigenous religious life was both practical and uplifting, touching every part of a person’s day.

sd13.talk: Can you think of a time when you felt sad because someone you love was making a bad choice?
sd13.child: Long ago, the people of the Andes believed in a kind creator named Viracocha, who made the sun, moon, stars, and people. They said he loved his children so much that he cried when they were sad or did wrong things.
sd13.learn: The story of Viracocha teaches us that the concept of a compassionate and sorrowful creator is not unique to one culture or religion. It reminds us that Heavenly Father has revealed His nature to various peoples in ways they could understand. This understanding encourages us to respect and learn from the spiritual insights of different cultures, recognizing the universal truths that connect us all as children of God.
sd13.matters: The story of Viracocha is significant because it illustrates a universal theme: a creator who loves and feels sorrow for his children. This resonates with the scriptural account in Moses 7:28-29, where God weeps for the wickedness of the earth. For families of faith, this parallel underscores the idea that Heavenly Father has revealed aspects of His loving nature to all His children, regardless of time or place. Recognizing these shared truths can deepen our appreciation for the diverse ways in which God's love has been manifested throughout history.

sources.name: Viracocha - World History Encyclopedia
Viracocha - Wikipedia
Viracocha: The Nature and Antiquity of the Andean High God | Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology

sd13.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as the monumental structures at Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca, provide insights into the religious practices of pre-Inca cultures. The Gateway of the Sun, a significant artifact at Tiwanaku, features a central figure that some scholars associate with Viracocha, depicted with a crown and holding staffs. However, interpretations vary, and some argue that this identification may be influenced by later Inca traditions. Additionally, Spanish chroniclers recorded accounts of Viracocha, describing him as a bearded man who traveled among the people, teaching and performing miracles. While these accounts offer valuable information, they were documented after the Spanish conquest and may reflect a blend of indigenous beliefs and European interpretations.
sd13.happened: Long ago, in the Andean regions of present-day Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador, the people revered Viracocha as their supreme creator deity. According to their beliefs, Viracocha emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca and brought forth the sun, moon, stars, and humanity. He was often depicted wearing the sun as a crown, holding thunderbolts, and with tears streaming from his eyes, symbolizing rain. After creating the world, Viracocha traveled across the lands, teaching people the arts of civilization and imparting wisdom. Once his work was complete, he departed across the sea, promising to return one day. This narrative highlights a creator who not only formed the world but also deeply cared for his creation, expressing sorrow and compassion for humanity.
sd13.scripture: In Moses 7:28-29, we read of Enoch witnessing God weeping over the wickedness of His children: 'And it came to pass that the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept.' This passage reveals a God who is deeply compassionate and sorrowful over the choices of His children. Similarly, the Andean depiction of Viracocha as a weeping creator reflects this profound truth—that our Creator is not distant or indifferent but is intimately concerned with our well-being and choices.
sd13.background: Before the rise of the Inca Empire, the Andean region was home to various cultures, each with its own traditions and beliefs. The people lived in close harmony with nature, relying on agriculture, particularly the cultivation of maize and potatoes, and domesticated animals like llamas and alpacas. They built impressive structures and developed complex societies. The concept of a creator god like Viracocha was central to their worldview, reflecting their understanding of the universe and their place within it. This belief system provided a foundation for the later Inca civilization, which integrated and expanded upon these earlier traditions.

sd14.talk: Why do you think some people kept the idea of a loving, great God a special secret?
sd14.child: Many, many years ago, the Maori people had a special name for God: Io. They believed He was the father of everything and the source of all light. Only special leaders knew this name and taught about Him very carefully.
sd14.learn: From the story of Io, we learn that truth can be found in many places, prepared by God in ways that fit different people and their needs. It teaches us to be humble and curious about how others have experienced the divine, and to honor the quiet faith that often grows in unexpected places. It also helps us see that our Heavenly Father is loving and aware of all His children around the world.
sd14.matters: For families of faith today, stories like that of Io remind us that Heavenly Father’s truth is sown in many places, often long before missionaries or scriptures reach a land. It matters to our world because it shows respect for the faith and searching hearts of all peoples. In the case of the Maori, their belief in a supreme and loving Father God helped prepare the way for the restored gospel when missionaries finally arrived. For families, it’s a gentle witness that God knows His children across the earth and prepares them in ways that are right for them.

sources.name: Te Ara - The Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Io – supreme being
Encyclopædia Britannica: Maori
Church News: Maori and the Book of Mormon

sd14.evidence: Historians and anthropologists have found that the tradition of Io was recorded in Maori oral histories and first written down by Maori elders in the nineteenth century, especially as Christian missionaries arrived and asked more about traditional beliefs. Some scholars debate whether the concept of Io was as ancient as claimed or whether it was shaped partly by contact with Christian ideas, as Io was not publicly spoken of before the 1800s. However, respected Maori sources and cultural leaders have maintained that the tradition of Io was kept sacred and secret for many centuries. Modern scholarship affirms that knowledge about Io existed among Maori priests before widespread European contact, though exactly how far back it goes is still studied and discussed.
sd14.happened: Around 1000 BCE, deep in the Pacific, the Maori and other Polynesian peoples carried with them a sacred tradition of a supreme being named Io. Unlike the gods commonly spoken of in day-to-day stories—gods who governed the winds, seas, or forests—Io was different. Io was seen as above all others, eternal and uncreated, the father and source of all life. This knowledge was so sacred that only the highest priests, the tohunga, were taught of Him, and then only after a long and careful preparation. These teachings were passed on quietly from one generation to the next, held close and respected as the deepest spiritual truth. Io was described as the God of light and truth, dwelling in the highest heaven, and seen as the source of wisdom, order, and all that was good. This belief guided the priests in their prayers, rituals, and understanding of life itself, giving a foundation of faith that something above and loving watched over them, even if ordinary people did not always hear the name Io in their everyday lives.
sd14.scripture: While the Bible teaches plainly of one God, the Father of all, such as in Malachi 2:10 (“Have we not all one father?”), and the Book of Mormon testifies that God is “the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Mormon 9:9), there is no direct mention of Io or Polynesian beliefs. However, the principle in Alma 29:8 speaks to this: the Lord “doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word.” Doctrine and Covenants 1:2 also assures us that God speaks to all “the nations of the earth.”
sd14.background: The people living in the Pacific islands at this time were master navigators, traveling across vast stretches of ocean in great double-hulled canoes. They settled islands from Hawai’i in the north, to Easter Island in the east, and New Zealand in the south. Their days were shaped by fishing, farming, and caring for their families, but also by a deep trust in the unseen world of spirits and ancestors. Religion was at the heart of community life, guiding decisions, ceremonies, and connections to the land. Among the Maori and other Polynesian groups, stories of the gods were passed in chants and songs, but the special knowledge of Io was kept in sacred trust by the chosen few. Life was not easy, but it was rich in meaning and ties to each other and to the divine.

sd15.t: Universal: The Flood in Every Culture
sd15.talk: Why do you think so many different cultures have stories about a big flood?
sd15.child: Long ago, many people told stories about a big flood that covered the world. In these tales, a good person built a big boat to save their family and animals. After the flood, they started life anew.
sd15.learn: These flood stories teach us about the resilience of the human spirit and the importance of preparedness and faith in the face of adversity. They remind us that while challenges and disasters may arise, hope and renewal are always possible. For families, these narratives can serve as lessons in morality, obedience, and the consequences of actions, emphasizing the importance of living righteously and being mindful stewards of the earth.
sd15.matters: The widespread presence of flood stories across various cultures highlights a shared human experience and the importance of water in shaping civilizations. For families of faith, these narratives can be seen as evidence of a common ancestry and shared history, reinforcing the belief that humanity is interconnected. Recognizing these shared stories can foster a sense of unity and understanding among diverse peoples, emphasizing the universal themes of survival, renewal, and divine intervention.

sources.name: List of flood myths
Evidence for a Flood
Is There Proof of Noah's Flood?

sd15.evidence: While many cultures have flood myths, scientific evidence for a global flood covering the entire earth is lacking. Geological studies indicate that sedimentary layers and fossil records were formed over millions of years through various processes, not a single catastrophic event. However, there is evidence of significant regional floods in history. For instance, research suggests that around 7,500 years ago, the Mediterranean Sea breached a natural dam, leading to the rapid flooding of the Black Sea basin. Such events could have inspired local flood legends, which over time, may have been adapted into the broader narratives found in various cultures.
sd15.happened: Long ago, many cultures around the world told stories about a massive flood that covered the earth. These tales often describe a divine being who, displeased with humanity, sent a great deluge to cleanse the world. In these narratives, a righteous person or family is warned in advance, builds a vessel, and saves themselves along with various animals. After the waters recede, they repopulate the earth. For example, the Mesopotamian "Epic of Gilgamesh" tells of Utnapishtim, who was instructed by the gods to build a boat to survive a flood meant to destroy humanity. Similarly, in Hindu tradition, the story of Manu describes a man who is forewarned by a fish about an impending flood and builds a boat to save himself and the seven sages. These stories, though differing in details, share a common theme of a catastrophic flood and a chosen survivor, suggesting a shared memory or experience among diverse peoples.
sd15.scripture: The Bible recounts the story of Noah's Ark in Genesis 6-9, where God, seeing the wickedness of humanity, decides to bring a flood to cleanse the earth. Noah, a righteous man, is instructed to build an ark to save his family and pairs of every animal species. After the floodwaters recede, God establishes a covenant with Noah, symbolized by a rainbow, promising never to destroy the earth by flood again. This narrative underscores themes of obedience, faith, and God's mercy.
sd15.background: In ancient times, civilizations often settled near rivers and bodies of water, which were vital for agriculture, transportation, and sustenance. However, these areas were also prone to flooding. Such natural disasters could be devastating, destroying homes, crops, and lives. The unpredictability and magnitude of these floods left a significant impact on these societies, leading them to incorporate such events into their oral traditions and myths. Over generations, these stories evolved, reflecting each culture's values, beliefs, and experiences, but the core narrative of a great flood remained consistent.

sd16.talk: Can you think of a time today when someone treated you with kindness, or when you did that for someone else?
sd16.child: Everywhere people have lived, they've learned to be kind to others because they wanted kindness too. Treating others how you want to be treated makes the world a better place.
sd16.learn: We can learn that every person, no matter when or where they lived, has been given a sense of right and wrong by Heavenly Father. The Golden Rule reminds us to pause and consider the feelings and needs of those around us. When we live by this principle, we carry forward an ancient truth that binds communities and families together in safety and peace.
sd16.matters: The Golden Rule matters because it teaches us that kindness and respect are not only good but essential for all to flourish. For a family of faith, it is a sign that Heavenly Father cares for all His children, planting in every heart the desire to treat others fairly. This principle builds trust in homes, schools, and nations, and helps us see others as He sees them, no matter where they live or what they believe. Teaching our children the Golden Rule helps them become peacemakers and good friends, both in our families and in the world beyond.

sources.name: BBC Ethics - The Golden Rule
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Golden Rule
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - Bible Dictionary: Golden Rule

sd16.evidence: Scholars have collected versions of the Golden Rule from every major civilization with written records, including ancient Egypt, Greece, China, India, and the Americas. Although these cultures were often separated by great distances and had no contact, their core teaching to treat others with fairness and kindness appears independently. Historians believe this reflects a shared human capacity for empathy, which psychologists have observed even in young children. Although some details differ, the core message is the same. Archaeological evidence, such as ancient texts, scrolls, and inscriptions, confirms that kindness and fairness were taught long before the modern era. This widespread presence suggests that the Golden Rule is one of humanity’s earliest and most lasting moral ideas.
sd16.happened: Long before there were cities, countries, or even written language, people all around the world began thinking about how to treat one another. In every major culture, from ancient Egypt and China, to the first people of India and Greece, something wonderful happened: each community found their own way to say that we should treat others as we hope to be treated. This simple idea became known as the Golden Rule. Some taught it in wise sayings passed from parents to children; others wrote it in sacred books or shared it as stories and parables. In China, Confucius shared it around 500 BC. Buddhists and Hindus taught their own versions about the same time. A bit later, it is found in Jewish teachings, and then in the teachings of Jesus Christ, who said, 'All things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.' Later, Islam and many other faiths passed on this same wisdom. These people lived in different places and times, often without knowing of each other's existence, yet they discovered this golden truth on their own.
sd16.scripture: In the Bible, Jesus teaches the Golden Rule in Matthew 7:12, 'Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.' The Book of Mormon shares related counsel, such as in Mosiah 2:17, where King Benjamin says, 'when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.' Doctrine and Covenants 59:6, about loving one another, and Moses 7:18 in the Pearl of Great Price, where the people of Zion are described as being 'of one heart and one mind,' also touch on this principle.
sd16.background: Early humanity lived in small villages or tribes, working together to gather food, care for animals, and find shelter. Life was often uncertain, so people depended on one another for survival. Most did not have writing or schools, but they learned by watching, listening, and sharing stories around their fires. As families grew into larger communities, rules for living together became more important. Spiritual leaders, wise elders, and parents tried to help everyone get along and be safe. Their advice was shaped by their experiences and their desire to make life better for everyone. In time, their simple rules of kindness, fairness, and respect became core teachings passed down through generations.

sf_a01.talk: Why do you think God wants us to learn about both the world and His teachings?
sf_a01.child: A long time ago, the church started the first universities so people could learn about both God and the world. They argued ideas kindly and studied together. Because of this, we have schools and science today.
sf_a01.learn: We can learn that faith and science can work together as friends, not enemies. The honest search for answers and the careful practice of debate and study were seen as ways to honor God. Being curious, asking questions, and using our minds can be faithful acts. This makes it possible for families to see the classroom as a place where faith and learning walk together.
sf_a01.matters: This story teaches us that the places where science is taught began with people of faith. Universities did not grow apart from the church, but out of it. For families who believe that God gives us tools to learn and build, this history is a reminder that seeking knowledge is part of our faith. It also shows how ideas can grow stronger when people learn to ask hard questions in a spirit of respect and honesty. As we send our own children into today's classrooms, we can trust that learning deeply about the world is not just a modern idea, but one that faithful people have loved and defended for centuries.

sources.name: Britannica Kids – University
Oxford University – History and Heritage
Vatican Museums – Medieval Universities: A Church Invention
Church of Jesus Christ – Seek Learning by Study and by Faith

sf_a01.evidence: Historians have good records showing the founding of the University of Bologna around 1088. Documents from the time mention its special charter and its right to set its own rules. The University of Paris may have roots earlier or later, but records from the 1100s show a community of teachers recognized by both kings and popes. Oxford has evidence of teaching by the late 1100s. Scholars have found copies of charters, letters between school leaders and popes, and old course lists that included logic, philosophy, math, medicine, and law. These sources confirm that universities were church-connected, self-governing, and protected centers of learning.
sf_a01.happened: In the late 1000s, a new kind of school appeared in Europe—one that did not belong to a single church or noble family, but stood by itself. The University of Bologna, started in 1088, was the first of its kind. After Bologna, Paris and Oxford soon followed. These universities were deeply connected to the Christian church. Most of their teachers were not just masters of learning but priests or monks, and many students were training to serve in the church. Classes were not divided like today; instead, they gathered in groups to listen, discuss, and especially to debate. One key method was disputation—where everyone learned by arguing different sides of important questions, searching for the best answer together. Students learned about God, but also about nature, math, stars, medicine, and law. Soon, universities earned special charters from popes and kings, giving them the right to teach and grant degrees. By 1500, the idea had spread across Europe. This way of teaching—open, questioning, and careful—was unlike anything that had come before, and it created a new space for science to grow.
sf_a01.scripture: Scriptures encourage the pursuit of knowledge and learning. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it says, “seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” The Bible, in Proverbs 4:7, reminds us, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.” While the Bible does not mention universities, these teachings reflect Heavenly Father's desire that we seek understanding of both spiritual and earthly things. The principle of gathering to learn and teach is found many times in scripture (Acts 17:11, 2 Nephi 9:29).
sf_a01.background: Before universities, most learning in Europe happened in monasteries or small church schools. Only a few people could read or write, and most books were copied by hand. The church was the main protector of learning after the fall of Rome. Life was hard for most families, who worked the land and faced dangers from illness, war, and famine. Faith was woven into every part of life. When the first universities were founded, much of Europe was rebuilding. People wanted more knowledge—as more trade, cities, and new ideas began to spread. The university grew out of a longing to organize this learning, make it safer, and to train leaders for both church and community.

sf_a02.t: Ibn al-Haytham and the Scientific Method
