sf_a02.talk: Can you think of something you wondered about, and how you could do a little experiment to learn more?
sf_a02.child: A long time ago in Egypt, Ibn al-Haytham showed that light goes into our eyes to help us see. He taught people to test their ideas with real experiments, not just trust what others say. Today, scientists everywhere try to learn truth by testing things, just like he did.
sf_a02.learn: From Ibn al-Haytham we learn the importance of questioning what we hear, testing it for ourselves, and letting evidence guide us. Faith and science do not need to be rivals; both encourage careful seeking after truth. His life teaches us that every honest question and humble experiment can help us learn more about God’s world and share those discoveries with others, no matter where or when we live.
sf_a02.matters: What happened in Cairo with Ibn al-Haytham changed the world’s approach to learning. His method—test, observe, question—spread across cultures and centuries. When his Book of Optics was translated into Latin, European scholars, including Roger Bacon and later Isaac Newton, built studies on his way of thinking. His story shows that great discoveries can come from careful, humble searching, and reminds us that science can flourish when people of faith seek to understand God’s world and share with others. For families of faith, his example encourages us to welcome learning and test what we’re taught against truth, trusting that all real knowledge comes from God.

sf_a02.evidence: Historians have carefully studied Ibn al-Haytham’s original Arabic manuscripts, as well as early translations of his work into Latin that spread through Europe. His detailed experiments are described plainly in the Book of Optics, which survives in many versions. Researchers agree that his method was new for his time. While science has grown since then, his insistence on experimental proof rather than authority alone set a lasting example. Museums and universities hold his early works, and scientific historians credit him directly with influencing later giants like Kepler and Newton. This is considered solid history, built on many primary documents and scholarly studies.
sf_a02.happened: Around the year 1021 in Cairo, Egypt, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham wrote a book called the Book of Optics. Ibn al-Haytham was deeply curious about how vision worked. People before him believed our eyes sent out rays to see, but he disagreed. Through careful thinking and experiments, he showed how light actually travels from what we see into our eyes. What made Ibn al-Haytham’s work extra special was his approach. He insisted that just believing what someone said—even famous thinkers like Aristotle—was not enough. He thought that every idea, even his own, should be tested with real-life experiments to see if it was true. He wrote that a seeker after truth must check everything carefully, trusting experiments over tradition. His Book of Optics wasn’t just about light and vision, but about how to seek knowledge. It invited others to test, observe, and learn from the world itself, and this way of learning would become the heart of science everywhere.
sf_a02.scripture: Scriptures teach us to seek knowledge, to ask questions, and to test all things. In James 1:5 of the New Testament, we are encouraged, “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 counsels to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” Alma 32:27 in the Book of Mormon compares truth-seeking to planting a seed, testing to see if it grows. These verses remind us that seeking truth—by experiment, faith, and reason—is a pattern the Lord approves, and that all good and truth can be sought courageously.
sf_a02.background: Ibn al-Haytham lived during what many call the Islamic Golden Age, a time when science, math, and learning flourished in places like Cairo and Baghdad. Scholars gathered in libraries and exchanged ideas, translating works from Greece, Persia, and India. Many of these thinkers were people of faith who believed that studying nature was a way to appreciate God’s creation. Daily life in Cairo bustled with trade, learning, and worship. Books were copied by hand, and scholars often worked for wealthy patrons or in grand public houses of learning called "houses of wisdom." Until Ibn al-Haytham’s time, much scientific thinking relied on ancient texts more than observation. He changed that by urging everyone to look at the world directly and test their ideas.

b01.happened: Around 600 BC, a prophet named Lehi lived in Jerusalem. One night, Lehi had a powerful dream or vision, which he shared with his family. In this dream, he saw himself in a dark and dreary wilderness. After praying for mercy, he was led by a man in a white robe to a beautiful and spacious field. In the middle of this field was an extraordinary tree, its fruit was white and sweet, bringing immense happiness to all who tasted it. Lehi wanted his family to taste this fruit because it filled him with joy. As he looked around, he saw a river, a rod of iron leading to the tree, and a great and spacious building filled with people who mocked those trying to reach the tree. Some people pressed forward, grasping the iron rod, and tasted the fruit. Others became lost because they let go or paid attention to those mocking them. Lehi described all these things to his family, hoping they would understand how to find the greatest happiness. His son Nephi wanted to know what his father saw, so he prayed for understanding. Nephi not only saw the vision himself but was taught by an angel that the tree represented the love of God—seen most clearly in the mission and Atonement of Jesus Christ.
b01.background: Lehi’s family lived during a time of great change and danger in Jerusalem, just before the Babylonian conquest. The city was troubled by wise men warning of destruction if people did not repent. Most worked hard for their daily bread, lived in stone houses, and gathered at the temple for worship. In this world, having visions was uncommon, but not unheard of among prophets. Lehi and his family would soon leave everything behind, traveling through desert lands toward a new home. Jerusalem was a center of learning and religion, but also of strife and pride. Life was often uncertain, so seeking guidance from God through dreams or visions brought real comfort and hope.
b01.matters: The vision of the Tree of Life matters deeply because it gives a picture of how God’s love is offered to everyone through Jesus Christ. For families of faith, this dream helps teach children about choosing to follow the path that leads to Christ, even when doing so is hard or others make fun. It reminds us that the path to true happiness is clear, but sometimes difficult, and that Heavenly Father wants us all to reach the joy found in His love—together as families. The image of holding to the iron rod has become a cherished symbol of staying true to God’s teachings, no matter the world around.
b01.scripture: This vision is found in 1 Nephi chapters 8 and 11 in the Book of Mormon. The direct interpretation is given in 1 Nephi 11:21-22, where it says the tree is the love of God, which is "most desirable above all things." Doctrine and Covenants 6:23 and John 3:16 from the Bible both echo the same message—God’s love is freely offered, and following His guidance leads to peace. Other scriptures also encourage us to seek and share that love so it can bless many lives.
b01.evidence: There is no direct archaeological evidence confirming the Tree of Life vision as a historical event. Scholars note that dreams and visions were a known spiritual experience in the ancient Near East, and the symbols Lehi described—such as a tree of life, a river, and a path—fit real cultural and religious themes of the time. Some research suggests that imagery of sacred trees as symbols of life, wisdom, or divine love was widespread from Mesopotamia to Israel. While historians can confirm that Jerusalem existed in Lehi’s day and understand the background, the specific details of Lehi’s vision are best supported within the faith community and its texts, rather than from external records or archaeology.
b01.learn: We can learn that God loves us deeply, and His greatest hope is for us to find happiness through Jesus Christ. The journey toward the tree teaches us to hold onto the things that help us stay close to God, like scripture and prayer, and to help others along the way. While the vision may not be proven history, its message can shape the way we live and love each other.
b01.child: Lehi saw a bright, happy tree in a dream, and its fruit made people feel full of joy. He wanted his family to eat the fruit and be happy. The tree shows how much Heavenly Father loves us all.
b01.talk: What do you think the fruit on the tree tasted like, and why did it make people so happy?

sf_a03.happened: In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus, who was not only a skilled astronomer but also a faithful canon (church leader) at Frombork Cathedral in Poland, published a book that changed how people understood the heavens. His book, "On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres," made the bold claim that the sun, not the earth, sits at the center of the universe and that the planets—including Earth—move around it. This idea was very new and surprising at the time, because for centuries most people believed that everything revolved around Earth. Copernicus worked on his book for many years, often sharing drafts with bishops and cardinals. He dedicated his work to the Pope, showing great respect for his faith. Far from hiding his beliefs, Copernicus served his church every day while quietly changing the way people would see the sky forever. His book was printed in the last year of his life and passed quietly among scholars and churchmen for decades, becoming one of the most important works in the history of science, and only became controversial long after Copernicus had died.
sf_a03.background: In the early 1500s, Europe was full of learning but also of questions. Most people believed what they saw—the sun seemed to rise and set around them—but astronomers kept careful notes and noticed things that didn't quite fit with old ideas. Before Copernicus, a wise astronomer named Ptolemy had taught that the Earth stood still at the universe's center, and this view matched what people read in their Bibles and saw with their eyes. Copernicus grew up in a world where the church was the center of learning, keeping libraries and teaching at universities. Life in Frombork, Poland, was shaped by the church, with bells ringing through the day and people gathering for worship, but curious minds like Copernicus's spent long nights measuring the stars. He was respected by church leaders and served as a canon even as he studied and taught about the stars and planets.
sf_a03.matters: This event matters because it reminds us that seeking truth and loving God are not two separate paths. Copernicus’s story shows that sincere faith and good science can go hand in hand. For families who believe all truth comes from God, this is a comfort and a call to courage—sometimes the world changes not by setting faith aside, but by following its deepest call to learn and serve. It also reminds us to double-check our stories: history is sometimes more surprising and hopeful than we remember.
sf_a03.scripture: Scripture teaches us that God is the Creator of all things and encourages us to study His works. Psalm 19:1 says, “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handiwork.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:42–47 speaks of the laws that govern the heavens, given by God. While the scriptures don’t say how the planets move, they invite us to search for truth in all things and trust that God wants us to learn about His creations.
sf_a03.evidence: The evidence for Copernicus’s role as a canon at Frombork, and the writing and dedication of his book, is clear from church and scientific records of the time. We have his letters, the original printed book from 1543, and letters from bishops and cardinals who encouraged him. Historians agree that Copernicus’s book was quietly accepted among many leading churchmen for decades, and it did not instantly cause trouble. Only when Galileo’s work stirred a public debate, many years later, did the Church place Copernicus’s book on a list for review, and even then, it was not completely banned but paused for corrections. His life and work are well documented in libraries and museums.
sf_a03.learn: We can learn from Copernicus that faithful people can make amazing discoveries, sometimes by patiently working for years and never losing sight of either their faith or their curiosity. He teaches us that our callings, our science, and our faith can work together, just as God intended. It’s important not to rush to fear or judgment when new understanding comes, but to remember that truth grows brighter as we seek it.
sf_a03.child: Long ago, a man who worked in a church found out that the sun is in the middle, not the earth. He loved God, and he loved to study the stars. His work helped everyone see the sky in a new way.
sf_a03.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to learn about His creations?

sf_a04.happened: Between 1609 and 1619, Johannes Kepler made some of the most important discoveries in the history of astronomy. Kepler lived in Prague, Bohemia, and he was deeply committed to his faith, having trained for the Lutheran ministry before turning to science. He wanted to understand the heavens because he believed nature was God’s handiwork and that by studying it, he could learn more about the Creator. Kepler worked very hard, using observations made by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. He started with the belief, shared by many in his time, that the planets must move in perfect circles. As Kepler studied the data, though, he saw that nothing quite fit these circles. Instead of forcing the information to match his hopes, Kepler carefully measured and found that the planets moved in ellipses—shaped like squished circles, or ovals—around the sun. He was disappointed because he thought circles were more perfect, but he trusted what he saw. Kepler published his findings, which we now call Kepler's three laws of planetary motion. He once wrote that by studying astronomy, he was “thinking God’s thoughts after Him.” Kepler’s willingness to change his view when faced with new evidence helped pave the way for modern science.
sf_a04.background: Kepler worked during a time of major change in Europe, often called the Scientific Revolution. People were just starting to question long-held beliefs about the natural world. Before Kepler, people mostly followed the teachings of ancient thinkers like Aristotle and Ptolemy, who said the heavens must be made of perfect circles. Kepler was born in 1571 in what is now Germany, in a world shaped by the Protestant Reformation and frequent religious conflict. He grew up wanting to serve God as a minister, but eventually found his calling in mathematics and astronomy. Daily life was often hard, with wars, sickness, and little privacy or comfort by today’s standards. Still, people found wonder in the night sky, and some, like Kepler, believed that learning about the heavens was a way to honor God.
sf_a04.matters: Kepler’s discovery matters because it changed how people understood our place in the cosmos. For families of faith, his story shows that seeking truth—no matter where it leads—can be part of worshipping God. Kepler did not let his personal wishes for how God might have arranged the heavens overrule the evidence in front of him. This kind of honesty, humility, and courage is vital in both science and faith. The very laws he found later allowed scientists like Isaac Newton to explain how gravity holds the planets in their paths, showing how careful observations can reveal even greater wonders hidden in God’s creation.
sf_a04.scripture: While the scriptures do not talk about Kepler directly or name the planets' orbits, they do praise honest seeking and teach that God is the author of both spiritual and physical truth. James 1:5 encourages asking God for wisdom. Doctrine and Covenants 88: 42-47 speaks of God setting “all things, both in heaven and on the earth,” in order, and how the stars obey laws He has given. The process Kepler followed—seeking truth humbly, and changing his own ideas when evidence demanded—is a principle we see encouraged through scripture.
sf_a04.evidence: Historians have many of Kepler’s writings, including his famous books, where he explained his discoveries and the thinking behind them. Exact records show how he used Tycho Brahe’s careful measurements to reach his conclusions about ellipses and planetary motion. His three laws are taught all over the world and still help scientists today. Translations of his letters and journals show his deep faith and his struggle to accept ellipses instead of circles. Scientists can use modern telescopes and math to see that his way of describing the planets’ paths is correct. There is overwhelming evidence from both his own words and the skies themselves that Kepler’s work is trustworthy and correct.
sf_a04.learn: Kepler’s story teaches that true faith does not fear honest questions, and that it is good to check what we hope is true against what really is. Sometimes we might want things to be a certain way, but following the truth, even if it surprises us, can lead to bigger discoveries and deeper faith. In both science and faith, Heavenly Father wants us to seek, learn, and listen—trusting that His creation will always speak what is true.
sf_a04.child: Johannes Kepler loved God and wanted to understand how the planets move. He found out they go in ovals instead of perfect circles, even though he wished for circles. He taught that following the truth is important, even when it surprises us.
sf_a04.talk: Why do you think it is important to tell the truth, even if it isn’t what you hoped?

sf_a05.happened: In the year 1633, Galileo Galilei, a well-known scientist from Italy, stood trial in Rome before the Roman Catholic Church’s Inquisition. Galileo believed that the sun, not the earth, was at the center of the solar system—a view called Copernicanism after another scientist, Copernicus. Though the Pope had once allowed Galileo to discuss this idea as just a theory, Galileo’s book placed the Pope’s argument in the mouth of a character named Simplicio, which sounded like he called him simple-minded. This, along with the Church’s belief that no solid proof existed yet (since people of that time could not observe the tiny shifts in stars, called stellar parallax), led to trouble. Galileo was formally accused of heresy, or teaching against Church doctrine. He was forced to say he was wrong and was sentenced to live under house arrest for the rest of his life. Though never put in a dungeon or tortured, he was watched closely. Even so, he continued his work and wrote some of his most important science while at home. Over 350 years later, the Catholic Church officially said Galileo's treatment had been a mistake, admitting that he had been right and that science and faith can sometimes have honest disagreements.
sf_a05.background: Galileo lived during the Renaissance, a time of great learning in Europe when old ideas were being challenged and new knowledge flourished. Most people still believed the earth was the center of the universe, as Ptolemy had taught for over a thousand years. Daily life was shaped by religion and tradition, and the Church was a great authority not just in spiritual matters but also in science. Books were mainly read by scholars, and the telescope was a brand-new tool. Galileo was a teacher, inventor, and father who believed that learning about the world helped people understand God’s creation. The Pope knew of Galileo and once supported him, but the fear that scientific ideas could challenge the Church’s authority made the situation tense. Galileo’s trial didn’t just involve science; it mixed personalities, pride, faith, and the struggle for truth in a changing world.
sf_a05.matters: Galileo’s story matters for our families today because it shows that sometimes faith and science can seem to be at odds, but both are ways of seeking truth. It reminds us that even good people and good institutions can make mistakes when they are afraid to listen or change. This event does not prove the Church always opposed science; in fact, believers have often been great scientists! But it warns us that when any group refuses honest questions, it might silence people who find out new truths. For families of faith, it teaches us to be humble in what we know and brave enough to keep searching and learning, knowing all truth comes from God.
sf_a05.scripture: While the scriptures do not discuss Galileo or his discoveries, there are principles that match this story. Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79 teaches us to “teach one another the doctrine of the kingdom…and all things that pertain unto the kingdom of God, that are expedient for you to understand; of things both in heaven and in the earth.” The Lord invites us to learn about the heavens and the earth, showing that seeking science is a worthy part of faith. James 1:5 in the New Testament also reminds us, “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God,” encouraging us to seek understanding both spiritually and through study. We are counseled to love truth, wherever it is found.
sf_a05.evidence: Historians and scientists have many records and letters that show what happened to Galileo. His book, 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems', his trial documents, and his own letters have survived, letting us read some of his own words. Later, scientists were able to observe the parallax Galileo could not, confirming the sun-centered model. The Vatican itself has made these historical papers open to scholars. Modern research shows he was not tortured and continued to correspond with friends and scientists while under house arrest. The story is well established in serious histories and church records, so we have strong evidence for what occurred and why.
sf_a05.learn: Galileo’s trial can teach us the importance of being willing to seek truth, even when it is hard or unpopular, and to be patient and respectful with those who disagree. We learn to listen with humility and not to fear new knowledge, trusting that all truth can come together in God’s plan. It is also a lesson in how even trusted leaders and institutions can err when they feel threatened by change, encouraging us as families to be hopeful, honest, and humble as we learn both from faith and from science.
sf_a05.child: A long time ago, a man named Galileo said the earth goes around the sun, but some leaders didn’t like this idea. They told him to stop saying it, so he had to stay at home. Galileo still learned and wrote wonderful things, even when it was hard.
sf_a05.talk: Why do you think it’s important to ask questions, even when others think differently?

sf_a06.happened: In 1687, Isaac Newton published a book called the Principia, which described new laws for how objects move and how gravity works everywhere in the universe. This book became one of the most important scientific works in all history. But what many people don’t know is that Newton, who taught at Cambridge University in England, also wrote many thousands of pages about theology—his thoughts about God, the Bible, and how the world fits together. In fact, more of his written work was about faith and the study of scripture than about mathematics or physics. Newton tried to create a timeline of events in the Bible and spent a lot of time thinking about how God’s plan could be seen in the order and beauty of the natural world. He believed deeply in God but had some unusual beliefs for his time, especially about the nature of the Trinity, which he kept mostly private to avoid trouble with the church or government.
sf_a06.background: During Newton’s lifetime in the late 1600s, England was a place of great change and discovery. The scientific revolution was underway, and people were starting to use careful experiments and mathematics to understand nature better. Before Newton, famous scientists like Galileo and Kepler had made big advances in understanding the planets and motion, but no one had found one set of rules that could explain both an apple falling and planets moving in the sky. People in Newton’s time lived without electricity or modern technology; life centered around faith, farming, and the rhythms of the church and the seasons.
sf_a06.matters: Newton shows us that faith and science are not enemies; they are different ways of seeking the truth. His life reminds us that curiosity about the world can lead us to wonder about God and His designs. For a family of faith, Newton’s story encourages us to see science as a tool that helps us appreciate God’s power and order in creation, rather than something that takes away from faith.
sf_a06.scripture: Several scriptures teach that God is a God of order and that studying His creations brings us closer to Him. For example, Doctrine and Covenants 88:47–49 explains that all things testify of God. Psalm 19:1 in the Bible says, 'The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.' While scripture doesn’t mention Newton, it encourages us to seek learning by study and by faith, as taught in Doctrine and Covenants 88:118.
sf_a06.evidence: Many of Newton’s original handwritten manuscripts survive today and can be seen in museum collections. Scholars have carefully studied these pages and confirmed that Newton wrote much more about biblical chronology and theology than he did about science and math. Historians also know from Newton’s private letters and notes that he held some beliefs that were different from most Christians in his day. The Principia itself is clear about his belief in a Creator, especially in the General Scholium at the end of the book. Modern research has confirmed all these parts of his life through direct evidence from his own hand.
sf_a06.learn: From Newton, we learn that exploring the world and faith can go hand-in-hand. We can be curious and love to learn about how things work while still believing that all knowledge is part of Heavenly Father’s plan. Newton’s example reminds us not to put limits on faith or learning, and to be humble about incomplete understanding. Sometimes, the people who discover the most about our world are also looking hardest for God’s hand in it.
sf_a06.child: Isaac Newton loved learning about how the world works and about God’s teachings. He wrote lots and lots about both science and the Bible. He believed the amazing order in the world shows how wise and powerful Heavenly Father is.
sf_a06.talk: Why do you think Newton felt that learning about how the world works could help him learn about God?

sf_a07.happened: In the year 1831, Michael Faraday, a man known for his deep faith and gentle character, made a discovery that quietly changed the world. Working in his laboratory in London, Faraday showed that when a magnet moves inside a coil of wire, it can create an electric current. This principle is called electromagnetic induction. His experiment was simple: he wrapped wire into coils and moved a magnet through them, finding that electricity appeared in the wire whenever the magnet moved. This finding became the foundation for electric motors and generators—the machines that help power nearly every corner of our world today, from homes and schools to hospitals and factories. Faraday was not a man of wealth or high social standing; he began as a bookbinder’s apprentice and taught himself much of what he knew. Despite invitations to accept important government jobs or become a knight, he chose to remain humble and serve in his church as an unpaid preacher, living his faith quietly even while his discoveries sparked a revolution in science and technology.
sf_a07.background: England in the early 1800s was a place of rapid change. The Industrial Revolution was transforming how people worked, traveled, and learned. Gas lamps were lighting city streets, and the idea of “electricity” was just starting to move from science experiments into daily life. Michael Faraday grew up in a modest home in London, the son of a blacksmith. He belonged to a small Christian group called the Sandemanians, who focused on simplicity, humility, and living the teachings of Jesus. Most people at that time knew little about science, and Faraday himself had only a basic education, learning mainly through hard work and curiosity. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, he approached problems with fresh eyes and deep faith, believing that the world was filled with order that could be discovered and understood.
sf_a07.matters: Faraday’s discovery matters because it is the foundation of all electricity generation today. Where there is a power plant, a wind turbine, or even a hand-cranked flashlight, the same principle that Faraday found in his lab is at work. For families of faith, Faraday’s life is a reminder that the Lord can work through humble and faithful people, not just the rich or the famous. He chose to turn down offers of power and wealth to stay true to his beliefs. His example shows us that scientific discovery and faith can go hand in hand, blessing people’s lives without compromise.
sf_a07.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention electricity or Faraday’s work, several passages teach about the beauty of learning and the gifts God gives His children. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are told to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." In the Bible, James 1:5 encourages us to ask God for wisdom. Faraday’s faith, humility, and desire to serve align well with these teachings—showing that one can seek knowledge and still rely on the Lord, using that knowledge for good.
sf_a07.evidence: Historians have thoroughly documented Michael Faraday’s experiments, letters, and public lectures. His notebooks describing electromagnetic induction are preserved at the Royal Institution in London, and replicas of his early apparatus can be found in science museums today. Scientists have repeated his experiments worldwide for nearly two centuries, always finding the same results: moving a magnet through coils of wire generates electricity. Faraday’s life and work were also recorded by those who knew him, including his lectures and faith service. There is no serious doubt among historians about what he discovered or how he lived.
sf_a07.learn: From Faraday, we learn that faith and curiosity can go together. Heavenly Father can inspire us as we study the world, and that knowledge can be used to bless others. We also learn that greatness is not about public honors or riches, but about quietly doing good, staying true to our values, and serving others. Like Faraday, we can find joy in discovery and use our talents for the benefit of those around us.
sf_a07.child: Michael Faraday discovered how to make electricity by moving a magnet in a coil of wire. He loved Jesus and chose to help his church instead of becoming rich or famous. Even today, the electricity in our homes comes from what he found.
sf_a07.talk: What would you have done if you discovered something important and people wanted to honor you, but your faith asked you to be humble?

sf_a08.happened: In 1866, a gentle and curious Augustinian friar named Gregor Mendel finished years of careful work in the garden of his monastery in Brno, Moravia. Mendel spent long hours planting and watching over thousands of pea plants, noticing how certain traits, like flower color and seed shape, passed from one generation to the next. He kept notes on every plant and every cross he made, then counted the different results. Mendel did not use guesses but math: he was one of the first scientists to realize that some traits followed patterns that could be predicted. He described what he found in a paper called 'Experiments on Plant Hybridization' and even shared it with several other scientists. His monastery encouraged him, with the abbot providing land and support. Despite the value of his findings, almost no one paid attention at the time. People simply didn’t see how important Mendel’s laws of inheritance were, so his work sat quietly in library shelves, nearly forgotten. It took more than thirty years before scientists searching for answers to their own questions rediscovered Mendel’s notes and realized how much they explained. His patient, quiet study laid the groundwork for the new science of genetics, changing how we understand plants, animals, and even our own families.
sf_a08.background: Europe in the 1800s was full of change and curiosity. People were beginning to ask more questions about the natural world using careful study and experiments. Schools and universities were growing, but many scientific discoveries still happened in homes, farms, and even in religious communities. Gregor Mendel lived in a monastery, a quiet place where friars studied, prayed, taught, and helped their neighbors. The monastery was also a center for learning, with a large garden and rooms for research. Mendel was trained at a university, but returned to the peaceful monastery to continue his work among the peas. Daily life for him meant a mix of worship, community service, and quiet observation of God’s creations. In Mendel’s world, faith and science were not enemies, but worked together to help people understand truth.
sf_a08.matters: Mendel’s discovery matters to the world, and to families of faith, because it shows that careful, honest work can bring great blessings, even if those blessings are not seen for many years. His findings are the roots of modern genetics, which influences everything from how we grow food to how doctors understand illnesses passed through families. For people who try to follow Christ, Mendel’s story reminds us that our efforts, especially in the service of others and in learning, are not wasted—even if we do not see the results right away. A garden in a quiet monastery became the starting place for knowledge that helps millions today.
sf_a08.scripture: While the scriptures do not describe scientific experiments or the discovery of genetics, they do teach about seeking knowledge, patience, and the importance of small things. For example, Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages us to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." The parable of the mustard seed in Matthew 13:31-32 reminds us how something tiny can grow large and bless many. The scriptures teach that knowledge is part of God’s work and that even unnoticed acts of good can bring great results in His time.
sf_a08.evidence: Historians and scientists agree that Mendel’s experiments are well documented. His original papers exist, and copies can be seen in scientific libraries. Scientists have repeated his pea plant experiments many times and have found the same patterns of inheritance Mendel described. Later discoveries in biology, like DNA, have shown that Mendel’s observations were the first steps toward understanding genes, even though he did not know about DNA himself. Records from the monastery also show that Mendel’s abbot supported and encouraged his careful work, which was rare for the time. Today, Mendel is widely recognized as the father of modern genetics.
sf_a08.learn: Mendel’s story teaches us that discovery and faith can work side by side. True knowledge comes through both careful study and trust in God’s timing. Even quiet, patient work—sometimes done in the background—can lead to blessings for many people, even far into the future. We can remember that working honestly and faithfully matters, even when no one notices at first.
sf_a08.child: A monk named Mendel grew lots of pea plants to figure out why plants look like their parents. He didn’t give up, even when no one cared for a long time. Because of his careful work, we now know how traits are passed down in families.
sf_a08.talk: What is something kind or helpful you have done that maybe nobody noticed, but you know was good?

sf_a10.happened: The story that people in the Middle Ages believed the earth was flat is a myth. This tale became popular in the 1800s but has little to do with what really happened. In truth, most educated Europeans since the time of the ancient Greeks knew the earth was shaped like a sphere. Written works by respected scholars such as Bede, Thomas Aquinas, and the poet Dante Alighieri show that they took the roundness of the earth for granted. When Christopher Columbus asked for support to sail west to reach Asia, his critics did not argue that he would fall off the edge of a flat earth. Instead, they correctly pointed out that the earth was much larger than Columbus claimed, and that his journey would be too long to survive without stopping for supplies. If America had not been there, Columbus and his crew would have run out of food and water in the middle of the ocean. But by the 1800s, writers like Washington Irving, who wanted to make Columbus sound heroic, invented meetings where religious leaders warned him about sailing off the world’s edge. This story was repeated in books, schools, and speeches, even though it isn’t true. Today, historians have shown that the flat earth myth is one of the best examples of a made-up fact that everyone seemed to believe.
sf_a10.background: Medieval Europe was a world of kingdoms, monasteries, and bustling towns where knowledge from Greece and Rome was taught in cathedral schools and universities. Many people were farmers and craftsmen, while monks and priests preserved and copied ancient books. By the time Columbus sailed in 1492, astronomy and mathematics were important subjects, and scholars read old works by people like Aristotle, who wrote that the earth was round. Some sailors and ordinary folk surely didn’t understand how big the world was, but most educated people did. Books and art from that time even show globe-shaped earths, and the stars’ movements across the sky were explained using a round earth.
sf_a10.matters: This story reminds us to check the facts before we believe what everyone says, even about history. For families who want to learn and teach truth, it shows that faith and science can live together, and that both are blessed when we seek knowledge honestly. Believing myths about the past can make us misunderstand both the faith of earlier Christians and how science grows. Sharing real stories helps us honor those who came before, and teaches our children to love truth—an important part of Heavenly Father’s plan for learning and growing in wisdom.
sf_a10.scripture: There is no scripture that says what shape the earth is, but the principle of seeking truth is found throughout. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches, 'Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.' This fits well with examining both the scriptures and honest discoveries from science and history. When we look for true knowledge, whether it comes from faithful believers or careful scientists, we are using one of the many gifts Heavenly Father has given us.
sf_a10.evidence: Historical scholarship shows overwhelmingly that educated people in the Middle Ages did not believe in a flat earth. Medieval scholars and churchmen owned and read works from Greek and Roman times that taught the earth was round. Artworks, literature, and even some church writings from the period use and depict a spherical earth. The legend that medieval people thought otherwise only became popular in the 1800s through writers like Washington Irving, and has since been corrected by historians. We now have access to original documents and many studies showing the continuity of this knowledge into the Middle Ages. Modern encyclopedias and university research confirm this as settled history.
sf_a10.learn: We can learn that things 'everyone knows' may not always be true, and that it’s wise to check what we hear, especially about faith and history. Teaching children how to think carefully and look for good evidence helps them become wise and humble. This helps us trust that truth, wherever it is found, is part of God’s light, and that our minds are meant to grow bright as we learn what really happened in the world.
sf_a10.child: A long time ago, people already knew the earth was round, even before Columbus sailed. The story that people thought the world was flat is made up. We can remember to check if the stories we hear are really true.
sf_a10.talk: Can you think of a time when something you heard turned out not to be true after you learned more about it?

sf_a09.happened: In 1874 in New York, a man named John William Draper published a book called History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science. Draper’s book painted a vivid picture of religion and science as two great forces locked in a never-ending battle. He suggested that religion had always tried to stop science from making progress, and that whenever science made a discovery, religious belief would fight back. His book was full of strong opinions and dramatic stories, and it became very popular, printed in fifty different editions. About twenty years later in 1896, another writer, Andrew Dickson White, released his own book, A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom. White also told stories of fights between science and religion, giving example after example of supposed conflicts—many of which he took from old legends and rumors more than careful history. Both authors made the idea popular that science and faith are natural enemies. These books were read by many people and helped shape a common belief that these two ways of thinking racially oppose each other.
sf_a09.background: The late 1800s were a time of great change in America and Europe. The world was being transformed by new inventions, discoveries, and ideas. Trains and telegraphs made travel and communication faster than ever. People were learning about electricity, and scientists like Charles Darwin were sharing new ideas about life and nature. At the same time, many people still attended church each week, and religion played a big role in their lives. Draper was a scientist and a professor in New York, while White was the first president of Cornell University. Both men believed in progress, and some of their own personal experiences with church leaders made them feel that religion could get in the way of science. Most everyday people, however, saw faith and discovery as parts of the same good life, and homes often held both scripture and science books.
sf_a09.matters: This topic matters because the idea that faith and science must always clash was taught by just a few writers, but it has continued to affect how people talk and think today. For families who see technology as a gift and want to use truth from every source to bless their lives, it helps to know that this story of war between faith and science was an invention, not a fact. Both ways of seeking truth—asking questions about the world and seeking God in prayer—can work together to help us grow. Recognizing this helps us teach our children to value learning from every good book, including both scripture and science, and to seek how the Lord’s gifts can work together for good.
sf_a09.scripture: The scriptures do not talk about Draper or White or their books, but they do teach principles that apply. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:77-80, the Lord commands people to “teach one another words of wisdom” and to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” This shows that gaining knowledge through both spiritual and scientific means is valuable. Alma 30:44 in the Book of Mormon reminds us that ‘all things denote there is a God,’ suggesting that learning about the world and recognizing God’s hand in it go together. The scriptures encourage unity and seeking truth from all sources, not conflict.
sf_a09.evidence: Today, nearly all historians who study the history of science agree that the story told by Draper and White is mostly false. Careful studies show that many of the clashes they described did not actually happen or were exaggerated. Scholars point out that most scientists throughout history have been religious themselves, and many discoveries happened within religious cultures or were supported by people of faith. For example, the Catholic Church supported many scientists, and great scientists such as Isaac Newton and Gregor Mendel were deeply guided by their faith. The majority of historians now teach that the relationship between faith and science is complex, including both cooperation and disagreement at times, but not a story of unending war.
sf_a09.learn: We can learn to be careful about popular stories, especially when they make grand claims about people or groups being natural enemies. Even ideas that sound sensible can be mistaken if they are not carefully studied. As families, we can teach children to look for truth in both science and faith, to treat both with respect, and to be patient with questions. When we know the real history, we are better able to build bridges between our beliefs and our learning, using all the gifts Heavenly Father has given us.
sf_a09.child: A long time ago, two men wrote books saying science and religion were always fighting. But later, people looked carefully and found this story wasn’t true. Faith and learning can work together to help us grow and do good.
sf_a09.talk: Can you think of a time when learning something new helped you understand something in the scriptures better?

sf_a11.happened: In July 1925, a small town in Tennessee became the center of a national debate about science, religion, and education. John Scopes, a high school teacher, was put on trial for teaching his students about evolution, which was against a new state law. This law, called the Butler Act, made it illegal to teach anything that denied the Biblical account of creation. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) wanted to challenge this law and arranged for Scopes to be put on trial. The case drew famous lawyers to Dayton: Clarence Darrow defended Scopes, and William Jennings Bryan, a well-known politician and Christian speaker, led the prosecution. The trial was held in the local courthouse, but it quickly grew into a nationwide event, with reporters from all over the country arriving to cover it. In the end, Scopes was found guilty and fined one hundred dollars. However, the verdict was later reversed, not because the law was changed, but on a technical detail. The trial became famous as the 'Scopes Monkey Trial,' and it showed just how deeply Americans could disagree on what should be taught in schools.
sf_a11.background: The world in 1925 was changing quickly. Scientific discoveries about fossils and evolution were being talked about in newspapers, and some people believed these ideas disagreed with what the Bible says about God creating the world. At the same time, many Americans still lived in small towns where church teachings shaped daily life. John Scopes was a young teacher who usually taught math and coached sports, not just science. Clarence Darrow was known for defending unpopular causes, and William Jennings Bryan had run for president three times and was a respected voice for traditional Christian beliefs. Many people in Dayton, Tennessee, hoped the trial would bring attention and business to their town, and they welcomed the reporters and crowds that came. Radios broadcast pieces of the trial, making it one of the first major news stories carried live to the whole country.
sf_a11.matters: The Scopes Trial became a moment when many Americans felt they had to choose between faith and science, even though most Christians in the world did not see such a sharp divide. For families of faith today, it reminds us that serious people can have honest disagreements about how to read scripture and understand science, and that loving God and learning about His creations do not have to compete. The trial’s echo is still heard in discussions about what should be taught in schools, showing why it is important to discuss how science and faith can work together.
sf_a11.scripture: The question at the heart of the Scopes Trial touches on how we interpret the creation accounts in Genesis chapters 1 and 2, as well as in Moses chapters 2 and 3 and Abraham chapters 4 and 5 in the Pearl of Great Price. Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79 encourages us to teach one another “of things both in heaven and in the earth,” suggesting that both spiritual and scientific learning are valued. While the scriptures do not mention evolution by name, they do affirm that God is the Creator of all things. Latter-day Saint leaders have often encouraged members to seek understanding in both spiritual and scientific studies.
sf_a11.evidence: Records from the Scopes Trial are carefully preserved, including the court transcript, newspaper articles, and personal writings from the people involved. There is no doubt that the events happened as reported. Historians agree that the trial did not settle the debate about evolution and creation but instead made it national news. Scientific evidence for evolution has grown steadily since then, with discoveries like DNA and fossils helping us understand how life on earth has changed over time. At the same time, many people of faith find ways to accept both scientific discovery and belief in God's creative power.
sf_a11.learn: From this trial we see the importance of being able to talk kindly with those who believe differently, and of valuing both faith and knowledge. It shows that questions about science and faith do not need to divide us, and that seeking truth is an ongoing part of following God. Being respectful and curious about others' views can help families learn and grow together.
sf_a11.child: A long time ago, a teacher went to court because he talked about a science idea called evolution in school. People everywhere talked about it, and it made many people think about how we can believe in God and learn about the world at the same time.
sf_a11.talk: What do you think it means to both love God and learn about His creations?

sf_a12.happened: In 1927, a Catholic priest and scientist named Georges Lemaître made a remarkable discovery in Belgium. Using Albert Einstein’s new ideas about gravity and space, Lemaître proposed that the universe was not static, but expanding. He went even further by suggesting that everything began from a single, incredibly dense point, which he called the “primeval atom.” This idea planted the seed for what we now call the Big Bang theory. At first, many leading scientists, including Einstein himself, pushed back against Lemaître’s proposal. Einstein once said Lemaître’s math was good but his physics was “abominable.” However, as more evidence emerged, even Einstein changed his mind and publicly praised Lemaître’s insight. This moment was not just a breakthrough in science, but an example of faith and curiosity working together, as Lemaître himself was both a priest and a physicist, deeply committed to both his faith and his work as a scientist.
sf_a12.background: When Lemaître introduced his idea, the world was still recovering from World War I. Science was changing rapidly, with physics leading the way into a new era. Albert Einstein’s theories had only recently turned old ideas about space and time upside down. Lemaître was living in Leuven, Belgium, enjoying academic life and serving as a Catholic priest. Most people in the world at the time imagined the universe as eternal and unchanging. Daily life in 1927 was shaped by new inventions like cars, radios, and planes, but people still relied on older ways too. Scientists gathered at universities in lively discussions, though faith and science often stayed in different circles.
sf_a12.matters: The Big Bang theory changed how we think about our place in the universe. For families who believe in God, it is meaningful that the person who first described the universe’s beginning was a man of faith. Lemaître’s respect for both science and scripture reminds us not to force one to prove the other, but to value both as gifts from Heavenly Father. The way scientists slowly accepted the Big Bang also shows that truth can take time to be recognized and that humility helps us learn.
sf_a12.scripture: There is no scripture that directly explains how the universe began in scientific terms, but the scriptures teach that God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1; Moses 2:1). Doctrine and Covenants 88:47–47 encourages us to study and appreciate creation, saying that all things testify of God. Latter-day Saints believe that both spiritual and scientific truths come from God and that we are encouraged to seek knowledge in all areas of life (Doctrine and Covenants 88:78–79).
sf_a12.evidence: Lemaître’s idea was supported by new observations showing that galaxies are moving away from each other, called the redshift, first measured in the late 1920s by Edwin Hubble. Over the years, many lines of evidence have built up for the Big Bang, including the discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965, sometimes called the afterglow of creation. Today, the Big Bang is the foundation of cosmology, and Lemaître’s early work is honored as its beginning. His careful separation of faith and science is still respected.
sf_a12.learn: We can learn to respect both faith and science, knowing each can help us learn about Heavenly Father’s creation. Lemaître’s life also teaches the value of humility. He listened carefully to both criticism and new discoveries, which made him a better scientist and a faithful believer. Families can be open to learning from both scripture and the wonders of the universe, trusting that all truth comes from God in His own time.
sf_a12.child: A priest named Georges Lemaître said the universe began from a tiny, very hot point. At first, people didn’t believe him, but later evidence showed he was right. He loved both God and science and used both to learn about the world.
sf_a12.talk: Why do you think Georges Lemaître was careful to say science and faith answer different questions about how the world began?

sf_a13.happened: In 1986, two historians named David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers published a book called God and Nature. This book took a deep look at the history of science and religion and explained that most stories of a constant battle between the two weren’t really true. In the past, many people believed in something called the conflict thesis, which said science and religion had always been at war. Lindberg and Numbers showed with careful research that this wasn’t accurate. They found that the relationship was much more complicated. Sometimes, faith and science worked together, sometimes they stayed apart, and only occasionally did they really clash. John Hedley Brooke continued this work in 1991 with his book Science and Religion, laying out what is now called the complexity thesis. This idea says their relationship is very changeable—sometimes friendly, sometimes distant, and sometimes stressed. Later, Ronald Numbers also gathered other experts to write about these topics in a 2009 book called Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths About Science and Religion, showing many famous stories of conflict were misunderstood or exaggerated. Today, historians mostly agree with this complexity view, even though you still see simplifications in popular culture and news.
sf_a13.background: Before these historians wrote their books, many people took it for granted that science and religion could not get along. This was called the conflict thesis, and it became popular especially in the 1800s in Europe and America, when science was making big advances. Back then, daily life for most people didn’t include much science, so it was easier to believe stories that made religion and science sound like enemies. Historians like Lindberg, Numbers, and Brooke were trained in reading old letters, scientific papers, and church documents closely. They worked in universities and spent years checking the real story behind famous events, like Galileo’s trial or Darwin’s discoveries. Their careful digging showed that real history is hardly ever so simple.
sf_a13.matters: This matters for families of faith because it corrects an old idea that can cause confusion or worry. If we think science is always against faith, we might fear scientific learning. But if we know the real story is more complex, we can approach both faith and science with trust and curiosity. For the world, it means scholars aim for a fair, honest view of our past. Families can feel encouraged to learn science and remember that many great scientists were also people of deep faith. Understanding this helps children see they don’t have to choose between loving God and loving learning.
sf_a13.scripture: The scriptures teach us in several places to seek knowledge by study and by faith. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we find, 'Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.' This principle is echoed in the Bible, where Proverbs 4:7 says, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' Both passages remind us to value learning both spiritual and worldly truths, and to do so with open hearts. While no scripture describes historians’ work directly, the idea of seeking truth from many good sources is a strong theme.
sf_a13.evidence: Historical research since 1986 has carefully re-examined the most famous stories of science and religion in conflict. For example, it is now clear that Galileo’s case was far more about politics and misunderstandings than a simple science-versus-religion fight. Likewise, many early scientists were deeply religious, including Isaac Newton who wrote more about religion than science. Detailed studies of their letters, books, and the times they lived show many examples of cooperation or parallel growth. While conflicts did happen, they were rare and shaped by details of the time and place, not by some natural fight between faith and science. The evidence is strong that the conflict thesis oversimplified things, and today’s historians generally reject it.
sf_a13.learn: We can learn that truth-seeking is best done with patience and humility. Not every story is simple, and it is wise to listen to different points of view. The best historians admit what is known and what is still debated. As we grow in faith and learning, we don’t have to be afraid that knowledge from good sources will threaten what we believe; often, it brings more wonder and trust in God’s plan. Families can build confidence in exploring science together.
sf_a13.child: A long time ago, some people thought science and faith were always fighting. Now, historians say that’s not true. Sometimes they helped each other, sometimes they didn’t talk much, and only sometimes did they argue.
sf_a13.talk: Can you think of a time when you learned something new and it helped you understand something at church better?

sf_a14.happened: In April 2003, the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium announced the successful completion of the Human Genome Project, a monumental scientific endeavor that mapped the entire human DNA sequence. This project, initiated in 1990, aimed to identify and map all the genes in human DNA, determining the sequences of the three billion chemical base pairs that make up the human genome. Under the leadership of Dr. Francis Collins, the project was completed ahead of schedule and under budget, providing a comprehensive reference for human genetics. The completion of this project marked a significant milestone in understanding the genetic blueprint of human life, paving the way for advancements in medicine and biology.
sf_a14.background: Before the Human Genome Project, scientists had limited knowledge of the human genetic code. The 1980s and 1990s saw rapid advancements in DNA sequencing technologies, but the task of mapping the entire human genome was daunting. Daily life during this period was witnessing the rise of personal computers and the internet, which facilitated global collaboration among scientists. Dr. Francis Collins, a physician-geneticist, was appointed director of the National Human Genome Research Institute in 1993. His leadership was instrumental in coordinating the international effort to sequence the human genome, bringing together researchers from around the world to achieve this ambitious goal.
sf_a14.matters: The completion of the Human Genome Project has profound implications for medicine and our understanding of human biology. It has enabled researchers to identify genes associated with various diseases, leading to improved diagnostics and targeted therapies. For families of faith, this achievement underscores the harmony between scientific discovery and belief in a divine Creator. Understanding the genetic code can be seen as uncovering the intricate design with which Heavenly Father created life, offering a deeper appreciation for the complexity and beauty of His creations.
sf_a14.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the divine creation of life. In the Book of Moses, we read, "And I, God, created man in mine own image" (Moses 2:27). This passage emphasizes that humans are created in the image of God, reflecting His divine nature. The study of the human genome can be viewed as exploring the intricate details of that divine image, deepening our understanding of God's handiwork.
sf_a14.evidence: The completion of the Human Genome Project is well-documented in scientific literature and official reports. The National Human Genome Research Institute provides detailed information about the project's goals, progress, and outcomes. The project successfully mapped 99% of the human genome with an accuracy of 99.99%, covering the euchromatic regions of the genome. This monumental achievement was the result of international collaboration and technological innovation, setting the stage for future research in genetics and personalized medicine.
sf_a14.learn: The Human Genome Project teaches us the value of perseverance, collaboration, and the pursuit of knowledge. It demonstrates how scientific endeavors can uncover the mysteries of life, aligning with our faith in a Creator who designed the universe with purpose and order. This achievement encourages us to seek understanding and wisdom, recognizing that science and faith can complement each other in revealing the wonders of creation.
sf_a14.child: Scientists worked together to read all the instructions in our DNA, like a big book that tells our bodies how to grow and work. This helps doctors understand how to help people when they are sick.
sf_a14.talk: How do you think understanding our DNA helps doctors take care of us?

sf_a15.happened: In 2026, real tension remains between faith and science, not because these two ways of understanding the world must always fight, but because there are still subjects where they come to different conclusions. Some of the sharpest disagreements come up around topics like how old the earth actually is and how life came to be. Many scientists accept that the earth is billions of years old and that life slowly changed over time through evolution. But some people of faith, including members of several Christian denominations, believe the earth and its life are much younger and were created in ways different from what most scientists describe. Other areas of tension include bioethics—questions about what is right and wrong when it comes to research on embryos, when life begins and ends, and new medical technologies. These are not just technical debates, but heartfelt issues touching people’s deepest beliefs about life and what it means to be human. Surveys also show that, in some countries, people who work in science are less likely to say they are religious compared with the general population, which sometimes adds to the sense that science and faith belong to different worlds. At the same time, historians warn against claims that faith created modern science single-handedly, or that they can never get along. Instead, they find that science grew from many roots, including ancient Greeks, Muslims, and medieval thinkers. Faith and science are not natural enemies, but it is honest to admit they still sometimes disagree.
sf_a15.background: The world in which this tension is acknowledged is a highly connected, deeply scientific, but also deeply religious place. Billions of people still find meaning in faith, even as technology changes daily life in almost every country. People’s days are filled with information from the internet, advanced medicine, and a growing understanding of the universe. Yet, their traditions, stories, and values often come from sacred texts. Scientists now often work in large teams across countries, and discoveries about genes, the cosmos, and the brain spark hope and new questions. Parents and children may pray together in the morning, then read the latest news about scientific discoveries at night. Many want both truth from science and wisdom from faith but find the two do not always seem to speak the same language, especially on topics that matter a great deal to their communities.
sf_a15.matters: This ongoing disagreement matters for several reasons. For families of faith, it means there are some questions where loving God and respecting science do not give neat, matching answers. Parents must teach their children to value honest questions, humility, and careful listening—very important skills in today’s world. The debate also shows that neither faith nor science has all the answers or gets everything right all at once. This can help families pause, pray, and study out important issues together, relying on both revelation and reason. For the world, it is a call to treat people’s convictions with respect, even if we disagree, and to keep learning from both spiritual and scientific insights.
sf_a15.scripture: The scriptures do not directly address modern scientific debates, but they give principles to guide us. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, the Lord asks us to seek learning by study and also by faith. The Bible teaches to love God with all our heart, soul, and mind (Matthew 22:37), and to prove all things and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Book of Mormon tells us to ask God for guidance (Moroni 10:5), trusting that truth, whether discovered through nature or revelation, will ultimately come from Him. These verses encourage a humble, searching attitude in every area of life.
sf_a15.evidence: Historical and scientific evidence shows both conflict and cooperation between faith and science. For example, most geologists and biologists agree that the earth is about 4.5 billion years old and that all living things share common ancestry—a view tested and supported by many lines of evidence, from fossils to DNA. Yet, many sincere believers interpret sacred texts differently, and continue to hold to a young earth or special creation by God. Bioethical questions, like research on embryos, raise serious moral disagreements shaped by different religious backgrounds. Surveys from the Pew Research Center reveal that scientists are, on average, less religious than others in some places, but far from universally so—many scientists still believe in God. Historians like Noah Efron and Lawrence Principe show that the scientific revolution was shaped by many cultures and times, not just the western Christian world.
sf_a15.learn: We can learn that both faith and science are gifts from God, meant to help us grow in understanding. But like any tool, each has limits and strengths. Admitting there is real disagreement allows us to treat each other kindly, to honor the journey of learning, and to keep asking questions instead of shutting down discussion. This humility and curiosity can strengthen families, encourage discovery, and invite God’s Spirit as we search for greater truth, trusting He will guide us step by step.
sf_a15.child: Sometimes people who love God and people who love science do not agree on everything, like how the world was made. That is all right. We can ask questions, listen kindly, and remember that both faith and science help us discover new things.
sf_a15.talk: What is something you wonder about where the answers from faith and science seem different?

sf_a16.happened: Throughout history, many of the world's most renowned scientists have been deeply religious individuals. Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed the heliocentric model of the universe, served as a cathedral canon. Johannes Kepler, known for his laws of planetary motion, initially trained for the ministry. Isaac Newton, famous for his laws of motion and gravity, wrote extensively on theology, producing more works on religious topics than on physics. Gregor Mendel, the father of modern genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Michael Faraday, a pioneer in electromagnetism, was a devout Christian and served as a lay preacher. Georges Lemaître, who formulated the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. Francis Collins, the geneticist who led the Human Genome Project, is an outspoken believer. Ibn al-Haytham, a medieval Muslim scientist, made significant contributions to optics and was deeply devout. Despite these strong connections between faith and scientific inquiry, historical records indicate that the Church formally prosecuted only one scientist, Galileo Galilei, for his scientific ideas. This suggests that, contrary to popular belief, the relationship between religion and science has often been collaborative rather than adversarial.
sf_a16.background: In the periods leading up to the Scientific Revolution, Europe was deeply influenced by religious institutions. The Church played a central role in education, governance, and daily life. Many universities were established by religious organizations, and clerics were among the most educated individuals of the time. This environment fostered a worldview where studying nature was seen as a way to understand God's creation. The belief that the universe was orderly and governed by laws set by a rational Creator provided a foundation for systematic scientific inquiry. This perspective was not unique to Christianity; in the Islamic world, scholars like Ibn al-Haytham pursued scientific studies as a means to comprehend the divine order. Daily life was intertwined with religious practices, and the pursuit of knowledge was often considered a form of worship.
sf_a16.matters: Understanding the historical interplay between faith and science highlights that religious belief has often been a driving force behind scientific exploration. For families of faith, this underscores the idea that seeking knowledge about the natural world can be a way to honor and understand God's creation. It challenges the notion that science and religion are inherently in conflict, showing instead that they can coexist and even complement each other. Recognizing this harmony can inspire both scientific curiosity and spiritual growth, encouraging individuals to explore the world with a sense of wonder and purpose.
sf_a16.scripture: The scriptures encourage the pursuit of knowledge and understanding. In Proverbs 25:2, it is written, "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter." This suggests that seeking to understand the mysteries of the universe is a noble endeavor. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:79 advises to learn "of things both in heaven and in the earth, and under the earth; things which have been, things which are, things which must shortly come to pass." These passages support the idea that studying the natural world is aligned with divine instruction.
sf_a16.evidence: Historical records show that many pioneering scientists were deeply religious and viewed their scientific work as a means to understand and glorify God. For instance, Isaac Newton's theological writings reveal his belief that studying the natural world was a way to uncover divine truths. Similarly, Johannes Kepler saw his astronomical work as uncovering the geometric plan of God's creation. The case of Galileo Galilei, often cited as evidence of conflict between science and religion, was complex and involved political and personal factors beyond his scientific theories. Modern historians recognize that, while there have been instances of tension, the overall relationship between Christianity and the development of science has been largely positive. The Church's support for education and the establishment of universities provided a fertile ground for scientific inquiry.
sf_a16.learn: Recognizing the historical collaboration between faith and science teaches us that curiosity and belief are not mutually exclusive. It encourages us to explore the world with an open mind, seeking to understand the natural laws that govern it while maintaining a sense of spiritual purpose. This perspective fosters a holistic approach to learning, where scientific discovery and religious faith enrich each other.
sf_a16.child: Many famous scientists loved God and wanted to learn about His world. They believed that by studying nature, they could understand more about God's creation. This shows us that learning about science can be a way to get closer to God.
sf_a16.talk: Can you think of something in nature that makes you feel amazed about God's creation?

fa01.happened: Judaism began about 4,000 years ago, around the time of Abraham, in a land called Canaan, which is now mostly Israel and nearby places. According to Jewish tradition and the Bible, Heavenly Father made a sacred promise called a covenant with Abraham and his family. The Lord promised to bless Abraham, give him many descendants, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abraham, his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob are often called the patriarchs of Judaism. Over centuries, their families grew and became a people—later called Israelites—who believed in one God and followed His teachings. God gave them special laws and commandments, most famously through Moses, including the Ten Commandments. Life was not easy: they were sometimes slaves, sometimes wanderers, sometimes kings and then exiles. Even when scattered across many lands, Jews kept their faith, traditions, and hope in God's promises. Judaism remains a living faith, practiced by families all over the world, sharing many stories also found in the Christian Old Testament.
fa01.background: Before Judaism, most people in the world worshipped many gods and followed the customs of their tribe or city. Canaan, where Abraham traveled, was filled with small villages and towns, each with their own idols and ways of life. Families lived in tents or small houses, raised animals like sheep, and grew crops. Society was organized around clans and families, and traditions were passed down by word of mouth. The idea of one God who cared for all people was very different from the beliefs of their neighbors. Since there were no written scriptures yet, stories of Abraham and his family were shared by telling and retelling them, especially as they traveled and moved to new places. Over time, these stories were written down and became the Jewish scriptures.
fa01.matters: Judaism matters because it introduced the powerful idea that all people are children of one loving God who makes promises and calls people to live righteous lives. For families of faith, every story in the Old Testament is part of this history. Christianity comes from these same roots, believing Jesus is the fulfillment of God's promises to Abraham. Learning about Judaism helps us understand our own spiritual family tree, to respect others' faiths, and to see how God's work can move across centuries and cultures. It also teaches about staying true to beliefs even when living among those who believe differently.
fa01.scripture: Many scriptures speak of the covenant the Lord made with Abraham. Genesis 12:1-3 describes God calling Abraham and promising to bless all nations through him. Galatians 3:8-9 in the New Testament teaches that this covenant found its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon often refers to the house of Israel and the promises given to Abraham and his children (see 1 Nephi 15:18, 3 Nephi 20:25-27). Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 mentions the return of the keys of the gathering of Israel, further connecting this ancient promise to the latter days.
fa01.evidence: Most historians agree that the stories of Abraham and the earliest patriarchs were passed down by word of mouth for many generations before being written. Archaeologists have found evidence of towns and practices in ancient Canaan that fit what the Bible describes. However, there is no direct archaeological proof for Abraham himself. Later figures, like King David and the existence of ancient Israel, have strong evidence, including inscriptions and buildings. The Jewish people's survival and traditions, even after thousands of years of being scattered and sometimes persecuted, are a testament to their deep faith and commitment. While the story's details are debated, Judaism’s ancient roots and influence are well supported historically.
fa01.learn: We can learn that being faithful, even when it’s hard or unpopular, can bless families and many others, just like Abraham’s family did. Technology, like scripture apps or family history tools, can help us remember and share our own family covenants and stories. Understanding Judaism reminds us that God keeps His promises and that every family is important in His plan.
fa01.child: A long time ago, Heavenly Father made big promises to Abraham and his family. They trusted God, even when things were hard. Because of them, we have many stories and blessings, too.
fa01.talk: Why do you think God keeps telling families His promises, instead of just one person?
