fa02.happened: Around 563 BC, in a place called Bodh Gaya in India, a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama lived in a palace with every luxury. Yet, he was troubled by suffering he saw in the world—pain, old age, and death. Leaving behind his royal life, he traveled and sought answers through deep thinking and meditation under a tree known now as the Bodhi Tree. After much effort and reflection, Siddhartha gained insight, or 'enlightenment,' understanding the causes of suffering and how to overcome them. He became known as the Buddha, meaning 'The Awakened One.' The Buddha spent the rest of his life teaching others a path called the Dharma, which centers on living with wisdom, compassion, and moderation to end suffering and find true peace. His teachings spread widely, and today, millions follow this way of life, called Buddhism, striving to be kind and mindful wherever they live.
fa02.background: India in the sixth century BC was a land of many kingdoms, each with its own rulers, customs, and beliefs. Most people lived in small villages, farming the land or trading goods in busy town markets. Society was divided into castes, or social classes, with strict rules about one’s place and duties. Religion was important, centered largely on many gods, rituals, and sacrifices led by priests. It was also a time of great questioning, as some people started to wonder about deeper meaning beyond everyday struggles. The Buddha grew up during this period, surrounded by both great wealth and the stark realities of suffering, which made him wonder if there was a better way to live. He was not the only philosopher of his age; in other parts of the world, teachers like Confucius and Pythagoras were asking big questions, too.
fa02.matters: Buddhism’s way of teaching compassion and wisdom has influenced how entire cultures think about respect, peace, and kindness for thousands of years. For families of faith, it offers a view of God’s love at work, planting seeds of truth in many places. Even though most Buddhists do not speak of Heavenly Father in the ways Christians do, their focus on kindness echoes what Jesus taught: to love others and care for those who suffer. Learning about Buddhism helps children see how Heavenly Father’s light can be found in every nation and culture, preparing people to receive more truth.
fa02.scripture: While the scriptures of the Church do not talk directly about the Buddha, several teachings from the Bible and Book of Mormon relate to the Buddhist focus on compassion and ending suffering. The Savior taught, "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Matthew 5:7) and commanded, "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39). In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 invites believers to "bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light" and to "mourn with those that mourn." These principles encourage us to feel and show compassion, just as Buddhism teaches.
fa02.evidence: Most historians agree that Siddhartha Gautama, later known as the Buddha, was a real person who lived in northern India and taught the ideas that we now call Buddhism. Ancient texts, such as the Pali Canon, were written down several hundred years after his life, preserving his teachings. Archaeological sites like Bodh Gaya, where he is said to have reached enlightenment, are visited by pilgrims to this day. Artifacts, such as ancient sculptures and carvings, show how early followers honored his memory. While the exact dates and some details of his life are still debated, scholars generally believe he lived in the sixth century BC and shaped world religion through his teachings.
fa02.learn: Buddhism teaches us that seeking peace and compassion is good for everyone. We learn that every person struggles, and that being gentle and understanding—rather than judging or ignoring others' pain—can help heal hearts. For Latter-day Saint families, seeing what is good and true in other religions helps us respect our neighbors and recognize God’s hand across the world. It reminds us to act with love, just as Christ would.
fa02.child: A long time ago, a man named the Buddha taught people how to be kind and wise so they could be happy and help others. Even today, many people try to follow his example and make the world a kinder place. Loving and helping others is something Jesus taught too.
fa02.talk: What is one way we can show kindness or help someone who is having a hard time?

fa03.happened: In the early 7th century, a man named Muhammad lived in Mecca, a bustling city in present-day Saudi Arabia. Around the year 610 AD, during a period of deep reflection in a cave called Hira, Muhammad experienced a profound event. He reported that the angel Gabriel appeared to him, delivering messages from God. These messages, emphasizing the oneness of God and calling for moral and social reform, were later compiled into the Quran, the holy book of Islam. Initially, Muhammad shared these revelations privately, but as he began to preach publicly, he and his followers faced increasing opposition from Meccan leaders who felt threatened by his teachings. In 622 AD, to escape persecution, Muhammad and his followers migrated to the city of Yathrib, later known as Medina. This migration, called the Hijra, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina, Muhammad established a community based on the principles revealed to him, uniting various tribes under the new faith. Over the next decade, Islam spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. By 632 AD, when Muhammad passed away, Islam had become a significant religious and social force in the region.
fa03.background: Before Islam's emergence, the Arabian Peninsula was a land of diverse tribes and cultures. Mecca, Muhammad's birthplace, was a significant trade hub, attracting merchants and travelers from various regions. The city was also home to the Kaaba, a sacred sanctuary housing numerous idols worshiped by different tribes. Society was predominantly tribal, with loyalty to one's clan being paramount. While some communities practiced monotheistic beliefs, such as Judaism and Christianity, polytheism was widespread. The region lacked a centralized political authority, leading to frequent inter-tribal conflicts. Economically, the area relied heavily on trade, with caravans transporting goods like spices, textiles, and incense across vast deserts. Socially, there were stark inequalities, with a clear divide between the wealthy elite and the impoverished. Practices like infanticide, especially of female infants, and the marginalization of certain groups were common. This was the world into which Muhammad was born, a society ripe for the transformative messages he would later convey.
fa03.matters: The founding of Islam has had a profound impact on world history, shaping cultures, laws, and societies across continents. For families of faith, understanding Islam's origins offers insights into the shared values and teachings among Abrahamic religions. Islam's emphasis on monotheism, compassion, and social justice resonates with principles found in other faith traditions. Recognizing these commonalities fosters mutual respect and understanding among diverse religious communities. Additionally, Islam's reverence for figures like Jesus and Mary highlights the interconnectedness of religious narratives, encouraging families to appreciate the rich tapestry of global faiths.
fa03.scripture: While the scriptures of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints do not directly reference the founding of Islam, they emphasize principles of seeking truth and understanding among all people. The Book of Mormon teaches, "All are alike unto God" (2 Nephi 26:33), underscoring the importance of recognizing the worth and contributions of diverse cultures and beliefs. Doctrine and Covenants encourages believers to "seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom" (D&C 88:118), promoting the pursuit of knowledge and understanding from various sources. These teachings inspire an attitude of respect and learning towards all of God's children, including those of different faith traditions.
fa03.evidence: Historical records provide a detailed account of Muhammad's life and the early development of Islam. Islamic tradition, preserved through oral and written histories, offers insights into his experiences and the societal changes he initiated. Archaeological findings, such as early Quranic manuscripts, support the textual preservation of the Quran. The rapid expansion of Islam after Muhammad's death is documented through various historical sources, illustrating its significant influence on subsequent civilizations. While some aspects of early Islamic history are debated among scholars, the core events surrounding Muhammad's life and the establishment of Islam are well-documented and widely accepted.
fa03.learn: Studying the founding of Islam teaches us the power of faith to inspire societal transformation. It highlights the importance of compassion, justice, and community in addressing social inequalities. Recognizing the shared values among different faiths encourages mutual respect and understanding. This knowledge empowers families to engage in meaningful dialogues with people of diverse backgrounds, fostering a more inclusive and harmonious world.
fa03.child: Long ago, a man named Muhammad received messages from God, teaching people to be kind and fair. These teachings grew into the religion of Islam, which many people follow today.
fa03.talk: What can we learn from other people's beliefs that helps us be better friends and neighbors?

e01.happened: Around 2334 BC, Sargon of Akkad rose to power in Mesopotamia, uniting the previously independent Sumerian city-states under his rule. He established the city of Akkad as his capital, creating the world's first known empire. Sargon expanded his territory through military conquests, extending his influence across Mesopotamia, the Levant, and parts of Iran and Anatolia. His grandson, Naram-Sin, continued this expansion, declaring himself a living god and adopting the title "King of the Four Quarters." The Akkadian Empire centralized administration, standardized weights and measures, and developed a postal system. The Akkadian language became the empire's lingua franca, while Sumerian remained important in religious and literary contexts. The empire eventually faced internal revolts, dynastic instability, and external threats, leading to its collapse around 2154 BC.
e01.background: Before the rise of the Akkadian Empire, Mesopotamia was a region of independent city-states, each with its own ruler and governance. The Sumerians, who inhabited this area, developed one of the earliest known writing systems—cuneiform—and made significant advancements in agriculture, architecture, and law. Daily life was centered around agriculture, with communities relying on the fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Trade was vital, connecting Mesopotamia with neighboring regions. The Akkadian people, a Semitic group, lived alongside the Sumerians, sharing and blending cultural practices over time.
e01.matters: The Akkadian Empire's establishment marked a significant shift from city-states to a centralized imperial system, setting a precedent for future empires. It facilitated cultural and technological exchanges across a vast region, influencing subsequent civilizations. For families of faith, the empire's role in preserving and transmitting writing and legal traditions is noteworthy, as these developments eventually contributed to the recording and dissemination of sacred scriptures.
e01.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the Akkadian Empire, they reference the city of Ur, a significant Sumerian city that became part of the Akkadian Empire. Abraham, a central figure in the Bible, was born in Ur (Genesis 11:31). This connection highlights how the Lord placed His covenant family within the heart of early civilizations, positioning them to influence and be influenced by the broader cultural and historical contexts of their time.
e01.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as cuneiform tablets and inscriptions, provide substantial evidence of the Akkadian Empire's existence and its administrative and cultural practices. Notable artifacts include the Bassetki Statue, which bears inscriptions from Naram-Sin's reign. Despite extensive research, the exact location of the city of Akkad remains undiscovered, adding an element of mystery to this ancient empire. Recent studies have also explored the impact of climatic changes on the empire's collapse, suggesting that severe droughts may have contributed to its downfall.
e01.learn: The story of the Akkadian Empire teaches us about the complexities of governance, the importance of cultural integration, and the challenges of maintaining a vast, diverse empire. It also underscores the significance of preserving knowledge and traditions, as these efforts have long-lasting impacts on future generations.
e01.child: Long ago, a king named Sargon united many cities to create the first empire. His grandson, Naram-Sin, continued to expand this empire, bringing many people together under one rule.
e01.talk: Why do you think it's important to learn about ancient empires like the Akkadian Empire?

e02.happened: Around 1894 to 1595 BC, the Babylonian Empire rose to power in the land that is now called Iraq. Babylon started as one city among many in an area called Mesopotamia, where people had farmed and traded along the big rivers for thousands of years. Hammurabi, the king who ruled from 1792 to 1750 BC, became known as the leader who united these separate city-states into one growing empire. Hammurabi was a wise and determined ruler. He led armies to bring other cities under Babylon's control, but he also cared about his people and wanted everyone to have protection and fairness. Hammurabi’s most lasting achievement was his law code, which he had carved into huge stones for everyone to read. These laws covered many parts of daily life—from trade and property to marriage and justice. By making his laws public, Hammurabi set an example: the law stood above even the king. People could know what was expected and trust that judgments would be fair. This strong government helped Babylon prosper in trade, building, and learning for generations.
e02.background: The world where Babylon rose was ancient and full of change. Mesopotamia means 'land between the rivers'—the Tigris and Euphrates—where some of the earliest cities and writing began. Before Babylon grew strong, many small city-states like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash had taken turns being powerful. People worked as farmers, traders, craftsmen, and soldiers, and families lived in mud-brick houses. Religion shaped daily life; people honored gods through temples and feasts. Travel was slow, mostly by foot or on animals, and stories were told in pictures on clay tablets. Into this busy world came Hammurabi, who taught that good laws could help everyone live in peace, even when they were different from each other.
e02.matters: The Babylonian Empire matters today because it showed, early in history, that a fair and organized set of laws could help a whole nation hold together. Families of faith notice that laws like Hammurabi’s taught ideas of fairness and taking care of the weak—principles that later influenced the way the Israelites made laws under Moses. When laws are fair and known by everyone, people can trust each other and feel safe. The way Hammurabi set up his code helped prepare the world for later laws that protect freedom, including the freedom to worship.
e02.scripture: In Genesis 11, the Bible describes the city of Babel (later Babylon) and the scattering of peoples and languages. Abraham, an important prophet, was born in Ur, a city within this world. While the scriptures do not mention Hammurabi or his laws, the Law of Moses in Exodus 20–24 shares some similar rules about justice, care for others, and fairness—showing how God values just laws. Doctrine and Covenants 134 also teaches that good laws help keep peace and protect our rights.
e02.evidence: Archaeologists have found the remains of Babylon and many of its written tablets. The most famous object is the black stone stele showing Hammurabi receiving his laws from the sun god Shamash, with all 282 laws written below. This stele can be seen in the Louvre Museum in Paris. Copies of Hammurabi’s code turn up across the region, showing it was well known. Other tablets and ruins match what history tells us about Babylon’s power, trade, and daily life. Scholars generally agree that Hammurabi was a real person, and his empire and laws are well documented in these ancient records.
e02.learn: We learn from Hammurabi’s story that laws are meant to bless people’s lives—not just control them. When laws are fair to all, it builds trust and safety for families and neighbors. Even today, we remember that God wants us to treat others as we wish to be treated. Like the Babylonians, we can use our own talents and tools, including technology, to help make our communities stronger and kinder.
e02.child: A long time ago, a king named Hammurabi made rules to help people be fair and safe. He wanted everyone—even himself—to follow the same laws. That way, families could know what was right and trust each other.
e02.talk: Why do you think it is important for everyone to follow the same rules, even the king or the president?

e16.happened: Around 3100 BC, a leader named Narmer brought together two great regions along the Nile River: Upper Egypt to the south, and Lower Egypt to the north, near the Mediterranean Sea. Before this, people lived in smaller kingdoms along the river, but Narmer’s unification marked the birth of one of the world’s first long-lasting empires. Ancient Egypt became known for its powerful rulers, who were called pharaohs. Over the centuries, they built remarkable cities, massive stone pyramids, and temples that still stand today. Some pharaohs like Khufu, who built the Great Pyramid at Giza, or Ramesses II, known for his grand monuments, became legendary. Egypt’s society was organized, with scribes, artists, farmers, priests, and skilled builders. The Egyptians invented a written script called hieroglyphics and developed papyrus, an early form of paper that kept their knowledge alive for future generations. Their ideas about life after death were deep and hopeful; they believed in resurrection and the importance of living well. Ancient Egypt lasted as a civilization for almost three thousand years until 332 BC, when Alexander the Great conquered the land and Greek rulers like Cleopatra VII finally ruled, ending the ancient kingdom’s story.
e16.background: Before Egypt rose as a united kingdom, smaller groups lived along the Nile, making the most of the river’s rich soil for farming. Their daily lives centered on the rhythm of the Nile’s floods, planting crops like wheat and barley, and fishing in its waters. Egyptians built mud-brick houses and worshipped many gods, believing the land was sacred. Society had clear roles: while pharaohs and priests held power, most people were farmers, craftsmen, or builders. Egypt traded with neighbors and shared ideas as they fashioned a stable, protected society thanks to the deserts and seas surrounding them. Family and community were at the heart of life, and children learned their place in the world from a young age. Over time, villages turned into cities, and with the unification under Narmer, Egypt’s culture began to shine bright, setting the stage for centuries of achievement.
e16.matters: The story of Ancient Egypt matters because it shows how people, when united by good leadership and common purpose, can build something that lasts for ages. Egyptian inventions—like paper, the calendar, and early medicine—touch our lives even today. For families of faith, Egypt’s part in scripture, particularly with figures like Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, offers lessons of hope and deliverance. The Egyptians’ belief in the afterlife and resurrection echoes truths found in the gospel, reminding us of Heavenly Father’s care in every age. Learning about Egypt helps us see how the Lord prepares and preserves His people, even in unexpected ways.
e16.scripture: The Bible mentions Egypt many times. Genesis 12 recounts Abraham’s journey to Egypt. Genesis 37-50 tells Joseph’s story—how he was sold by his brothers, rose to power in Egypt, and helped preserve his family. Exodus 1-14 records Moses’ early life in Pharaoh’s household and the Israelites’ escape from bondage. Egypt’s role as both oppressor and protector is seen throughout scripture. Doctrine and Covenants 136:1-3 reminds us that the Lord guides and delivers His people in every dispensation. These stories teach that even in difficult places, God provides a way forward.
e16.evidence: Archaeologists have found many things from Ancient Egypt—temples, tombs, pyramids, and objects buried with the dead. The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, helped scholars finally read Egyptian hieroglyphics. This has let us learn about Egypt directly from its ancient records. The Great Pyramid of Giza still stands today, showing the Egyptians’ skill in building. Wall paintings and papyrus scrolls give us glimpses of daily life, religious beliefs, and the rulers who led Egypt through centuries. Evidence supports the key facts: Egypt united under one king roughly around 3100 BC and endured for millennia as a lasting civilization.
e16.learn: Studying Ancient Egypt teaches us about working together, honoring knowledge, and remembering our past. We also see how faith in something greater can shape a people’s choices and hopes. As we learn about their mistakes and successes, we can better understand ourselves and how Heavenly Father guides people in every time and place to do good.
e16.child: Long ago, people in Egypt worked together to build huge pyramids and write on special paper called papyrus. The Bible tells us stories about Joseph and Moses in Egypt, showing us that God cares for us, no matter where we are.
e16.talk: Why do you think God wanted Joseph and Moses to go to Egypt?

e03.happened: During the days of the Egyptian New Kingdom, from about 1550 to 1070 BC, Egypt became one of the most powerful empires the world had ever seen. It began when strong leaders drove out the Hyksos, a group of foreign rulers, and united Upper and Lower Egypt again. The pharaohs who ruled during this time—like Thutmose III, who led armies far beyond Egypt, and Ramesses II, known for his long reign and mighty building projects—expanded Egypt's control into neighboring lands. Akhenaten tried to change Egypt’s religion to worship one main god, Aten, while his son Tutankhamun is famous today for his tomb filled with treasures. People from many lands came to Egypt’s great cities, and the Nile River made the land rich with food. During this time, the Hebrews, led by Joseph and later Moses, lived in and eventually left Egypt. Stories of pyramids, mummies, and hieroglyphs come from this period, showing Egypt’s deep beliefs about life after death. The arts, sciences, and government of Egypt influenced the world for centuries.
e03.background: Before the New Kingdom, Egypt was weakened by the rule of the Hyksos, a foreign people who introduced new tools and ways of fighting. Egyptians from the south fought back, drove out the Hyksos, and reunited the land under a powerful line of kings called pharaohs. Egypt’s people lived by the Nile River, which flooded each year, making the soil good for farming. Most Egyptians were farmers, but there were also builders, artists, traders, and scribes. Kings and queens lived in palaces, but even poorer people had simple homes and rich religious lives. Families honored gods, told stories about the afterlife, and worked together to build mighty monuments. The kingdom stretched south into Nubia and north toward the Mediterranean Sea, making Egypt a connected, bustling place.
e03.matters: The Egyptian New Kingdom matters because it shaped so much of what we know about ancient civilization. Egypt’s story overlaps with the earliest parts of the Bible, and its rulers, buildings, and writing inspired later peoples all over the world. For families of faith, Egypt's story reminds us that even in powerful nations, God watches over His people, as He did with Joseph and Moses. The lessons of liberation from oppression and the importance of faith in hard times come from these years. Studying this era helps us see the patterns of pride, repentance, and deliverance in both history and our own lives.
e03.scripture: Many stories in Genesis and Exodus happen during Egypt’s mighty days, including Joseph’s rise to power (Genesis 41) and Moses leading the Israelites out of slavery (Exodus 1–14). The Book of Mormon mentions Egypt as a center of learning (1 Nephi 1:2), and Doctrine and Covenants 8:3 mentions Moses parting the Red Sea. Although the scriptures do not describe the New Kingdom’s history in detail, they show how God’s purposes continue even when His people live among other nations.
e03.evidence: Archaeologists have found many buildings, tombs, and objects from the New Kingdom, such as temples at Karnak and Luxor, and the nearly intact tomb of Tutankhamun. Hieroglyphic records tell us how pharaohs ruled, fought wars, and honored their gods. The Merneptah Stele, carved around 1208 BC, is important because it is the first Egyptian record to mention a people called "Israel" in Canaan, supporting the idea that Israelites lived in the land after leaving Egypt. Scholars use these records, pottery, and ancient writings to confirm the basic outline of Egypt’s power and influence, though specific links to individuals like Moses are still debated.
e03.learn: From Egypt’s New Kingdom, we learn how nations rise and fall, how families stay strong in changing times, and how God watches over people everywhere. We also see what happens when people use their talents to build, create, and worship, for good or for selfish reasons. This story encourages us to trust in God and to remember that even the mightiest empires are part of His larger plan.
e03.child: Long ago, Egypt was a place of kings and pyramids. Moses and Joseph lived there, and God helped His people when times were hard. Today, we can learn from their stories and trust that God helps us too.
e03.talk: How did God help His people when they were living in a powerful place like Egypt?

e04.happened: The Assyrian Empire became one of the most powerful empires of the ancient world, lasting from about 911 to 609 BC. It rose in Mesopotamia, the region known today as Iraq, and was known for its strong military and advanced use of iron weapons. Under rulers like Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib, and Ashurbanipal, the Assyrians conquered many lands, including parts of what are now Syria, Turkey, and Israel. Their armies were disciplined and often used fear to keep subjects in line. One of their most famous acts was the conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC. After this, many Israelites were taken from their homes and scattered throughout the empire, beginning what became known as the lost tribes of Israel. The Assyrian capital city, Nineveh, grew into one of the greatest cities of its day, with great walls and beautiful palaces. Ashurbanipal, one of the final strong kings, created a great library at Nineveh that kept thousands of clay tablets, including stories like the Epic of Gilgamesh. The empire eventually fell as Babylon and other peoples joined together to conquer it, but its influence shaped much of the region’s history.
e04.background: Before the Assyrian Empire, Mesopotamia had seen many rulers come and go, from the Sumerians and Akkadians to the Babylonians. The people of Assyria were known for building fortified cities along the Tigris River. Most people farmed, raised animals, or worked as craftsmen. Religion played a large part in daily life, with temples dedicated to gods like Ashur and Ishtar. Life could be hard, as the region often saw battles for control. Writing and reading were important for record keeping, and the rich and powerful could enjoy art, music, and beautiful gardens. Ordinary families often lived in small mud-brick houses and worked together to gather enough food, water, and safety for their children.
e04.matters: The Assyrian Empire shaped history by spreading people, ideas, and technology across a wide area. The scattering of the Israelites began a process that later prophets and modern scripture speak of as key to God’s plan for gathering His children. For families of faith, the story is a reminder that even when people are scattered or face hard times, Heavenly Father is aware of them and can use every part of history, both good and bad, for His ultimate purposes.
e04.scripture: Several Bible stories directly mention the Assyrians, especially 2 Kings 17, which tells how Assyria conquered Israel and took many people away. The story of Jonah visiting Nineveh is found in the Book of Jonah, showing that the Lord cared about the people living in Assyria, just as He cares for everyone. Modern scripture (such as Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 and 133:7-14) talks about the latter-day gathering of Israel, a promise that began with events like the Assyrian conquest. While the Book of Mormon does not mention Assyria by name, it speaks of scattering and gathering as God’s work.
e04.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered palace ruins, carved wall panels, and thousands of clay tablets from Assyria, especially in the ancient city of Nineveh. The Library of Ashurbanipal remains one of the most famous finds, helping us understand not only Assyrian history but also stories of that era. Ancient royal records, as well as records from other lands, confirm much of the written history about Assyria’s rule and its conquest of Israel. Archaeologists have also found inscriptions and artifacts that match people and places found in the Bible, helping historians be confident in much of what is written about the empire. For example, the British Museum and other institutions hold many such artifacts.
e04.learn: From the Assyrian Empire, we learn that power can rise and fall, and that the choices leaders make can change the lives of whole nations. We see that even when things are hard or seem scattered, Heavenly Father still remembers and works with all His children. Their story invites us to look for God’s hand in history and to remember that knowledge and records, like Ashurbanipal’s library, are precious gifts to be preserved.
e04.child: Long ago, the Assyrians were strong rulers who built big cities and won many battles. They took people from their homes, but God still loved and watched over everyone. Even hard times can be part of Heavenly Father’s big plan.
e04.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wanted Jonah to teach the people of Nineveh, even though they weren’t from Israel?

e05.happened: The Neo-Babylonian Empire was a powerful kingdom that rose up in Mesopotamia around 626 BC, following the decline of the Assyrian Empire. The story began when Nabopolassar, a Babylonian leader, led a revolt against the Assyrians, eventually defeating them and making Babylon the main power in the region. His son, Nebuchadnezzar II, became the most famous king. Nebuchadnezzar built impressive cities, led grand armies, and conquered lands nearby—including Jerusalem. In 586 BC, Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers captured Jerusalem, destroyed its beautiful temple, and took many Jewish people to live in Babylon. This time is called the Babylonian Captivity. While life in Babylon was strange and hard for those taken from Jerusalem, the city was full of wonders like the Hanging Gardens, said to be one of the ancient world’s greatest marvels. It was during this period that important Jewish scriptures and traditions were gathered and preserved, even while families learned to live in a new land and serve God in a foreign place.
e05.background: Before the Neo-Babylonian Empire, Mesopotamia was ruled by the Assyrians, known for their strong armies and large cities but also their harsh rule. The people of Babylon were part of a long line of civilizations that had lived between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers—one of the earliest places people built cities, wrote with marks on clay tablets, and traded goods like grain and wool. Daily life in Babylon was busy and impressive: tall ziggurat temples stood over bustling markets, artisans crafted jewelry and pottery, and everyone from powerful priests to farmers helped the city thrive. When Babylon became an empire, it reached west into the land of Judah, home to the Israelite people.
e05.matters: The rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire changed the ancient world forever. Babylon became a center of learning, culture, and power. For families of faith, this moment matters deeply because it set the stage for well-known Bible stories of faith and courage—like Daniel in the lions’ den—and the preservation of scripture that still blesses lives today. Even when hard things happen, like the loss of Jerusalem, Heavenly Father can help His people learn and grow in new places, preparing the way for future blessings.
e05.scripture: The story of the Babylonian Empire and its effect on Jerusalem can be found throughout the Old Testament. Daniel, Ezekiel, and later Esther, each lived and served Heavenly Father in Babylon (see Daniel 1; Ezekiel 1; Esther 1). 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39:1–10 describe the capture of Jerusalem and the beginning of the exile. The Book of Mormon refers to the scattering and gathering of Israel (1 Nephi 5:13–14), echoing the events of the Babylonian captivity. The Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 speaks of the gathering of Israel in the last days—a promise first made in these ancient times.
e05.evidence: Archaeologists have found many clay tablets called the Babylonian Chronicles that record major events of this empire, including the conquest of Jerusalem. These chronicles match with what the Bible says about the destruction of Jerusalem. The ruins of Babylon—massive walls, gates, and the base of the ziggurat—can still be seen in present-day Iraq. The British Museum holds some of these tablets and other artifacts. While the existence of the Hanging Gardens is still debated by scholars, other evidence strongly supports the history of the empire and Nebuchadnezzar’s rule.
e05.learn: We learn that even in times of trial and change, God’s hand can be seen. The Jewish people learned to worship, study, and remember God even far from home, and their faith grew stronger. Today, we can remember that changes and challenges—big or small—can help us draw closer to Heavenly Father as we seek to do what’s right, no matter where we are.
e05.child: Long ago, Babylon was a big, busy city with strong kings. God’s people were taken far from home, but He never forgot them. They learned to love Him anywhere they lived!
e05.talk: What are some ways we can remember Heavenly Father, even when things around us change?

e06.happened: In the mid-6th century BC, Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire, uniting the Persian tribes and swiftly conquering neighboring regions. He overthrew the Median Empire around 550 BC, then defeated the wealthy kingdom of Lydia in 546 BC, and finally captured Babylon in 539 BC. His conquests were notable for their speed and the relatively humane treatment of the conquered peoples. Cyrus is particularly remembered for his policy of religious and cultural tolerance. After taking Babylon, he issued a decree allowing exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return to their homelands and rebuild their temples. This act is documented in the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay artifact inscribed with his proclamations, which many consider an early declaration of human rights. Under his rule, the empire expanded to encompass a vast territory, including parts of the Middle East, Central Asia, and Egypt, governing over 40% of the world's population at the time.
e06.background: Before the rise of the Achaemenid Empire, the region was a mosaic of powerful kingdoms and city-states, including the Medes, Lydians, and Babylonians. The Medes had established dominance over Persia, while Lydia, located in modern-day Turkey, was known for its wealth and the invention of coinage. Babylon was a major center of culture and learning. Daily life in these societies varied but often included agriculture, trade, and craftsmanship. The Persian people, originally a collection of nomadic tribes, lived in the region of present-day Iran. They practiced Zoroastrianism, a monotheistic religion emphasizing the duality of good and evil and the importance of individual choice. This religious background influenced their governance and cultural practices.
e06.matters: The establishment of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great marked a significant turning point in world history. It was one of the first empires to implement policies of cultural and religious tolerance, setting a precedent for future governance. For families of faith, Cyrus's actions resonate deeply. His decree allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple is seen as a fulfillment of divine prophecy and an example of how God can use individuals, regardless of their background, to accomplish His purposes. This story underscores the belief that Heavenly Father guides history to fulfill His promises and that leaders can be instruments in His hands.
e06.scripture: The Bible specifically mentions Cyrus in Isaiah 45:1, where the Lord refers to him as His anointed: "Thus says the Lord to His anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, to subdue nations before him..." This prophecy, made approximately 150 years before Cyrus's birth, highlights his role in God's plan to restore Israel. Additionally, the books of Ezra and Nehemiah detail the return of the Jewish exiles and the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem, events made possible by Cyrus's decree. These scriptures illustrate how God can work through leaders to fulfill His promises to His people.
e06.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as the Cyrus Cylinder, provide concrete evidence of Cyrus's policies and conquests. Discovered in 1879 in Babylon, the cylinder records his capture of the city and his subsequent decrees, including the restoration of temples and the return of displaced peoples. The Royal Road, an extensive network of highways built during the Achaemenid Empire, facilitated communication and trade across the vast empire. Remnants of this road have been identified through archaeological surveys, confirming historical accounts of its existence and significance. These artifacts and structures corroborate the historical narratives of Cyrus's reign and the administrative sophistication of the Achaemenid Empire.
e06.learn: From Cyrus's story, we learn the importance of leadership that respects and values the diversity of its people. His policies of tolerance and restoration demonstrate that power can be exercised with compassion and respect for different cultures and beliefs. For families of faith, it serves as a reminder that God can work through anyone to accomplish His purposes, and that leaders who act justly and honorably can have a lasting positive impact on the world.
e06.child: Cyrus was a king who helped people return to their homes and rebuild their places of worship. He showed kindness to many different groups, allowing them to live peacefully.
e06.talk: How can we show kindness and respect to people who are different from us?

e07.happened: Between 336 and 323 BC, Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, led his armies on a journey that stretched from Greece, through Egypt, across Persia, and reached into India. At only twenty years old, Alexander inherited the throne of Macedonia after his father, King Philip II, was assassinated. Alexander was not only strong and brave, but he was also an excellent planner and thinker, trained by the philosopher Aristotle. Using a new way of fighting called the Macedonian phalanx, his armies moved quickly and worked together better than any before them. In only thirteen years, Alexander defeated many strong empires, including the mighty Persians. Everywhere he went, Alexander founded cities named after himself, like Alexandria in Egypt, where people from many lands could meet, trade, and share ideas. But Alexander didn’t only want to conquer lands—he wanted to bring Greek ways of speaking, learning, and living to people everywhere. When he died at just thirty-two years old, his empire was the largest the world had ever seen, though it soon broke into smaller kingdoms ruled by his friends.
e07.background: Before Alexander’s time, the Greek world was made up of small city-states like Athens and Sparta, who often fought each other instead of working together. Most Greeks knew only their own land, and the great Persian Empire to the east ruled over many other peoples. Life for most was simple; people farmed, gathered in marketplaces, and honored their gods. Macedonia, in the north, was seen as rough and less cultured, but its kings built a strong army and learned from Greek ways. Under Philip II, the Macedonians united Greece for the first time. Alexander grew up in this new world, with wild lands to the north and the mystery of Persia and Egypt beyond. The people he conquered spoke many different languages and had different customs, but Alexander wanted to pull all these lands together under one rule and one shared way of life.
e07.matters: Alexander’s conquests changed the world in ways that still matter to families of faith today. Because he spread the Greek language everywhere, it became the language of learning, trade, and even the New Testament. When the time came for Jesus’s teachings to be written down, koine Greek was the tool that let people from Spain to Persia read the same words. For those who believe Heavenly Father prepares the way for His work, Alexander’s story is a reminder that even far-away events can help the gospel move forward. His empire mixed people and ideas in new ways, some good and some difficult, but the open path for the gospel remains one of his most lasting gifts.
e07.scripture: The Bible never names Alexander the Great, but the prophet Daniel sees visions of a great king who will rule swiftly and then have his empire divided (see Daniel 8:5-8, 21-22; Daniel 11:3-4). Many scholars believe these visions describe Alexander and his successors. In the Book of Mormon, the principle that God prepares the way for His purposes (1 Nephi 9:6) fits well: Alexander didn’t know it, but by spreading Greek, he helped make ready the world for the Savior’s gospel to be shared far and wide. No scripture teaches directly about Alexander, but the hand of preparation can be seen through the language and roads his empire left behind.
e07.evidence: The story of Alexander the Great is supported by many ancient writings, coins, statues, and archaeological finds. His own men and later Greek historians wrote about his campaigns, and the places where he built cities—like Alexandria in Egypt—can still be visited today. Inscriptions and coins showing his image or name have been found from Greece to India. However, some stories about his life are mixed with legends or added later, so historians look at the oldest sources most closely. The use of koine Greek across the Mediterranean and the influence of Greek art, architecture, and culture in former Persian lands are visible in both texts and ruins. Modern studies and excavations continue to deepen what we know, but the main outline of his conquests and their effects is firmly supported by multiple sources.
e07.learn: From Alexander's life, we learn that one person’s choices and actions, whether they know it or not, can shape history in ways no one can foresee. It also teaches that God can use even the actions of those who do not know Him to prepare the world for great blessings later on. Language, learning, and the sharing of ideas can open paths for good—like how the Greek language was ready when it was time for the teachings of Jesus to go out to all nations.
e07.child: Alexander marched across many countries and shared the Greek language with people everywhere. Later, the Bible’s New Testament was written in this language so many could read it. Even big events long ago can help us share good things today.
e07.talk: How could one person’s choices help others even hundreds of years later?

e18.happened: In 321 BC, Chandragupta Maurya established the Maurya Empire by overthrowing the Nanda dynasty in the Indian subcontinent. With guidance from his advisor Chanakya, he unified much of northern India and extended his rule westward. Around 305 BC, Chandragupta engaged in a conflict with Seleucus I Nicator, a successor of Alexander the Great. This confrontation concluded with a treaty in which Seleucus ceded territories in exchange for 500 war elephants, strengthening Mauryan influence in the northwest. Chandragupta's reign laid the foundation for a centralized administration and a unified currency system. His grandson, Ashoka the Great, ascended the throne in 268 BC. Initially, Ashoka expanded the empire through military conquests, notably the Kalinga War around 261 BC. The immense suffering caused by this war led Ashoka to embrace Buddhism and adopt a policy of nonviolence. He issued edicts promoting moral principles and religious tolerance, inscribed on pillars and rocks across the empire. These edicts, some written in Greek and Aramaic, indicate the empire's extensive reach and its interactions with neighboring regions. Ashoka's efforts significantly contributed to the spread of Buddhism beyond India, reaching areas like Afghanistan, Syria, and Egypt.
e18.background: Before the rise of the Maurya Empire, the Indian subcontinent was fragmented into various kingdoms and republics. The Nanda dynasty, known for its wealth and military strength, controlled a significant portion of northern India. Daily life during this period was largely agrarian, with communities engaged in farming, trade, and local crafts. The region was also influenced by the remnants of Alexander the Great's campaigns, leading to interactions between Indian and Hellenistic cultures. This period set the stage for the emergence of a centralized authority capable of unifying the diverse political entities of the subcontinent.
e18.matters: The Maurya Empire's establishment marked the first time much of the Indian subcontinent was unified under a single political entity, setting a precedent for future empires. Ashoka's transformation from a conqueror to a proponent of nonviolence and moral governance highlights the profound impact of personal change on leadership. For families of faith, Ashoka's journey underscores the importance of compassion, repentance, and the pursuit of peace, reflecting principles that resonate across various religious teachings.
e18.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly reference the Maurya Empire, the principles demonstrated by Ashoka align with teachings found in the Bible. For instance, in Isaiah 2:4, it is prophesied that nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." This vision of peace and transformation mirrors Ashoka's commitment to nonviolence after witnessing the devastation of war.
e18.evidence: Historical understanding of the Maurya Empire is derived from various sources, including Ashoka's edicts, archaeological findings, and accounts from Greek historians like Megasthenes. The edicts, inscribed on pillars and rocks, provide direct insight into Ashoka's policies and moral directives. Archaeological excavations at sites like Pataliputra have uncovered remnants of the empire's infrastructure, such as fortifications and urban planning. Additionally, Greek records offer external perspectives on the empire's administration and culture. These combined sources offer a comprehensive view of the Maurya Empire's history and its significance.
e18.learn: The story of the Maurya Empire teaches us about the power of leadership grounded in moral principles. It illustrates how personal transformation can lead to societal change and the importance of compassion and nonviolence in governance. These lessons remain relevant, encouraging us to reflect on our actions and their impact on others.
e18.child: Long ago, a king named Ashoka saw how much pain war caused and decided to be kind and peaceful instead. He told everyone to treat each other nicely and to live without fighting.
e18.talk: Why do you think King Ashoka chose to stop fighting and be kind to others?

e08.happened: In 27 BC, the Roman Republic changed forever when Augustus became the first emperor. This ended years of fighting and confusion among Roman leaders who could not agree. Augustus brought stability by making sure that power was held by one leader: himself, though he kept many parts of the old Republic, like the Senate, to help him rule. Over time, the empire grew and included places across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Cities flourished, trade grew along safe Roman roads, and millions of people lived under Roman law. The Romans built strong armies and powerful ships, and they designed roads and bridges that connected their lands for trade and travel. By about the year 100 AD, the Roman Empire was at its strongest, ruled by emperors like Augustus, Trajan, and Hadrian. The peace, safety, and laws of Rome allowed new ideas and cultures to spread far and wide. Rome's hand reached even to Jerusalem, where the life of Jesus and the early Christian Church were shaped under its rule.
e08.background: Before Rome became an empire, it was a republic where citizens voted for leaders and decisions. The Roman people farmed, traded, and worshipped many gods. Life in a Roman city was crowded and busy, with markets, temples, and baths. Soldiers guarded the borders, and families gathered for meals in small homes or grand villas. In the countryside, Romans grew crops like wheat, olives, and grapes. Many people were free, but some were slaves, working in homes, fields, and mines. Other great powers, like Egypt and Greece, already influenced the world’s science and stories, but Rome’s army and organization made it the most powerful. Before Augustus, Rome had suffered many civil wars, with rival leaders fighting for control. The people were tired of chaos, making Augustus’ long, peaceful rule a welcome change.
e08.matters: The Roman Empire matters because it shaped much of Western civilization. Its laws became the base for many countries’ legal systems. Much of our language, architecture, and calendar come from Roman ideas. For families of faith, Rome mattered even more: it was in the Roman world that Jesus was born, lived, and taught, and early Christians spread their message. Families today still feel these effects when they read the New Testament or walk along a road built by Romans.
e08.scripture: Luke 2:1 tells us that 'a decree from Caesar Augustus' sent Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, fulfilling prophecy. Matthew 27:1-2, Mark 15:1, and Luke 23:1-25 describe Jesus’ trial before the Roman governor Pilate. Acts and Paul’s letters show the gospel spreading on Roman roads, like Acts 16:9-10. Doctrine and Covenants 133:8–9 encourages gathering from all nations, a work made possible because of things like Roman roads and laws. While the Book of Mormon does not mention Rome, it shares principles of God preparing the way for His work (1 Nephi 9:6).
e08.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found strong evidence for the Roman Empire, from its many ruins—like the Colosseum, Roman roads, and aqueducts—to thousands of inscriptions, coins, and writings by Romans and their neighbors. Documents from the time, such as those by Roman historians Tacitus and Suetonius, record the reigns of the emperors and the empire’s reach. Scholars also study ancient laws, letters, and official records. Modern technology, like ground-penetrating radar and satellite imaging, helps experts map old Roman cities and roads still visible beneath the soil. Artifacts and architecture are found not just in Italy, but all over Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, proving the size and influence of the empire.
e08.learn: From the Roman Empire, we can learn how people and nations can create order, beauty, and connection, but also how power can be misused. We see that good ideas, like strong roads and helpful laws, can last for centuries and help others do good—just as Heavenly Father can use the world’s systems and inventions to bless His children. We also learn that a single person’s choices, like Augustus’s, can change the world in ways both great and small, for many years to come.
e08.child: Long ago, Rome was the biggest empire in the world. It built safe roads and made rules so people could travel and share ideas, even the story of Jesus. The Romans helped prepare the way for many things we use today, like roads, languages, and calendars.
e08.talk: How do you think Heavenly Father helps people use good things from the world, like roads or inventions, to share His love?

e09.happened: In 618 AD, Li Yuan overthrew the Sui Dynasty and established the Tang Dynasty, ushering in a period of remarkable cultural, political, and economic growth in China. Under the leadership of emperors like Taizong and Xuanzong, the Tang Dynasty expanded its influence across Central Asia, becoming a hub of international trade and cultural exchange. This era is often referred to as the golden age of Chinese poetry and art, with significant advancements in literature, painting, and sculpture. Notably, the invention of woodblock printing during this time revolutionized the dissemination of knowledge. Additionally, the Tang Dynasty's openness to foreign cultures facilitated the arrival of Nestorian Christian missionaries from the Church of the East. These missionaries traveled along the Silk Road and reached China, where they established communities and shared their faith. A significant artifact from this period is the Nestorian Stele, erected in 781 AD, which documents the presence and activities of these early Christians in China.
e09.background: Before the Tang Dynasty, China experienced a period of fragmentation and turmoil following the fall of the Han Dynasty. The Sui Dynasty briefly reunified the country but was marked by heavy taxation and forced labor, leading to widespread dissatisfaction. The Tang Dynasty emerged from this backdrop, bringing stability and prosperity. The capital, Chang'an (modern-day Xi'an), became one of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities in the world, bustling with merchants, scholars, and diplomats from various regions. Daily life during the Tang era was characterized by a rich cultural milieu, with people enjoying poetry, music, and art. The Silk Road played a crucial role in facilitating trade and cultural exchanges, connecting China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and beyond. This environment of openness allowed for the introduction and assimilation of foreign ideas, religions, and technologies, including Nestorian Christianity.
e09.matters: The Tang Dynasty's embrace of diverse cultures and religions highlights the importance of openness and inclusivity. For families of faith, this period serves as a reminder of how the gospel can reach distant lands and touch lives across different cultures. The arrival of Nestorian missionaries in China demonstrates that even during times of limited communication and travel, the message of Christ found its way to new regions. This historical event underscores the belief that Heavenly Father guides the spread of His gospel, planting seeds of faith in various parts of the world, even during periods when the fullness of the gospel was not present.
e09.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the Tang Dynasty or the spread of Christianity to China, the principle of the Lord's work reaching all nations is evident. In Doctrine and Covenants 1:30, it states that the Church is "the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth." This suggests that the Lord's work is intended for all people, regardless of their location or culture. Additionally, in Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus commands His disciples to "go ye therefore, and teach all nations," emphasizing the global nature of the gospel message. These passages reflect the ongoing effort to share the gospel with all of Heavenly Father's children.
e09.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide substantial evidence of the Tang Dynasty's achievements and the presence of Nestorian Christianity in China. The Nestorian Stele, erected in 781 AD, is a significant artifact that details the arrival and establishment of Christian communities in China during the Tang era. This stone monument, inscribed in both Chinese and Syriac, describes the teachings of Christianity and acknowledges the support of the Tang emperors. Additionally, the Daqin Pagoda in Shaanxi province, believed to be a Christian monastery from the Tang period, features Christian-themed artwork, further attesting to the presence of early Christians in China. These artifacts, along with historical texts, confirm the cultural and religious exchanges that took place during the Tang Dynasty.
e09.learn: The history of the Tang Dynasty teaches us the value of cultural openness and the impact of sharing beliefs across different societies. It reminds us that the gospel can reach and influence diverse cultures, even in times and places where we might not expect. This encourages us to be open to learning from others and to share our faith in ways that are respectful and considerate of different cultural contexts.
e09.child: A long time ago, in China, there was a time called the Tang Dynasty when people from different places came together to share ideas and learn from each other. Some Christians traveled a long way to tell the people in China about Jesus, and they built special places to worship there.
e09.talk: How do you think people from different places can learn from each other and share their beliefs?

e10.happened: Around the year 1206, a great leader named Genghis Khan united many feuding tribes on the grassy plains of Mongolia. He became the first Great Khan and began a series of campaigns that would stretch across Asia and into Eastern Europe. By the year 1260, the Mongol Empire stood as the largest land empire in human history. The Mongol armies were known for their disciplined and swift horsemen, as well as their ability to adapt new technologies and tactics from conquered peoples. Under Genghis Khan and, later, his grandson Kublai Khan, the Mongols conquered vast territories, including the old heartlands of China, Persia, Russia, the Middle East, and parts of Eastern Europe. Their conquests sometimes brought great destruction, like the 1258 sack of Baghdad, which ended the Islamic Golden Age and led to the loss of enormous libraries and ancient knowledge. However, from about 1260 onward, a period known as Pax Mongolica, or "Mongol Peace," began. During this time, the empire made the Silk Road safe for travelers and traders, allowing ideas, inventions, cultures, and goods from China, the Middle East, and Europe to mix as never before.
e10.background: Before the Mongol Empire, the Mongolian steppe was home to many tribes who often fought each other for land, animals, and honor. These nomadic people tended herds of horses, sheep, and goats, and lived in felt tents called yurts, moving often to find fresh grass. Outside Mongolia, great empires and centers of learning thrived, especially in China, Persia, and the Islamic world. In cities like Baghdad, scholars studied science, medicine, and philosophy, and merchants traded across continents. Daily life depended on the seasons and local rulers, but many people farmed, traded, or practiced crafts, while others traveled the Silk Road for trade. The world was already connected in pockets, but risky for long-distance travel. Generations of wars, local rulers, and shifting alliances shaped what the Mongols would encounter and, eventually, change.
e10.matters: The story of the Mongol Empire matters because it changed the map of the world and the lives of millions. Its conquests caused much suffering but also created new ways for ideas, inventions, and beliefs to travel between distant cultures. For families who see the hand of God in history, it reminds us that even in times of upheaval, unexpected good can come. The Mongol Empire’s era of peace helped knowledge and technology spread, preparing the world for future growth and discovery. It also teaches about the dangers of pride and cruelty, but the blessings that can arise when people are able to listen to and learn from each other.
e10.scripture: Although the scriptures do not mention the Mongol Empire directly, the principle of God being aware of all nations can be found in 2 Nephi 29:7, where the Lord says He remembers all His children, wherever they are. Doctrine and Covenants 1:33 also teaches that the Lord is able to bring about His purposes even in times of chaos. The downfall of mighty nations, such as what happened to Baghdad, reminds us of Daniel 2:21 in the Old Testament, which says God "removeth kings, and setteth up kings." These teachings help us see that history is always in God's view, and He can use even difficult events to prepare the world for His work.
e10.evidence: Much is known about the Mongol Empire from both Mongol and non-Mongol sources, including chronicles written by those who saw the conquests, as well as archaeological finds such as city ruins and Mongol-era coins. Modern historians use old letters, trade records, and the ruins of towns across the Silk Road to understand how far Mongol influence reached. While parts of Mongol records were lost, especially after the destruction of many cities, Chinese, Persian, and European writers described their armies and leaders in great detail. The paths of the Silk Road can still be traced, and there is evidence of new inventions and cultural ideas spreading faster because of Mongol protection. Scientists and archaeologists continue to study these changes through what has survived from the 13th and 14th centuries.
e10.learn: From the Mongol Empire, we learn that both harm and good can come from great power. Even after great loss, Heavenly Father can use times of peace to bring people and knowledge together. It is a reminder to use our means and talents wisely—just as the Silk Road under Mongol rule became a bridge between very different nations, we too can build bridges of understanding in our own homes and communities.
e10.child: Long ago, a powerful ruler named Genghis Khan brought many tribes together and made the biggest land empire ever. The Mongols could be fierce, but they also helped people travel safely and share ideas. Some cities were destroyed, but some good things grew because people could talk and trade more easily.
e10.talk: How could Heavenly Father use something that seems hard or scary to help His work move forward?

e17.happened: In the 1200s, a great story unfolded in West Africa where families and villages lived along the Niger River. Around 1235, a leader named Sundiata Keita rose to strength after his people, the Mandinka, had suffered under the harsh rule of the Sosso Empire. Sundiata's courage and leadership led his army to defeat the Sosso at the Battle of Kirina. This marked the start of the Mali Empire, which grew to be one of the wealthiest and most powerful empires in the world by the year 1350. Later, a king named Mansa Musa would shine as one of Mali’s most famous rulers. In 1324, Mansa Musa traveled on a pilgrimage to Mecca with a caravan so grand, filled with gold and gifts, that it amazed all who saw it, spreading Mali’s fame across continents. His actions, and his generosity with gold, even changed the prices of things all across North Africa. And at home, the city of Timbuktu blossomed into a famous center for learning, where thousands of students studied math, science, faith, and ancient texts.
e17.background: Before the Mali Empire, West Africa was home to different tribes and smaller kingdoms. The land was rich with gold, salt, and vibrant rivers, providing busy markets and farms. The people spoke many languages but shared traditions of storytelling, music, and devotion to family and faith. The Ghana Empire, Mali’s predecessor, had already shown how powerful a West African kingdom could be. Daily life was filled with farming, trading, and family chores, and there was always respect for wise leaders and elders. Most people practiced faiths rooted in their land and ancestors, but as time went on, Islam spread through traders, slowly blending with local ways and bringing new literacy and scholarship.
e17.matters: The Mali Empire matters because it shows how faith, knowledge, and leadership can lift a people. For a family of faith today, it is inspiring to see how learning and wisdom were treasured and protected. Heavenly Father’s hand can be seen in blessing people everywhere with not just riches but also with knowledge and a thirst for understanding. Remembering Mali’s story helps us recognize the beauty and value found in all peoples and reminds us to seek learning, by study and also by faith, as the Lord commands.
e17.scripture: Though the scriptures do not mention the Mali Empire, their story stands as an example of the principle in Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, which teaches us to seek learning 'by study and also by faith.' Proverbs 4:7 in the Bible also tells us, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' The scholars of Timbuktu valued wisdom and learning, echoing the scriptural call to treasure knowledge as a gift from God, no matter where in the world it blossoms.
e17.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found strong evidence about the Mali Empire, from written records by Arab travelers like Ibn Battuta to manuscripts and maps from the time. The wealth of Mali, especially in gold and salt, is well documented. Ruins in Timbuktu and other ancient cities still show that they were great centers of learning, full of libraries and mosques. The story of Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage comes from many sources and is supported by records showing the effect his riches had. Manuscripts from Timbuktu have been studied by scholars all over the world, giving us direct insight into the deep learning and sophistication of the Mali Empire.
e17.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father loves all His children and provides opportunities for learning and growth everywhere on earth. The Mali Empire’s love of wisdom shows us the importance of education and the sharing of knowledge. When we honor learning, lift others, and remember God, we can help make our world brighter, just as Timbuktu shone with scholarship long ago.
e17.child: Long ago in Africa, there was a kingdom called Mali. Its people learned many things and shared them with others, because God loves learning everywhere. A kind king named Mansa Musa showed the world faith, kindness, and giving to others.
e17.talk: What do you think Heavenly Father wants us to learn every day, especially from people who are different from us?

e12.happened: Between 1438 and 1533 AD, a remarkable civilization grew in the Andes Mountains of western South America. The Inca Empire, led at first by Pachacuti, began as a small kingdom but soon expanded into one of the largest empires ever seen in the Americas. Pachacuti reorganized his people, led conquests of neighboring lands, and set up systems that made the empire strong and efficient. The Inca built vast networks of roads and bridges across mountains and valleys, helping them connect distant cities. They developed advanced ways to farm the steep slopes, making use of terracing to grow food for millions. After Pachacuti, Inca rulers such as his son and later Huayna Capac continued to expand the empire. The capital, Cusco, became a powerful city filled with temples, palaces, and busy markets. But in the early 1500s, the arrival of Spanish conquerors changed everything. After years of battles and disease, the Inca Empire was overtaken by the Spanish, who introduced new ways of life, including the Christian faith.
e12.background: Before the Inca rose to power, the Andes were home to many smaller kingdoms and tribes. People here had learned to live high in the mountains, where the land was rocky and the air thin. Families worked together to grow crops like potatoes and maize on steep hillsides, using clever farming methods passed down through generations. They lived in stone houses and wove beautiful cloth from llama and alpaca wool. Communities shared resources and celebrated festivals honoring their gods and ancestors. Life for most was about farming, tending animals, and helping each other. The Inca, calling themselves 'Children of the Sun,' united these groups into one empire, with Quechua as the main language. Their leaders were known for their wisdom and organization.
e12.matters: The story of the Inca Empire is important because it shows how people, even without horses or written books, could build a great civilization through faith, cooperation, and innovation. Their achievements in farming, architecture, and building roads have lasted centuries and still help people today. For families of faith, it reminds us that the Lord works among all His children, wherever they live. The blending of Inca traditions with new teachings brought by the Spanish shaped the culture, language, and beliefs of millions. It is also a story about change—how new ideas and beliefs can come and bless new lands and people.
e12.scripture: The scriptures teach that Heavenly Father knows and loves all His children, no matter where they live (Acts 17:26-27; 2 Nephi 26:33). The Book of Mormon often speaks of God's love for people on the 'isles of the sea' and in distant lands (3 Nephi 16:1-3). While the Inca are not mentioned directly, these scriptural teachings remind us that Christ's invitation is for everyone, including the people who lived in the Andes. D&C 1:2 also teaches that the gospel will be proclaimed to every nation and language.
e12.evidence: Archaeologists have discovered much about the Inca from ruins like Machu Picchu, stone roads that still cross the Andes, and artifacts found in cities such as Cusco. Historical records from early Spanish writers describe the power and organization of the empire, though these sources are not always complete. Modern studies confirm that the Inca built one of the most complicated road networks in the ancient world and that their terraced farms could feed large populations. The Quechua language, still spoken today, and traditions kept alive by Andean families also show the living legacy of the Inca. Scientists continue to study and learn from the advanced engineering and agricultural practices the Inca developed.
e12.learn: From the Inca, we can learn the importance of working together, caring for the earth, and being open to learning new things. Their ability to build and organize shows what can happen when a community uses its knowledge and faith to solve difficult problems. We are also reminded to respect the beliefs and cultures of others, knowing that God watches over all His children.
e12.child: Long ago, the Inca people lived high in the mountains and built amazing cities and farms. They shared what they had and worked together. Today, people still remember and learn from the things the Inca made.
e12.talk: Why do you think working together helped the Inca people become so strong?

e13.happened: The Aztec Empire was one of the most remarkable civilizations in the Americas. In the year 1500, the empire was at its height in central Mexico. The Aztecs formed a group called the Triple Alliance, joining with the cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan to become the most powerful force in the area. Under rulers like Moctezuma II, they conquered many neighboring peoples and built a magnificent city, Tenochtitlan, on an island in a lake. Their city boasted grand temples, canals, markets, and houses. People from far and wide brought goods to trade, and there were spectacular festivals and rituals. However, when Spanish explorers led by Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519, everything changed quickly. The Spanish had horses, guns, and carried new diseases the Aztecs had never seen, which spread quickly through the population. The fighting and sickness weakened the Aztec defenses, and by 1521, the city of Tenochtitlan fell. Over time, the city became what we now know as Mexico City, and the culture and language of the Aztecs continued to shape the country even after the Spanish conquest.
e13.background: Before the Aztec Empire, many cultures lived in the region, like the Toltecs and the Maya. The Aztecs, who called themselves Mexica, originally came from the north and settled in the valley of Mexico. Their daily life was filled with farming, building, and family. Corn was their main food, and they grew beans, squash, tomatoes, and chilies. Children went to school to learn craft, trade, or religion. Religion was very important; people believed that pleasing the gods helped the sun rise and brought rain for their crops. Aztec society was complex, with nobles, priests, warriors, traders, and farmers, all working together to build a vibrant community.
e13.matters: The story of the Aztec Empire reminds us how powerful civilizations can rise and fall. It shows how cultures can blend after great hardships, and that faith and resilience matter when everything else changes. For families of faith, it invites us to reflect on how Heavenly Father watches over all His children, even in times of suffering. Today, the language, foods, and traditions from the Aztecs still enrich lives around the world, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ has reached their descendants in modern Mexico.
e13.scripture: Although the Bible and Book of Mormon do not mention the Aztecs directly, scripture teaches us about God's love for all His children (Acts 10:34-35) and the gathering of Israel from all nations (Isaiah 49:6; 2 Nephi 10:8-22). Doctrine and Covenants 1:20 also reminds us that the gospel is for all families of the earth. These truths help us see that the Lord remembers and cares for every people, even through great trials.
e13.evidence: Archaeological discoveries in Mexico, such as the ruins of Tenochtitlan beneath Mexico City, codices (folded bark books), and artifacts, confirm much about Aztec society, their achievements, and their relationships with others. Spanish records from the conquest, despite being written by outsiders, also provide firsthand accounts. Modern studies of Aztec language and DNA connect today’s people to their ancestors. Historians agree that smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans killed millions after first contact. Ongoing excavations reveal more about Aztec lives, art, and beliefs, continually enriching our understanding.
e13.learn: From the Aztec Empire, we learn the dangers of pride and the costs of conflict, but also the power of endurance and change. Heavenly Father’s purposes can still move forward, even after tragedy. We can work to remember the good in every culture, and help heal what has been broken.
e13.child: A long time ago, the Aztecs built a huge city on a lake and grew all sorts of food. When new people came, there was a lot of trouble, and many got sick, but some of their words and foods are still with us today.
e13.talk: What good things do you think we can learn from people who lived long ago, like the Aztecs?
