fp22.happened: Benjamin Franklin was born in 1706 in Boston, and his life became one of the most remarkable stories in American history. As a young man, Franklin was curious and always eager to learn, despite only having two years of formal schooling. He moved to Philadelphia where he became a printer, then an inventor, scientist, writer, and finally a statesman who helped shape a new nation. He experimented with electricity and proved lightning was a form of electrical energy by flying a kite in a storm, which led to his invention of the lightning rod—an important safety device. Franklin also invented everyday things like bifocal glasses and created the first public lending library in America, making books accessible to everyone, not just the wealthy. His life was not just about science and invention; he played a vital role in the founding of the United States. Franklin helped draft the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution. He is the only person to sign all four of the major documents that founded the country, showing his central role in building ideas like freedom, democracy, and public service into the nation’s fabric.
fp22.background: When Franklin was born, America was a set of British colonies with growing towns and cities. Life was much harder than today; most people worked on farms or as craftspeople. Books were rare and expensive, most travel was by foot or horse, and there was no electricity, running water, or public health care. The colonies were bustling with energy but also uncertain about their future. People were beginning to think more about freedom and rights. Franklin’s world was shaped by Enlightenment ideas from Europe; thinkers everywhere were talking about science, reason, and ways to make society better. These ideas gave Franklin inspiration for his inventions and for his belief that education and community help everyone rise.
fp22.matters: Franklin’s life and work matter for many reasons. His discoveries in science helped people understand how the world works and made life safer. His inventions and public projects—like the public library and fire department—set examples that are still followed today. Franklin’s leadership helped create a form of government, based on laws and the idea that people’s voices matter, that protects freedom and invites everyone to participate and learn. For families of faith, his story is a reminder that using our minds and working together in our communities can be ways of serving God and helping His children. Our gifts, used well, can answer prayers and help people in lasting ways.
fp22.scripture: The scriptures speak often about wisdom, service, and building strong communities. Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 tells us that God raised up wise men to help establish the principles of liberty in the U.S. Constitution. Franklin, though not of any particular church, believed in Providence (God’s care) and acted with values like honesty and service that the Bible teaches; for example, Proverbs 4:7 praises seeking wisdom, and Mosiah 2:17 in the Book of Mormon teaches that serving others is serving God. Franklin’s work in public institutions and government connects to these principles.
fp22.evidence: Historians have a great deal of evidence about Franklin’s life. There are thousands of his letters, books he published, inventions he made (many of which can still be seen in museums), and firsthand accounts from friends and colleagues. His experiments with electricity, such as the famous kite and key, were documented in his own words and those of others who knew him well. The institutions he formed—the first public library, the first fire insurance company, and hospitals in Philadelphia—are still operating or have direct descendants today. Franklin’s writings, including his autobiography and political essays, give us a clear window into his thoughts and times. Scholars generally agree about the key events and his impact, although some details and motivations are still studied and debated as new documents are discovered.
fp22.learn: We can learn from Benjamin Franklin that curiosity, hard work, and the desire to help others can lead to great things. He reminds us that no one has to start out important to make a difference; it’s our choices and how we use our talents that matter. By building libraries and helping set up ways for everyone to learn and be safe, he showed that serving others can bless whole communities. Franklin’s story lights the path for using our minds and hands to solve problems and lift others, while remembering we are all children of God with spiritual gifts to share.
fp22.child: Benjamin Franklin was a smart and kind man who invented things and helped America become its own country. He made things like libraries and fire stations so people could be safer and smarter. He believed in helping everyone have a chance to learn and live better.
fp22.talk: What is something you could invent or create to help your family, school, or city?

fp31.happened: Around 1805, Te Pahi, a respected Māori chief from the Bay of Islands in New Zealand, embarked on a significant journey to Sydney, Australia. Accompanied by four of his sons, he aimed to establish peaceful relations and explore opportunities for his people. Upon arrival, they were warmly received by Governor Philip Gidley King and stayed at Government House for nearly three months. During this time, Te Pahi observed various European industries, including wool processing and cloth making, and attended court proceedings, where he expressed his views on justice. He also met with Reverend Samuel Marsden, discussing religious matters and the potential for missionary work in New Zealand. Before departing, Governor King presented Te Pahi with gifts such as a silver medal, livestock, and a prefabricated house, symbolizing the mutual respect and alliance formed during the visit.
fp31.background: In the early 19th century, New Zealand was experiencing increased contact with European traders and settlers. The Māori people, known for their seafaring traditions, were keen to engage with Europeans to acquire new technologies and goods. European whalers and traders frequented the Bay of Islands, leading to a burgeoning exchange of cultures and commerce. Daily life for the Māori involved communal living, with a strong emphasis on kinship and tribal affiliations. The introduction of European tools and crops began to influence traditional practices, prompting leaders like Te Pahi to seek knowledge and resources that could benefit their communities.
fp31.matters: Te Pahi's visit to Sydney was a pivotal moment in Māori-European relations. By choosing to engage peacefully and seek mutual benefits, he set a precedent for future interactions between the two cultures. His openness to new ideas and technologies demonstrated a forward-thinking approach, aiming to enhance the well-being of his people. For families of faith, Te Pahi's actions exemplify the importance of building bridges and seeking understanding with others, reflecting the principle of loving one's neighbor and embracing opportunities for growth and learning.
fp31.scripture: The scriptures teach the value of seeking wisdom and understanding. In Proverbs 4:7, it states, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' Te Pahi's proactive approach to learning from others aligns with this principle, emphasizing the importance of acquiring knowledge to benefit one's community. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages us to 'seek learning, even by study and also by faith,' highlighting the balance between spiritual and temporal knowledge.
fp31.evidence: Historical records, including accounts from the Sydney Gazette and writings by Governor Philip Gidley King, document Te Pahi's visit and interactions in Sydney. Artifacts such as the silver medal presented to him have been preserved and are displayed in museums, providing tangible evidence of the event. Additionally, portraits and engravings from the period depict Te Pahi, further corroborating his significant role in early Māori-European relations.
fp31.learn: Te Pahi's journey teaches us the value of open-mindedness and proactive engagement with others. By seeking knowledge and forming alliances, we can create opportunities for mutual benefit and understanding. His example encourages us to embrace new experiences and learn from different cultures, fostering harmony and progress.
fp31.child: A long time ago, a Māori chief named Te Pahi traveled to Sydney to meet new people and learn about their ways. He wanted to help his people by bringing back useful ideas and tools. This shows how being curious and friendly can help everyone get along better.
fp31.talk: Why do you think it's important to learn about other people's ways and ideas?

fp35.happened: Napoleon Bonaparte was born in 1769 on the island of Corsica. As a young man, he became a soldier in the French army and quickly rose through the ranks, thanks to his sharp mind and boldness. He became famous during the French Revolution, a time when France was changing its government. Soon, Napoleon became the leader of France and declared himself emperor. He led his armies across Europe, winning many battles and taking control of large parts of the continent. But his quest for power also led to great suffering. His wars caused the deaths of around 5 million people, and families all over Europe felt the loss. Napoleon even imprisoned the Pope, Pope Pius VII. While he brought new laws and ideas of fairness and freedom—like the Napoleonic Code, which shaped laws even in countries far from France—he did so by force. After years of fighting, other nations united against him. He was finally defeated and sent far away to the island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821, far from home.
fp35.background: France in the late 1700s was a place of big changes and deep troubles. For centuries, kings ruled with strict control, and most people were poor while a few were very rich and powerful. In 1789, the French Revolution broke out, as ordinary people demanded more rights and better lives. Daily life was hard for most, with food shortages and heavy taxes. As old ways were swept away, France became the center of hope for some—and fear for others. Napoleon, born to a modest family, grew up in these times. He trained as a soldier and found chances to move up quickly when many leaders lost their positions during the Revolution. By the time he was in his early thirties, he was leading armies and shaping the fate of countries across Europe.
fp35.matters: Napoleon’s story matters because it shows how one person can change the world, for better and worse. His leadership and laws helped end old, unfair systems and offered new hopes for freedom and fairness, but he also brought pain through wars and conquest. For families of faith, Napoleon’s story reminds us that great power brings great responsibility. The way he spread religious tolerance and equal laws is inspiring, but the suffering caused by his ambition is a warning. Remembering his life helps us seek peace and justice together.
fp35.scripture: Scriptures teach us that all people are children of God and should use authority with love and wisdom. In Doctrine and Covenants 121:39, it warns against unrighteous dominion, or using power to harm others. The Savior said, "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9), showing the value of spreading peace instead of war. Though no scripture mentions Napoleon, these principles remind us that God's way is to lift others up, not to rule by force or fear.
fp35.evidence: There is strong evidence from letters, public records, and many eyewitness reports about Napoleon’s life, military campaigns, and government reforms. The number of people who died in his wars—about 5 million—is estimated from army documents and population studies. Objects from his life, such as uniforms, personal belongings, and official papers, are kept in museums. Historians agree on the main facts of his story, and his legal reforms—especially the Napoleonic Code—are still studied and followed around the world. While some details about his motives and private life are debated, the key events and their effects are well documented in many countries’ archives and records.
fp35.learn: Napoleon’s rise and fall reminds us that using our talents can bring good to others—but only if we don’t let pride or ambition take over. Laws and freedoms matter a lot, but how we treat others—especially those with different beliefs or backgrounds—shows our true character. His story urges us to use any influence we have to build up, not tear down, and to be humble.
fp35.child: Napoleon was a smart and brave leader from France who won many battles, but his wars hurt lots of people. He changed many rules in Europe, helping make things fairer, but he also made some big mistakes and was sent away to live alone until he died.
fp35.talk: What do you think is more important—being powerful, or using power to help others?

fp39.happened: Maximilien Robespierre was a key figure during the French Revolution, particularly known for his role in the Reign of Terror. In 1793, he became a leading member of the Committee of Public Safety, which held significant power in revolutionary France. Under his leadership, the committee initiated the Reign of Terror, a period marked by mass executions of those deemed enemies of the revolution. Estimates suggest that over 17,000 people were officially executed, many by guillotine, and thousands more died in prison without trial. Robespierre also sought to replace traditional Christianity with the Cult of Reason, a state-sponsored secular belief system. However, his radical policies and the escalating violence led to growing opposition. On July 27, 1794, Robespierre was arrested by the National Convention. The following day, he and 21 of his followers were executed by guillotine, effectively ending the Reign of Terror.
fp39.background: The late 18th century was a time of significant upheaval in France. The nation was burdened by economic hardship, social inequality, and widespread discontent with the monarchy. The French Revolution began in 1789, aiming to establish liberty, equality, and fraternity. However, as the revolution progressed, internal conflicts and external threats intensified. The radical Jacobin faction, led by figures like Robespierre, gained prominence, advocating for drastic measures to protect and advance the revolution. Daily life was fraught with uncertainty, as political alliances shifted rapidly, and the threat of violence loomed large.
fp39.matters: Robespierre's actions during the Reign of Terror serve as a stark reminder of the dangers of extremism and the abandonment of moral and ethical principles in pursuit of political goals. For families of faith, this period underscores the importance of upholding values of compassion, justice, and respect for human life, even amidst societal upheaval. It also highlights the perils of attempting to replace deeply held religious beliefs with state-imposed ideologies, which can lead to societal discord and suffering.
fp39.scripture: The scriptures caution against the perils of pride and the rejection of divine guidance. Proverbs 16:18 states, "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." Similarly, in 2 Nephi 9:28-29, it is written, "O that cunning plan of the evil one! O the vainness, and the frailties, and the foolishness of men! When they are learned they think they are wise, and they hearken not unto the counsel of God." These passages remind us of the consequences of turning away from God and relying solely on human wisdom.
fp39.evidence: Historical records from the period provide detailed accounts of the events during the Reign of Terror. Official documents from the National Convention and the Committee of Public Safety outline the policies and actions taken under Robespierre's leadership. Eyewitness accounts and contemporary writings offer personal perspectives on the atmosphere of fear and suspicion that pervaded France. Additionally, the extensive use of the guillotine and the establishment of the Cult of Reason are well-documented, reflecting the radical shifts in governance and societal norms during this time.
fp39.learn: The story of Robespierre and the Reign of Terror teaches us the importance of balancing the pursuit of change with adherence to moral principles. It warns against the dangers of allowing fear and extremism to dictate actions, leading to the loss of innocent lives. For families, it emphasizes the value of compassion, justice, and the preservation of faith as guiding lights during times of turmoil.
fp39.child: A long time ago in France, a man named Robespierre tried to change many things very quickly. He thought his way was best, but it led to a lot of sadness and hurt for many people.
fp39.talk: Why is it important to be kind and fair to others, even when we want to make big changes?

fp28.happened: Toussaint Louverture was born enslaved in Saint-Domingue, a French colony on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola, in 1743. Though he started life in chains, Toussaint became an extraordinarily wise and brave leader. Around 1780, the colony was one of the richest in the world, powered by the hard work and suffering of enslaved Africans. People in Saint-Domingue grew sugar, coffee, and other crops, but the enslaved made up most of the population. In 1791, when Toussaint was about 48, a great revolution started. The enslaved people rose up against their masters, risking everything for freedom. Toussaint, who could read and was deeply respected, soon became their general. He was a brilliant strategist, keeping his men safe and outmaneuvering much larger armies from France, Spain, and Britain. Toussaint’s leadership helped drive out foreign armies and abolish slavery in the colony. Though he was captured in 1802 and died the next year in France, the revolution he started succeeded: in 1804 Haiti became the first free Black republic and the first nation to permanently end slavery, blazing a path of hope for enslaved people everywhere.
fp28.background: Before the revolution, Saint-Domingue was a vital French sugar colony, worked by nearly half a million enslaved Africans. White colonists held almost unchecked power, and free people of color faced many restrictions despite sometimes owning land themselves. Life for most was filled with hard labor, especially on the plantations. Disease, hunger, and violence were common for the enslaved. News of the American Revolution and the ideas of equality from the French Revolution inspired hopes of freedom across the island. The church was important, but it did not oppose slavery at this time. There was a great divide between slaveholders and the enslaved in daily life, with almost no paths to possible freedom until the revolution began.
fp28.matters: The Haitian Revolution is a turning point in world history. Toussaint Louverture’s leadership showed that people everywhere deserve freedom, dignity, and respect, no matter where they were born. For families of faith, his story is a powerful reminder that each child of God holds great worth. Heavenly Father often works through small and humble people to accomplish great purposes. Toussaint’s stand for freedom not only changed Haiti but influenced movements for emancipation throughout the world.
fp28.scripture: The Bible teaches that all are alike unto God. Galatians 3:28 says, 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free… for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.' The Book of Mormon echoes this in 2 Nephi 26:33: 'all are alike unto God.' While the scriptures do not mention Toussaint or Haiti, the truth that everyone deserves liberty and dignity is clear. Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 reminds us, 'Therefore, it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another.'
fp28.evidence: Historians rely on letters, government records, eyewitness accounts, and writings from Toussaint himself to understand the revolution. His life and victories are well-documented in military reports and in the memories of those who fought beside or against him. Archaeological work in Haiti sheds light on plantation life, the harsh conditions people endured, and the battles during the revolution. Today, the impact of Haiti’s independence and the permanent abolition of slavery is recognized worldwide as a confirmed chapter in history. The revolution’s brutal battles and Toussaint’s determination are documented by both European and Haitian sources, making it one of the best-recorded stories of freedom from oppression.
fp28.learn: We learn that with courage, faith, and wisdom, great changes can be made—sometimes even by those least expected. Toussaint’s story teaches that Heavenly Father can work through anyone who stands for what is right, even in the hardest of times. Families can talk about how everyone’s freedom matters and how to stand up for what is true and just.
fp28.child: Toussaint Louverture was born a slave but helped all the other enslaved people in Haiti win their freedom. He showed that everyone should be treated fairly, because we are all children of God. Because of his bravery, Haiti became the first free Black country.
fp28.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father cares about the freedom and happiness of every person, no matter where they come from?

fp05:abraham-lincoln.happened: Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in Hodgenville, Kentucky. He grew up in a small log cabin and faced many hardships as a child, including the early death of his mother. Lincoln taught himself to read and write, and he became a lawyer. He was known for his honesty and care for others. In 1861, Lincoln became the 16th President of the United States, just as the nation was breaking apart over the issue of slavery. During his presidency, the Civil War broke out between the Northern states (the Union) and the Southern states (the Confederacy). Lincoln worked hard to keep the country together and to end slavery. In 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared all slaves in the Confederate states to be free. He also spoke powerful words about forgiveness and unity, especially in his Second Inaugural Address, where he called on Americans to act "with malice toward none, with charity for all." Sadly, Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, just after the war ended, but his actions helped shape the country forever.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.background: Abraham Lincoln lived at a time when America was still quite young and deeply divided over slavery. Most people in the North believed slavery was wrong, while many in the South depended on it for their way of life. Daily life then had no electricity or cars. People worked hard on farms or in small towns. Most children learned in one-room schoolhouses, and families often did not travel far from home. As the country grew, arguments about freedom, rights, and the future grew, too. Lincoln came from a humble background, and many could relate to his early struggles. His life shows how someone from an ordinary family could shape history through courage and faith.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.matters: Lincoln matters because he led the United States through its most dangerous crisis and helped end slavery. For families of faith, he shows how a leader can seek God’s help during dark times. Lincoln protected freedom of religion and freedom for all people, which are blessings we cherish. His words in the Second Inaugural Address remind us to be humble and empathetic, even when we are sure we are right. The choices he made and the price he paid for them continue to inspire people everywhere to seek justice and mercy together.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.scripture: The scriptures teach us to mourn with those that mourn and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, as found in Mosiah 18:9. The Bible tells us, "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9), and to "love thy neighbour as thyself" (Matthew 22:39). Lincoln’s call for forgiveness and his work to set people free reflects these teachings. Doctrine and Covenants 98:16 guides us to "renounce war and proclaim peace," which matches Lincoln’s hope to unite the country with peace and healing, even after war.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.evidence: Historians have studied Lincoln’s life through many sources: letters he wrote, speeches he gave, and testimony from those who knew him. Photographs and preserved buildings, like his birthplace log cabin, help us picture his life. The events of the Civil War are well-documented in military records and news reports from the time. There is no significant debate about Lincoln’s presidency or his contributions; his handwritten Emancipation Proclamation and the speech texts are preserved and widely available. We also know from eyewitnesses how he was assassinated and how the nation mourned. The evidence is deep and trustworthy, supported by museums and major universities.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.learn: From Lincoln, we learn that doing what is right is often hard and costly, but it is worth it. He taught us to care for everyone, even those we disagree with. Families can talk about how faith in God guides us to be peacemakers and helpers. Lincoln’s life shows that anyone can make a big difference, no matter where they start, by choosing courage, kindness, and honesty.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.child: Abraham Lincoln worked to keep the country together and end slavery. He was kind, brave, and tried to help everyone. Even when things were hard, he trusted God and tried to do what was right.
fp05:abraham-lincoln.talk: How do you think Abraham Lincoln felt when he tried to help free the slaves and keep the country together?

fp23.happened: Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a small log cabin in Kentucky. He grew up working hard on farms and reading whenever he could. As a young man, he moved to Illinois, became a lawyer, and taught himself much about the world. Lincoln entered politics, serving in the Illinois legislature and one term in Congress, but he became truly famous when he debated slavery in the 1850s. In 1860, Lincoln was elected the 16th President of the United States, just as the country was splitting apart over the question of slavery. When the southern states tried to leave the Union, Lincoln led the United States through a terrible war, the Civil War, from 1861 to 1865. In 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which freed millions of enslaved people. Lincoln believed the war was God’s judgment on the nation for the wrong of slavery. He worked to keep the nation together and helped change the United States so it promised freedom for all. Just as the war was ending, Lincoln was shot and killed by someone who did not agree with what he had done. He died in April 1865, only a few days after peace was finally restored.
fp23.background: The world Abraham Lincoln lived in was changing quickly. The United States was growing, adding new states and building railroads. People in the northern states mostly lived in cities and worked in factories or on small farms. In the South, many people grew cotton and tobacco and depended on enslaved workers. The question of whether new states should be free of slavery or allow it caused big arguments. Many families were divided on these issues. Most people traveled by horse or on foot, and families worked together to survive. Life could be hard, but people valued freedom and dreams of a better future.
fp23.matters: Abraham Lincoln changed history by helping to end slavery and keep the United States together. He showed that one person's courage and faith can make a big difference, even in the hardest times. For families of faith, Lincoln’s example invites us to remember that every person is a child of God and deserves to be treated with dignity. He also helped protect the freedoms, like religious liberty, that are very important in our faith and lives today.
fp23.scripture: The Bible, in Galatians 3:28, teaches that 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.' This principle reminds us that God values all His children equally. In modern scripture, Doctrine and Covenants 98:8-10 speaks about good leaders and righteous law, telling us to seek honest and wise leaders to uphold freedom. These teachings fit with how Lincoln worked to bless and free others and protect the Constitution.
fp23.evidence: Historians and scholars have studied thousands of Lincoln’s letters, speeches, photographs, and government records. Many artifacts, like his famous hat and his handwritten notes, are in museums today. There are official records of his presidency and the Civil War, including the text of the Emancipation Proclamation and his speeches. Eyewitness accounts and newspaper articles from the time describe his words and actions in detail. All of this evidence confirms what he did and shows how he affected the nation and the world.
fp23.learn: From Abraham Lincoln’s story, we learn that standing for what is right may be hard, but it can bless many lives. Honest leadership and gentle words, even in times of conflict, can help heal and unite. His example reminds us to look for courage and compassion as we try to follow God’s will. Lincoln didn’t see himself as a hero, but by trying to do what was right, he changed history.
fp23.child: Abraham Lincoln was a kind man who helped free people from slavery and kept America together. He tried to do what was right, even when it was really hard. People remember him for his wise words and gentle heart.
fp23.talk: Why do you think Abraham Lincoln believed it was important to treat everyone fairly, even when it cost him so much?

fp24.happened: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 in England, and she grew up in a wealthy family that expected her to live a comfortable life. But Florence felt a calling from God to help others, especially the sick and poor. When she learned how bad the hospitals were, she studied nursing, even though it was not considered a proper job for women at the time. During the Crimean War, she went with a group of nurses to care for wounded soldiers in Turkey. At first, the hospital was filthy and crowded, and many soldiers died from infections rather than their wounds. Florence worked day and night to clean up the hospital, wash the sheets, and make sure everyone had clean water and food. She kept careful records, using mathematics and new ways to draw pictures called diagrams, which helped her show the leaders how better hygiene saved many lives. Her work made her world-famous as "The Lady with the Lamp," and she set up the first official nursing school, teaching that caring for others meant using both hands and mind.
fp24.background: In Florence’s world, England in the 1800s was changing quickly. Cities were growing and people moved from farms to crowded towns. Most people did not know about germs, and hospitals had no real rules for cleaning or caring for patients. Nurses often had little or no training. Women from proper families were expected to marry, not work. Disease often spread fast, and many children and adults died young. During the Crimean War, thousands of British soldiers fought far from home, often not dying from battle, but from dirty wounds and sickness. Florence came from a loving but strict family but was determined to learn and serve despite the customs of her time. She studied mathematics, languages, and nursing, preparing for the work she felt God wanted her to do.
fp24.matters: Florence Nightingale’s work changed hospitals forever. By proving that cleaning, fresh air, and good records save lives, she helped doctors and nurses everywhere get better at caring for people. The way she used data and graphs to persuade leaders is still used in science and medicine today. For families of faith, Florence is a gentle reminder that God can help us notice the needs of others and use our gifts to serve them. Her life shows how faith leads to action, and that every good thing we do for one person can bless many.
fp24.scripture: The scriptures often teach that caring for the sick and needy is a sign of living faith. James 2:17 in the New Testament says, “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” Mosiah 2:17 in the Book of Mormon teaches, “when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.” Florence Nightingale lived these principles. Her sense that God called her to action is much like these scriptural invitations to serve others and put faith into loving work.
fp24.evidence: Historical records clearly show Florence Nightingale’s contributions. Letters, hospital reports, and government documents from the Crimean War confirm that she led a team of nurses and worked tirelessly to improve sanitation. Mortality statistics show that the death rate in the war hospital dropped dramatically after her reforms. Her notes, diagrams, and mathematical methods survive and are studied to this day. The Nightingale Training School in London opened in 1860 and has direct records of its founding. Modern historians and medical experts agree that her efforts marked the beginning of professional nursing as we know it, and that her use of statistics was groundbreaking.
fp24.learn: We can learn from Florence Nightingale that a person’s faith can inspire them to work hard and notice the needs around them. She showed that taking care of people can be both an act of love and a careful science. If we use our talents and education to serve, we may bless many lives, even in simple ways like keeping things clean, comforting others, or speaking up for those in need.
fp24.child: Florence Nightingale was a nurse who helped sick soldiers get better by keeping things clean. She worked hard because she believed God wanted her to help others. Her kindness and smart ideas changed hospitals forever.
fp24.talk: How can we help someone feel comforted or safe, just like Florence Nightingale did?

fp25.happened: Marie Curie, born Maria Skłodowska in 1867 in Warsaw, Poland, was a pioneering physicist and chemist who made groundbreaking contributions to science. In 1891, she moved to Paris to study at the Sorbonne, where she met Pierre Curie, whom she married in 1895. Together, they conducted extensive research on radioactivity, a term Marie coined. Their work led to the discovery of two new elements: polonium, named after Marie's homeland, and radium. In 1903, Marie and Pierre, along with Henri Becquerel, were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for their collective research on radiation phenomena. After Pierre's untimely death in 1906, Marie continued their work, and in 1911, she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for isolating pure radium. During World War I, she developed mobile X-ray units, known as "petites Curies," which were used on the battlefield to diagnose injuries, saving countless lives. Marie Curie's relentless pursuit of knowledge and her dedication to science left an indelible mark on the world.
fp25.background: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the scientific community was rapidly evolving, with significant discoveries reshaping our understanding of physics and chemistry. The concept of radioactivity was newly introduced, and the structure of the atom was still a mystery. Women faced considerable barriers in academia and scientific research, often being excluded from formal education and professional opportunities. Despite these challenges, Marie Curie's determination led her to pursue higher education in Paris, where she immersed herself in scientific studies. Her marriage to Pierre Curie formed a partnership that combined their expertise and passion for research, enabling them to make significant scientific breakthroughs together.
fp25.matters: Marie Curie's discoveries revolutionized science, leading to the development of nuclear physics and advancements in medical treatments, particularly in cancer therapy through radiation. Her achievements challenged societal norms, paving the way for women in science and demonstrating that perseverance and dedication can overcome significant obstacles. For families of faith, her life exemplifies the principle that seeking truth and knowledge, despite challenges, can lead to profound blessings and advancements for humanity.
fp25.scripture: The scriptures teach the value of seeking knowledge and truth. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it states, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." Marie Curie's life reflects this principle, as she diligently sought scientific understanding, contributing greatly to human knowledge and well-being.
fp25.evidence: Historical records, including her published research, personal letters, and contemporary accounts, provide extensive evidence of Marie Curie's life and work. Her laboratory notebooks, though still radioactive, are preserved and studied, offering insights into her meticulous research methods. The Nobel Prizes she received are well-documented, and her contributions to science are widely recognized and celebrated in scientific literature and history.
fp25.learn: Marie Curie's life teaches us the importance of perseverance, curiosity, and dedication in the pursuit of knowledge. It shows that overcoming societal and personal challenges can lead to significant contributions that benefit humanity. Her story encourages us to value education and to support and encourage those who seek to expand our understanding of the world.
fp25.child: Marie Curie was a scientist who discovered new elements and helped doctors see inside the body with X-rays. She worked very hard and never gave up, even when things were tough.
fp25.talk: What can we learn from Marie Curie's determination and curiosity?

fp29.happened: Wilbur and Orville Wright, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, did something no one had ever done before. On December 17, 1903, they flew an airplane they designed and built themselves. The flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered only 120 feet, but it changed the world forever. Their flying machine, called the Wright Flyer, had a small gasoline engine and wings made of wood and fabric. This first flight took place at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, a windy spot of sand and grass where the brothers had tested gliders for several years. After many tries and careful repairs, Wilbur and Orville swapped turns piloting the Flyer, four times that day. Many people at the time thought powered flight was impossible, but the Wright brothers’ careful work proved it could be done. Only a few witnesses were there, but the news quickly spread. In just twenty years, airplanes were flying people across oceans—distances never before possible in so short a time. The seeds of today’s global air travel and space exploration were planted that cold, windy day in 1903.
fp29.background: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, life in the United States was filled with big changes. The Wright brothers grew up during a time of invention and discovery. People were building the first practical bicycles, sewing machines, lights, phones, and machines for factories. Most Americans lived in cities or small farms, traveling by horse or train. The idea of flying in the sky was still a dream. Wilbur and Orville worked as bicycle mechanics, which taught them about balance and steering—skills they used to build their flying machine. People around the world were trying to make a working airplane, but the Wrights used careful experiments, tested over many years, and never gave up when things went wrong.
fp29.matters: The first powered flight matters because it opened the sky to everyone. Now, people and families can visit loved ones far away, and missionaries can travel almost anywhere in the world within hours, helping spread the gospel of Jesus Christ just as the Lord’s restored Church began its worldwide mission. The Wright brothers’ work also made space travel, satellites, and exploration of our planet possible. Their perseverance and faith in learning can inspire all of us to keep trying big things.
fp29.scripture: The scriptures do not mention airplanes, since they were written long before powered flight was possible. However, the Bible teaches that knowledge shall increase in the last days (Daniel 12:4), and the Doctrine and Covenants tells us that God will give us knowledge “by the unspeakable gift of the Holy Ghost” (D&C 121:26). These verses remind us that Heavenly Father helps people discover and invent new things that bless His children. The progress of flight is one way knowledge has grown to help gather Israel and bring families closer.
fp29.evidence: There is no doubt that the Wright brothers achieved the world’s first powered, controlled, and sustained human flight. Their own photographs, diaries, and letters documented the event. Witnesses, including local men from the nearby lifesaving station, testified to what they saw. Pieces of the original Wright Flyer are on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, and their design and engineering notebooks are preserved in museums and libraries. Historians have confirmed their achievement through newspaper reports, detailed engineering analysis, and physical remains of their planes. Over 100 years of research has only strengthened the story: the Wright brothers were truly first.
fp29.learn: From Wilbur and Orville’s lives, we can learn the value of careful study, working hard even when others doubt us, and not giving up after failure. Their example shows that small steps—like testing gliders and fixing broken parts—can lead to big changes that bless the world. We can also recognize that every good thing, including technology, can be used to help others and further Heavenly Father’s work. We should use the tools we’re given for good.
fp29.child: Wilbur and Orville Wright built the first airplane that could really fly. Because of them, we can travel far and even see family or serve others in distant places. Their hard work lets us fly in the sky today.
fp29.talk: How might Heavenly Father want us to use airplanes and other inventions to help others?

fp37.happened: Joseph Stalin became the leader of the Soviet Union after the death of Vladimir Lenin in 1924. He soon took nearly all control into his own hands and ruled as a dictator. During his time in power, Stalin was determined to create a strong communist state and rid society of any opposition. To do this, he organized large political purges, sent millions to forced labor camps called the Gulag, took food and land from farmers, causing widespread famine, and made it very dangerous for anyone to speak against him. Stalin's government sought to erase religion, particularly Christianity, from the country. He ordered almost all Orthodox churches destroyed or used for other purposes, and many church leaders were executed or sent to prison camps. Regular people caught worshipping faced serious punishment. For over seventy years, faith and public worship were serious risks for believers in the Soviet Union. Families could not openly pray, serve, or gather to worship God together. This period left deep wounds across several generations, and trying to rebuild faith, culture, and trust took decades even after Stalin's death in 1953.
fp37.background: Before Stalin rose to power, the Russian Empire was ruled by tsars for hundreds of years, with the Russian Orthodox Church playing a central role in daily life. Most families grew up in faith, attending church, celebrating religious holidays, and praying together. Life changed dramatically after the Russian Revolution of 1917, which replaced the tsar with a communist government. Lenin and the early Soviet leaders began to limit religious practice, but it was under Stalin that these efforts became ruthless and systematic. Most people lived very modestly, often working long hours in factories or on collective farms. Famine and fear were common as Stalin pushed for rapid industrial growth and punished millions for small acts of resistance.
fp37.matters: Stalin's attack on religion was not just about closing churches or punishing believers; it aimed to separate people completely from their faith and from God. For families, this meant the loss of traditions, hope, and the freedom to teach their children about Heavenly Father. Understanding this history helps us see the blessing it is to worship openly today, and invites us to protect the right to believe and teach our faith peacefully. It also reminds us that faith can survive even in dark times, though hearts and communities may suffer for generations.
fp37.scripture: Scriptures teach that faith cannot be truly destroyed by force, even when the world tries. In Daniel 3 (Old Testament), Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego faced the fiery furnace for refusing to deny God—yet their faith stood firm. In the Book of Mormon, Alma and others worshipped in secret when the law forbid it (Mosiah 18:1–3). Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 affirms that no government should control the conscience or force people to worship, but that every person should be free to choose their religious path. These passages show that God desires us to have agency, and that choosing faith under trial matters deeply.
fp37.evidence: Historians have extensively documented Stalin's rule using Soviet archives, survivor testimonies, and contemporary records. Research confirms the mass destruction of thousands of churches, the execution or imprisonment of tens of thousands of clergy, and the forced indoctrination of atheism in schools. The Gulag system's terrible toll has been shown through declassified documents and firsthand stories. The widespread famine of the early 1930s, especially in Ukraine, resulted in millions of deaths, much of it due to government policy. These facts are widely attested by modern historians and are not disputed among scholars.
fp37.learn: From this history, we learn the importance of standing up for faith and conscience, even when it is hard. We see how easily freedom can be lost, and how precious it is to be able to worship with family and friends. This story also shows the enduring power of faith even in the face of terrible opposition. It encourages us to appreciate and protect religious freedom in our own families and communities today.
fp37.child: Joseph Stalin was a very strict leader who closed churches and said no one could pray or talk about God. Many people who believed in God had to be very brave or worship in secret. This reminds us how special it is to be able to choose and share our beliefs.
fp37.talk: Why do you think people want to worship even if it is dangerous or forbidden?

fp06:albert-einstein.happened: Albert Einstein was born in 1879 in the city of Ulm, Germany. As a young boy, he was curious about how things worked, and he loved to ask questions. He became a brilliant physicist who changed the way people understand the universe. In 1905, Einstein published the theory of special relativity, introducing the famous equation E=mc2, which shows that energy and mass are different forms of the same thing. Later, he also developed the general theory of relativity, which explained how gravity is not just a force, but a warping of space and time itself. His ideas were so groundbreaking that they changed science forever. In 1921, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the photoelectric effect, helping scientists understand how light and matter interact. Einstein’s discoveries touched not only science, but also technology, and even how people think about God and the universe.
fp06:albert-einstein.background: Einstein was born at a time when Europe was filled with new inventions and scientific excitement, but people still went about life with candles, horses, and handwritten letters. Only a few decades before his birth, trains became common, and electricity was starting to light up cities. Scientific ideas about the universe were still based mostly on Isaac Newton’s laws from the 1600s, which explained the movement of planets and objects on Earth. Most people in Germany in the late 1800s lived as families with clear routines, valued education, and often gathered at home to read or play music. Many were Jewish, Christian, or influenced by a mix of religious and philosophical traditions.
fp06:albert-einstein.matters: Einstein’s work matters because it opened the door to many discoveries that shape our lives today, from the power in the sun to the GPS in your phone. For families of faith, Einstein’s awe at the beauty and order of the universe reminds us that learning and science are not enemies of faith, but expressions of it. When Einstein spoke of the universe being understandable, it can remind us of God’s invitation to seek knowledge in both spiritual and physical ways. His work has helped people appreciate the wonder of creation and the importance of curiosity.
fp06:albert-einstein.scripture: The scriptures do not mention Albert Einstein or the theory of relativity, but several passages encourage seeking light and understanding. In the Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, the Lord invites us to seek learning “by study and also by faith.” Psalms 19:1 in the Bible says, “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handiwork.” These teachings support the idea that exploring how the universe works can be a spiritual pursuit. They remind us that order and knowledge bless God’s children and can glorify Him.
fp06:albert-einstein.evidence: The evidence for Einstein’s life and discoveries is vast and thoroughly documented. Original manuscripts of his papers, personal letters, and photographs exist in museums and universities around the world. His theories were tested by experiments, like the bending of starlight measured during a solar eclipse in 1919, which confirmed general relativity. Science today continues to use and test Einstein’s ideas in areas like nuclear power and space exploration. Historians have written biographies, and his work is a foundational part of all physics education. There is no serious debate about his contributions or his importance.
fp06:albert-einstein.learn: We can learn from Einstein’s example that asking questions, seeking understanding, and using our minds are gifts from God. Whether we study science, art, or scripture, all truth fits together in God’s great plan. Being humble about what we don’t know can help us look for answers, trusting that learning more about the world brings us closer to our Heavenly Father.
fp06:albert-einstein.child: Albert Einstein wondered how the world works and found answers no one had thought of before. He showed us that learning is like solving a puzzle Heavenly Father made. His ideas help us understand light, time, and space.
fp06:albert-einstein.talk: What is something in the world that you wonder about, and how could we learn more about it together?
